questions.stem: An occupational therapist working in an inpatient rehabilitation unit begins the morning ADL session with a client who was cognitively intact the previous day. Today the client is visibly confused, unable to follow simple two-step commands, and cannot state the current year. What should the occupational therapist do FIRST?
questions.correct_rationale: An acute, unexplained change in cognitive status from a known baseline is a clinical red flag that may indicate a serious medical event such as stroke, infection, metabolic disturbance, or medication reaction. The OT's professional and ethical obligation within the interprofessional team is to escalate safety-relevant clinical observations to the nurse or physician immediately so that medical evaluation can begin without delay. Completing therapy tasks or charting before alerting the team could cause harmful delays in diagnosis and treatment.
questions.core_concept: Interprofessional communication requires the OT to recognise and promptly escalate clinically significant changes in a client's status to the appropriate medical team member. The OT functions as an active contributor to patient safety by serving as a critical observer during therapy and channelling urgent findings through the correct communication pathway — verbal report to nursing or medicine first, documentation second.
questions.explain_differently: Picture the interprofessional team as a relay race: the OT is holding the baton (the observation) and the nurse or physician is the next runner who has the medical tools to investigate and act. If the OT stops to write notes or calls the family instead of passing the baton immediately, the medical response is delayed and the client is at risk. "Report first, document after" is the safety rule whenever an acute clinical change is observed during therapy.
questions.topic: Interprofessional Communication — Escalation of Acute Clinical Changes

options.label: A
options.text: Stop the session and immediately report the acute change in cognitive status to the nurse or physician.
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct response — stopping the session and escalating to the medical team is the appropriate first action when an acute, unexplained cognitive change is observed.

options.label: B
options.text: Continue the ADL session using simplified one-step verbal cues and hand-over-hand assistance to maximise participation.
options.incorrect_rationale: Proceeding with the session treats the confusion as a functional adaptation problem rather than recognising it as a potential acute medical event requiring immediate escalation.

options.label: C
options.text: Document the observed cognitive changes thoroughly in the client's chart before taking any other action.
options.incorrect_rationale: Documentation is essential but is not the first action; written charting alone does not trigger the real-time medical assessment this change in status requires.

options.label: D
options.text: Contact the client's family to inform them of the observed changes and ask about any recent events at home.
options.incorrect_rationale: Family notification may be appropriate later, but the family cannot evaluate or treat an acute medical cause; the medical team must be alerted first.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old right-hand-dominant construction worker is referred to OT six weeks after a right crush hand injury. He has been medically cleared for light-duty work. Clinical evaluation reveals nearly full active ROM and grip strength sufficient for light tasks; however, he rates his fear of re-injury at 8/10 on a numeric scale, consistently guards the hand during activity, and has not returned to any tool use. He states, "Every time I try to use it, I'm sure something will snap." Which intervention approach BEST addresses the primary barrier to his occupational performance?
questions.correct_rationale: The client's primary barrier is fear-avoidance behavior (kinesiophobia), not residual physical impairment — ROM and strength are adequate for light tasks. Evidence supports graded activity exposure (systematically increasing task demand while keeping perceived threat manageable) paired with pain neuroscience education (correcting the catastrophic belief that use equals damage) as the first-line approach for kinesiophobia. This dual strategy reduces avoidance behavior, restores self-efficacy, and directly enables occupational re-engagement, which is the OT's core domain.
questions.core_concept: Fear-avoidance behavior (kinesiophobia) is a psychological barrier that can persist independently of physical recovery and is a primary driver of prolonged disability after musculoskeletal injury. OT addresses it through graded activity exposure and pain neuroscience education, targeting the client's maladaptive beliefs and behaviors rather than treating physical impairment that has already resolved.
questions.explain_differently: Think of this client like someone terrified to get back on a bicycle after a fall — the bike is mechanically fine and so are his legs, but his brain is sounding a false alarm. Handing him a helmet (splint) or telling him to take the bus for now (job modification) does nothing to fix the alarm. The only way to reset it is to get back on the bike, starting with just sitting on it while it is stationary, then rolling slowly, then riding — each successful step proves to his nervous system that use does not equal damage. That graduated re-engagement, paired with teaching him why the alarm fires falsely, is exactly what graded exposure plus pain education does.
questions.topic: Hand rehabilitation — fear-avoidance behavior and kinesiophobia following musculoskeletal injury

options.label: A
options.text: Thermal modalities and manual therapy before each session to reduce residual discomfort and prepare the hand for functional use
options.incorrect_rationale: Passive preparatory modalities address tissue-level symptoms, not the cognitive-behavioral fear-avoidance cycle; relying on them reinforces the client's belief that the hand requires external protection before it is safe to use.

options.label: B
options.text: Graded task exposure combined with pain neuroscience education, progressing systematically from low-load familiar tasks toward work-simulation activities

options.label: C
options.text: Custom resting hand splint worn during light-duty tasks to provide external support and reduce perceived risk of re-injury
options.incorrect_rationale: Splinting is not indicated when ROM and strength are adequate; providing a protective device validates and entrenches the client's catastrophic belief rather than building self-efficacy and tolerance.

options.label: D
options.text: Referral to vocational rehabilitation to identify modified job duties that eliminate hand use until confidence returns spontaneously
options.incorrect_rationale: Avoiding hand use reinforces fear-avoidance behavior and delays return to occupational performance; confidence does not return through avoidance — it is rebuilt through graduated, supported exposure.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman is referred to occupational therapy 6 weeks after a conservatively managed distal radius fracture. She reports pain rated 4/10 at rest, visible dorsal hand edema, and difficulty with IADL tasks including meal preparation and grooming. Active wrist ROM measures: flexion 30°, extension 20°, pronation 60°, supination 40°. Her primary goal is to return to her occupation as a hairdresser. Which intervention should the OT prioritize at this stage of rehabilitation?
questions.correct_rationale: At 6 weeks post-fracture, the tissue is in the proliferative-to-remodeling phase of healing. Residual edema is a primary driver of stiffness and pain, and active ROM within a pain-free range harnesses muscle pump action to reduce swelling while preventing scar and capsular adhesion. Addressing edema first creates the physiological conditions necessary for all subsequent ROM and strength gains. Bypassing this foundational step risks prolonged inflammation, increased pain with movement, and delayed return to function.
questions.core_concept: Rehabilitation sequencing in musculoskeletal OT follows a stage-based framework: edema and pain management must precede ROM restoration, which must precede strengthening, which must precede occupation-specific task training. Intervening out of sequence can delay healing and compromise long-term outcomes.
questions.explain_differently: Think of post-fracture rehabilitation like renovating a flooded room — you drain and dry it before sanding and painting. The edema is the standing water; until it is cleared, every other intervention (splinting, strengthening, task practice) is being done in a wet room. Edema management plus gentle active ROM is the "dry-out" phase that makes everything else possible.
questions.topic: Upper extremity rehabilitation — post-fracture intervention sequencing

options.label: A
options.text: Static progressive wrist extension splinting worn for 6–8 hours daily to restore end-range ROM
options.incorrect_rationale: Static progressive splinting is an appropriate adjunct when active ROM has plateaued despite adequate edema control, not as a first-line intervention when edema and pain are still the primary limiting factors.

options.label: B
options.text: Progressive resistive strengthening of wrist flexors and extensors using a dynamometer protocol
options.incorrect_rationale: Resistive strengthening is contraindicated until edema is controlled, ROM is functionally adequate, and the fracture site has sufficient structural integrity — typically not before 8–10 weeks post-injury in a conservatively managed distal radius fracture.

options.label: C
options.text: Edema management techniques combined with active range of motion exercises performed within a pain-free range

options.label: D
options.text: Functional task simulation replicating hairdressing activities such as combing and blow-drying
options.incorrect_rationale: Although occupation-based practice is ultimately the goal, simulating hairdressing tasks requiring sustained grip and repetitive wrist motion is premature when ROM deficits and edema have not yet been addressed, risking re-injury and increased pain.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist is conducting an initial evaluation with a 68-year-old woman who was recently discharged home following a total hip replacement. During the interview, the client states that her biggest concern is being unable to dress her lower body independently. Which assessment would BEST capture this client's self-perception of her occupational performance and her satisfaction with that performance?
questions.correct_rationale: The Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM) is a standardized, semi-structured interview tool specifically designed to identify occupational performance problems from the client's own perspective across self-care, productivity, and leisure. The client rates both their performance and their satisfaction on a 10-point scale. This directly aligns with the clinical need here: identifying what the client perceives as her most important concern (lower-body dressing) and establishing a baseline of her self-rated performance and satisfaction to track change over the course of intervention.
questions.core_concept: Client-centered assessment in OT requires tools that measure occupational performance from the client's perspective rather than solely from clinician observation. The COPM operationalizes this principle by using a structured interview to elicit the client's self-identified priorities and self-rated performance and satisfaction scores, making it the gold-standard tool when the goal is to understand what matters most to the client and measure meaningful change from their viewpoint.
questions.explain_differently: Think of it this way: if you want to know how a client feels about their own ability to do something important to them, you need a tool that asks the client directly. The COPM is essentially a structured conversation where the client names their problem, scores how well they think they are doing it, and scores how happy they are with that performance. The other tools here all involve a clinician watching or scoring the client from the outside — none of them hand the measuring tape to the client the way the COPM does.
questions.topic: Client-Centered Occupational Performance Assessment / COPM

options.label: A
options.text: Functional Independence Measure (FIM)
options.incorrect_rationale: The FIM measures functional independence using clinician-rated scores across self-care and mobility domains; it does not capture the client's own perception of performance or satisfaction.

options.label: B
options.text: Berg Balance Scale (BBS)
options.incorrect_rationale: The Berg Balance Scale assesses static and dynamic balance through clinician-observed tasks and does not address occupational performance priorities or client satisfaction.

options.label: C
options.text: Assessment of Motor and Process Skills (AMPS)
options.incorrect_rationale: The AMPS uses trained-rater observation of ADL task performance to evaluate motor and process skill quality; it does not elicit the client's personal priorities or self-rated satisfaction.

options.label: D
options.text: Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM)
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct answer and requires no distractor rationale.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman is referred to occupational therapy two weeks after a new diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis affecting both hands. She works full-time as a graphic designer and reports significant difficulty with prolonged computer use and meal preparation, both of which she identifies as essential to her livelihood and daily routine. She has no prior OT history. Which assessment should the occupational therapist administer FIRST?
questions.correct_rationale: The COPM is a semi-structured, client-centered interview that systematically identifies which occupations the client perceives as problematic, ranks them by personal importance, and captures baseline self-ratings of performance and satisfaction. Administering it first establishes the client's own occupational priorities — in this case distinguishing whether computer work or meal preparation is more urgent — before selecting performance-based measures. This sequence is consistent with OT's top-down assessment model, in which occupational needs are identified before component-level deficits are measured, preventing the therapist from investing time in tests that may not address what matters most to this client.
questions.core_concept: OT practice follows a top-down, client-centered assessment model: occupational priorities are identified through a client-centered interview before performance-based or component-level measures are selected. This sequence ensures that all subsequent assessment and intervention targets are anchored to what is occupationally meaningful to the individual client, reflecting the profession's foundational commitment to occupation-centered, client-directed care.
questions.explain_differently: Imagine a client walks into a restaurant and the server immediately brings dishes chosen by the kitchen before taking the order. A performance test like the Purdue Pegboard or Jebsen-Taylor is that pre-chosen dish — useful, but potentially irrelevant. The COPM is "taking the order first": the therapist asks the client which occupations she finds hard, how much each one matters, and how well she feels she performs them. Only after that conversation does the therapist know which performance tests will actually inform a meaningful treatment plan. Skipping the COPM risks spending the entire evaluation measuring something the client does not even identify as a problem.
questions.topic: Client-Centered Assessment and Top-Down Evaluation in OT

options.label: A
options.text: Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM)

options.label: B
options.text: Purdue Pegboard Test
options.incorrect_rationale: The Purdue Pegboard quantifies fine motor dexterity and is a useful component-level measure, but selecting it first imposes the therapist's assumption about which deficit to measure rather than letting the client identify her priority occupations.

options.label: C
options.text: Jebsen-Taylor Hand Function Test
options.incorrect_rationale: Although the Jebsen-Taylor assesses hand function across simulated daily tasks and is appropriate for RA, administering it first bypasses the client-centered step of confirming which occupations the client finds most limiting and meaningful.

options.label: D
options.text: Barthel Index
options.incorrect_rationale: The Barthel Index measures basic ADL independence (feeding, dressing, mobility) and lacks sensitivity to the IADL demands — sustained computer use and complex meal preparation — that define this client's primary concerns.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with moderate Parkinson's disease (Hoehn and Yahr Stage III) is referred to occupational therapy for difficulty completing morning ADLs. He takes carbidopa-levodopa at 7:00 AM. His wife currently assists him with bathing and dressing because he is too rigid and slow. During the OT evaluation at 7:30 AM, he requires maximal assistance for upper-body dressing and takes 10 minutes to fasten two shirt buttons. He ambulates independently with a rolling walker. Which action should the occupational therapist prioritize FIRST?
questions.correct_rationale: Levodopa typically reaches peak plasma concentration (the "on" period) approximately 45-90 minutes after oral ingestion, during which motor symptoms are most controlled. Scheduling ADL training and adaptive equipment trials during this window maximizes the patient's available motor function, improves skill acquisition, and provides a realistic baseline for recommending compensatory strategies. Adaptive equipment (button hook, elastic shoelaces) reduces the fine-motor demand that bradykinesia makes prohibitive, supporting independence within the client's actual functional capacity.
questions.core_concept: Occupational therapists working with clients on dopaminergic medications must integrate pharmacological timing into intervention scheduling — a practice called activity patterning around medication windows. Aligning skill-building and adaptive equipment trials with the client's optimal functional state maximizes learning potential and produces more clinically valid performance data.
questions.explain_differently: Think of levodopa like a window of opportunity that opens roughly an hour after the pill is taken and closes a few hours later. Trying to teach someone to button a shirt when that window is closed — when the medication has not yet kicked in — is like teaching someone to walk on ice without boots and expecting them to learn quickly. The OT's job is to time practice for when the window is open, and to use tools like a button hook to make success possible even when the window starts to narrow.
questions.topic: Parkinson's Disease ADL Intervention and Pharmacological Timing

options.label: A
options.text: Conduct ADL training sessions at 7:30 AM before the medication reaches peak effect to challenge the patient's motor capacity during off-periods.
options.incorrect_rationale: Training during an off-period, when rigidity and bradykinesia are maximal, undermines skill acquisition and does not reflect evidence-based scheduling for Parkinson's disease.

options.label: B
options.text: Reschedule ADL training to approximately 60 minutes after the morning levodopa dose and introduce adaptive equipment such as a button hook and elastic shoelaces during that on-period window.

options.label: C
options.text: Defer ADL intervention and refer the patient to physical therapy for balance and strengthening before initiating occupational therapy treatment.
options.incorrect_rationale: Deferring OT intervention is not indicated; OT and PT goals can be addressed concurrently, and delaying ADL intervention prolongs unnecessary dependence.

options.label: D
options.text: Teach the wife proper caregiver body mechanics and assistance techniques so she can safely and efficiently perform all morning ADLs for the patient.
options.incorrect_rationale: Training the caregiver to perform all ADLs fosters dependence rather than maximizing the client's residual occupational performance, which is a foundational OT principle.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with left hemiplegia following a right CVA is seen in outpatient OT. He reports that cooking meals for his family is his most meaningful occupational goal. During evaluation, he demonstrates intact cognition, fair sitting balance at the kitchen counter, and minimal functional use of his left (non-dominant) upper extremity. Which intervention approach is MOST appropriate to prioritize at this stage of treatment?
questions.correct_rationale: Cooking is the client's self-identified priority occupation, and he has intact cognition and adequate sitting balance to participate safely. A compensatory approach — one-handed technique training and adaptive equipment such as a dycem mat, rocker knife, and suction-cup bowl holder — enables immediate, meaningful occupation engagement. Evidence consistently supports occupation-as-means: performing the valued task itself drives neuroplasticity and functional recovery while honoring the client's goals. CIMT or remediation-only approaches are not contraindicated long-term but should not supplant occupation-based work when compensatory strategies can safely unlock the goal now.
questions.core_concept: Occupation-based, client-centered practice holds that meaningful occupation is both the goal and the primary therapeutic medium. When a client has intact cognition and the capacity to participate safely, the OT prioritizes enabling engagement in the stated goal occupation through compensatory strategies rather than sequencing restoration as a prerequisite.
questions.explain_differently: Think of it this way: the client did not come to OT to exercise his arm — he came to cook for his family. The OT's job is to get him back in the kitchen as soon as it is safe to do so. A one-handed approach with the right tools lets him achieve that goal today, while remediation work (strengthening, CIMT) can run alongside it. Making him wait until his affected arm "earns" its way into the kitchen is like telling someone who uses a wheelchair that they cannot go to work until they can walk — the adaptation solves the problem now.
questions.topic: Occupation-based intervention and compensatory strategy selection in post-stroke rehabilitation

options.label: A
options.text: Initiate constraint-induced movement therapy (CIMT) to restore bilateral upper extremity function before introducing any cooking tasks
options.incorrect_rationale: CIMT requires the client to meet specific motor threshold criteria and, even when indicated, delaying occupation engagement until restoration is complete contradicts client-centered, occupation-as-means principles.

options.label: B
options.text: Focus exclusively on resistive tabletop strengthening exercises for the left upper extremity until the limb is functional enough for bilateral kitchen tasks
options.incorrect_rationale: Remediation-first sequencing that postpones meaningful occupation is not supported by evidence; it delays engagement in the client's stated goal and reduces motivation and real-world skill transfer.

options.label: C
options.text: Train one-handed cooking techniques and introduce adaptive equipment so the client can begin preparing meals for his family now

options.label: D
options.text: Defer cooking intervention and refer the client to a community day program until sufficient bilateral arm function is demonstrated
options.incorrect_rationale: Deferring the client's priority occupation to await full restoration is inconsistent with OT scope and evidence; compensatory strategies allow occupation engagement regardless of limb status.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist is assigned to work with a First Nations client in a community health setting. Which action BEST demonstrates culturally safe practice?
questions.correct_rationale: Cultural safety is grounded in critical self-reflection by the practitioner. It requires the therapist to examine their own cultural identity, privilege, and biases and to analyse the power dynamics inherent in the therapeutic relationship. This internal work is what makes the encounter safe for the client — safety is defined by the client's experience, not by the therapist's cultural knowledge or environmental choices.
questions.core_concept: Cultural safety is distinct from cultural competence. While cultural competence involves accumulating knowledge about other groups, cultural safety requires practitioners to critically examine their own values, biases, and institutional power, recognising that harm can occur even with good intentions when power imbalances are unacknowledged. Safety is ultimately determined by the client, not the clinician.
questions.explain_differently: Cultural competence is about learning more about other people; cultural safety is about learning about yourself first. No matter how much a therapist knows about Indigenous cultures, if they have not examined how their own assumptions and the power they hold as a clinician might cause harm, the encounter is not yet safe. Self-reflection is the non-negotiable starting point.
questions.topic: Cultural Safety vs. Cultural Competence in OT Practice

options.label: A
options.text: Research Indigenous cultural practices and ceremonies before the first session to demonstrate cultural knowledge
options.incorrect_rationale: Acquiring knowledge about a cultural group describes cultural competence, not cultural safety; cultural safety shifts the focus from learning about others to critically examining one's own positionality and power.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask the client to describe their cultural background and traditions during the intake interview
options.incorrect_rationale: Placing the burden of cultural education on the client reinforces othering and an unequal power dynamic; culturally safe practice requires the practitioner to do their own reflective work rather than treating the client as a cultural informant.

options.label: C
options.text: Decorate the therapy room with Indigenous artwork and materials to signal a welcoming environment
options.incorrect_rationale: Environmental adaptations may contribute to a welcoming atmosphere but do not constitute cultural safety, which is fundamentally relational and rooted in power analysis rather than physical surroundings.

options.label: D
options.text: Examine personal biases, privilege, and assumptions and consider how these may shape the therapeutic relationship

questions.stem: An occupational therapist begins an evaluation with a 58-year-old woman recently discharged home after a total hip replacement. The therapist wants to identify which daily activities the client personally considers most important and is currently having difficulty performing, so that intervention goals can be set collaboratively. Which standardized assessment tool is MOST appropriate to administer first?
questions.correct_rationale: The COPM uses a structured interview to have the client identify and rate occupational performance problems across self-care, productivity, and leisure, then prioritize which problems matter most to her. It directly measures perceived performance and satisfaction from the client's perspective, making it the tool of choice when the explicit goal is client-centered, collaborative goal identification — precisely what this scenario describes.
questions.core_concept: Client-centered assessment is the practice of using the client's own values, priorities, and perceived difficulties — rather than clinician observation alone — as the starting point for evaluation and goal-setting. The COPM operationalizes this principle by placing the client in the role of expert on her own occupational performance, which aligns with the OT profession's foundational commitment to occupation-focused, person-centered care.
questions.explain_differently: Think of the COPM as handing the steering wheel to the client: she tells you which daily tasks feel broken and which ones she most wants fixed, then scores how well she thinks she is doing them and how happy she is with that performance. Every other tool on this list has the therapist doing the rating or measuring something broad like overall health — none of them ask the client to name and rank her own problem list the way the COPM does.
questions.topic: Standardized Occupational Performance Assessment / Client-Centered Evaluation

options.label: A
options.text: Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM)
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct answer.

options.label: B
options.text: Barthel Index
options.incorrect_rationale: The Barthel Index is a clinician-rated ordinal scale that measures functional independence across basic ADL tasks; it does not capture which activities the client personally prioritizes or how satisfied she is with her performance.

options.label: C
options.text: Functional Independence Measure (FIM)
options.incorrect_rationale: The FIM measures burden of care and functional independence across 18 items using clinician observation; it is not designed to elicit the client's own occupational priorities or support collaborative goal-setting.

options.label: D
options.text: Short Form-36 (SF-36)
options.incorrect_rationale: The SF-36 is a self-report measure of general health-related quality of life across eight broad health domains; it does not identify specific occupational performance problems or facilitate priority-setting with the client.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist working in an inpatient rehabilitation unit has completed a standardized functional assessment showing that a client recovering from a traumatic brain injury scores at a maximal assistance level for all instrumental ADLs and demonstrates poor safety awareness on objective testing. During the weekly interdisciplinary team meeting, the physiatrist announces a discharge date in three days because insurance authorization has been exhausted. The client, who retains decision-making capacity, states he wants to go home. His spouse reports feeling "too overwhelmed" to provide full-time caregiving and has not been trained in any assist techniques. The OT believes discharge in three days poses a serious safety risk. Which action should the OT take FIRST?
questions.correct_rationale: The OT is currently inside the interprofessional forum where the discharge decision is being reached. Interprofessional collaboration competencies require that each discipline contribute discipline-specific, evidence-based findings at the point of team decision-making — not after the fact. Presenting standardized, objective data (rather than opinion) gives the team actionable clinical information, honors the OT's professional accountability to client safety, and initiates collaborative problem-solving (e.g., extended stay, transitional care unit, intensive caregiver training) within the appropriate channel. All other options either skip a step, delay advocacy, or route around the team structure prematurely.
questions.core_concept: Interprofessional advocacy requires OTs to raise evidence-based safety concerns within the shared team forum at the moment the decision is being made, using objective, standardized data rather than subjective opinion. Raising concerns after the meeting or bypassing the team to escalate elsewhere first undermines collaborative practice standards and the OT's professional accountability for client safety.
questions.explain_differently: Picture the team meeting as the one open window where all clinical voices can change the outcome in real time. The OT holds a key — objective, standardized assessment data that no other discipline collected. Waiting to slip a note under the door after the meeting closes, or going directly to the insurance company or the chart, means the window has already shut. Speaking up now, with data in hand, is not confrontation — it is exactly what interprofessional teams are designed to do: integrate each discipline's unique findings before locking in a plan.
questions.topic: Interprofessional Team Communication and Clinical Advocacy at Discharge Planning

options.label: A
options.text: Contact the insurance company's utilization review department directly to request a continued-stay authorization on behalf of the client.
options.incorrect_rationale: Contacting the insurer directly bypasses the interprofessional team and is typically the responsibility of the case manager or social worker; the OT should work through the team structure before escalating outside it.

options.label: B
options.text: Present the objective functional assessment scores and specific safety concerns to the team during the current meeting, and propose that discharge alternatives be formally discussed before the date is finalized.
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct answer.

options.label: C
options.text: Document the OT's clinical concerns thoroughly in the medical record and request that the physiatrist review them before finalizing the discharge date.
options.incorrect_rationale: Charting is necessary but passive; because the OT is already present in the decision-making forum, deferring to a written note after the meeting forfeits the immediate opportunity for real-time interprofessional advocacy.

options.label: D
options.text: Arrange a home visit before the next team meeting to assess environmental safety and evaluate caregiver feasibility before weighing in on the discharge plan.
options.incorrect_rationale: A home visit may be a useful later step, but it is not feasible within a three-day window as a first action, and it delays the OT's obligation to raise safety concerns in the current clinical forum where the decision is actively being made.

questions.stem: Margaret reports ongoing difficulty with lower-body dressing despite having a reacher and sock aid. To identify the specific performance components contributing to this difficulty, what is the BEST next step for the occupational therapist?
questions.correct_rationale: Direct task observation in the natural environment is the gold standard for occupational performance assessment. Only by watching Margaret attempt lower-body dressing in her home can the therapist identify exactly where performance breaks down — whether the issue is tool technique, sequencing, fatigue, environmental barriers, or precaution violations. Interviews and body function measures yield complementary data but cannot reveal the dynamic interaction between person, environment, and occupation that observation captures.
questions.core_concept: Occupational performance assessment is optimally conducted through direct task observation in the client's natural environment. This approach identifies specific performance breakdowns at the person-environment-occupation interface, which interviews, chart reviews, and impairment measures alone cannot capture.
questions.explain_differently: Think of it like watching someone try to parallel-park in their actual neighborhood versus asking them to describe it or testing their steering strength in a parking lot. Only direct observation in context reveals where the real difficulty lives — and that is exactly where OT intervention begins.
questions.topic: Occupational performance assessment and task observation

options.label: A
options.text: Administer the Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM) to formally establish Margaret's occupational performance priorities.
options.incorrect_rationale: The COPM is an interview-based tool for identifying and rating priority occupations; it has already been accomplished through the initial interview and does not reveal the specific task-level breakdowns occurring during performance.

options.label: B
options.text: Measure Margaret's active hip flexion range of motion to determine whether precautions are limiting her reach to her lower extremities.
options.incorrect_rationale: ROM measurement quantifies body function but does not capture how Margaret uses her tools, sequences the task, or adapts to her environment; body structure data alone does not explain occupational performance failures.

options.label: C
options.text: Observe Margaret performing lower-body dressing in her home environment, noting where and how performance breaks down.

options.label: D
options.text: Review the acute care discharge summary to obtain the inpatient therapist's dressing training notes.
options.incorrect_rationale: Prior documentation provides background context but cannot substitute for direct observation of current performance in the client's actual home environment, where contextual factors and carry-over of training can be directly assessed.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist is selecting an intervention approach for an adult client recovering from a stroke. To practice in an evidence-based manner, the therapist integrates the best available research evidence with which TWO additional components?
questions.correct_rationale: The evidence-based practice model, as defined by Sackett et al. and adopted by AOTA, rests on three equally weighted pillars: (1) best available research evidence, (2) the practitioner's clinical expertise and critical reasoning, and (3) the client's values, goals, and preferences. Integrating all three ensures interventions are both scientifically sound and person-centered.
questions.core_concept: Evidence-based practice (EBP) in occupational therapy is defined by the integration of three components: best available external research evidence, practitioner clinical expertise, and client values and preferences. No single component alone is sufficient; all three must be synthesized to constitute true EBP.
questions.explain_differently: Think of EBP as a three-legged stool: research evidence, the therapist's clinical judgment, and the client's own goals and values. Remove any one leg and the stool falls over. Option B names exactly the two legs that must be added to research evidence to complete the stool. The other options bring in considerations (billing, protocols, physician orders) that belong to a different framework entirely.
questions.topic: Evidence-Based Practice — Three Pillars (Sackett Model)

options.label: A
options.text: The facility's reimbursement policies and the client's insurance coverage
options.incorrect_rationale: Reimbursement and insurance are administrative and financial considerations, not components of the evidence-based practice framework defined by Sackett et al.

options.label: B
options.text: The client's diagnosis and the referring physician's treatment recommendations
options.incorrect_rationale: While diagnosis and physician input are clinically relevant, they are not the two additional pillars of the EBP triad; they may inform clinical expertise but are not independent EBP components.

options.label: C
options.text: The therapist's years of experience and the facility's established treatment protocols
options.incorrect_rationale: Years of experience alone is not equivalent to clinical expertise (which requires critical appraisal and reasoning), and facility protocols are institutional standards rather than a pillar of the EBP model.

options.label: D
options.text: The therapist's clinical expertise and the client's values and preferences
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct answer; clinical expertise and client values are the two additional pillars that, combined with best research evidence, define evidence-based practice.

questions.stem: Given Marcus's TSK-17 score of 48 and his current light-duty clearance, which intervention should the OT prioritize FIRST in the RTW program?
questions.correct_rationale: A TSK-17 score of 48 indicates clinically significant kinesiophobia, which is a major psychosocial barrier to RTW. Evidence from the fear-avoidance model supports graded exposure combined with pain neuroscience education as the first-line approach: graded exposure systematically reduces fear by breaking the pain-catastrophizing-avoidance cycle, while education reframes pain as non-threatening, enabling Marcus to safely progress physical demands toward job requirements.
questions.core_concept: The fear-avoidance model explains how pain catastrophizing and kinesiophobia create a cycle of avoidance that perpetuates disability. OTs integrate graded exposure and pain neuroscience education to interrupt this cycle, addressing psychosocial barriers alongside physical rehabilitation in RTW programs.
questions.explain_differently: Think of kinesiophobia like a smoke alarm that keeps going off even when there is no fire — Marcus's nervous system is sounding danger signals for movements that are actually safe. Graded exposure is the process of showing his nervous system, step by step, that these movements are not harmful, while pain education teaches him why the alarm is misfiring. Starting work hardening without doing this first is like turning up the smoke in a room where the alarm is already stuck on — it makes the fear worse, not better.
questions.topic: Kinesiophobia and fear-avoidance intervention in RTW

options.label: A
options.text: Implement graded exposure to feared movements combined with pain neuroscience education.

options.label: B
options.text: Begin a full work hardening program immediately with progressive lifting up to job demands.
options.incorrect_rationale: Initiating high-demand work hardening without first addressing kinesiophobia risks reinforcing the fear-avoidance cycle and is unsafe given his current 8 kg functional lifting capacity.

options.label: C
options.text: Recommend indefinite light-duty work until his TSK-17 score normalizes before advancing any physical demands.
options.incorrect_rationale: Static light-duty without active intervention does not interrupt the fear-avoidance cycle and may prolong disability and deconditioning.

options.label: D
options.text: Refer Marcus to a psychologist for evaluation before initiating any OT intervention.
options.incorrect_rationale: Kinesiophobia in a musculoskeletal RTW context falls within OT scope of practice; deferring to psychology before any OT action causes unnecessary delay in appropriate care.

questions.stem: During the second week of rehabilitation, Mr. Chen consistently steers his wheelchair into door frames on his right side and omits right-sided items when setting up for grooming. He remains highly motivated to practice meal preparation and resists engagement in tabletop scanning exercises. The rehabilitation team notes his neglect poses a functional safety risk. Which intervention approach BEST balances neglect remediation with evidence-based, client-centered practice at this stage?
questions.correct_rationale: Evidence supports embedding neglect remediation strategies — including visual scanning training, trunk rotation cues, and left-anchor techniques — directly within meaningful occupational tasks rather than decontextualized tabletop exercises. Cooking provides a rich, ecologically valid environment where rightward scanning has immediate functional relevance (locating ingredients, monitoring the stove), which enhances attention, motivation, and generalization. This approach simultaneously uses occupation as the therapeutic means (the vehicle for scanning practice) and the therapeutic end (the goal Mr. Chen values), reflecting best practice in occupation-based intervention.
questions.core_concept: Occupation-based intervention embeds impairment remediation within meaningful daily tasks, using the occupation as both the therapeutic medium and the outcome goal. Evidence demonstrates superior skill generalization and client engagement when cognitive and perceptual strategies are trained in contextually relevant environments rather than isolated tabletop tasks.
questions.explain_differently: Imagine trying to teach a chef to season food by having him practice shaking a salt shaker over an empty plate. He could do the exercise perfectly and still miss the pot on the stove. The neglect needs to be addressed where it actually causes problems — in the kitchen, reaching for the cutting board on his right side, scanning the counter for missing ingredients. His love of cooking is not a distraction from therapy; it IS the therapy. The meaningful context is what makes the brain pay attention.
questions.topic: Neglect remediation through occupation-based intervention; occupation as means and end

options.label: A
options.text: Suspend cooking activities until Mr. Chen demonstrates consistent rightward scanning during structured tabletop exercises.
options.incorrect_rationale: Withholding a meaningful occupation until an impairment resolves contradicts occupation-based practice and evidence showing that neglect training generalizes better when embedded in contextually relevant tasks; it also undermines therapeutic alliance.

options.label: B
options.text: Use a structured meal preparation task as the therapeutic medium, embedding visual scanning cues and anchoring strategies within the cooking context.

options.label: C
options.text: Prioritize caregiver education, training his wife to compensate for his neglect across all daily tasks until discharge.
options.incorrect_rationale: Caregiver compensation as a primary strategy does not remediate neglect, promotes dependence, and does not address Mr. Chen's goal of independent cooking; it may be a supplementary safety strategy but is not the primary intervention at this stage.

options.label: D
options.text: Defer occupation-based intervention and refer Mr. Chen to neuropsychology for neglect management before resuming ADL training.
options.incorrect_rationale: Occupational therapists have full scope of practice to assess and treat hemispatial neglect within ADL contexts; deferral is not indicated, would delay functional progress, and misaligns with the interdisciplinary rehabilitation model.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist is completing a discharge planning assessment with a 68-year-old First Nations woman recovering from hip replacement surgery. The client's adult children are present during the session. When the OT begins discussing home modification goals, the client remains quiet and consistently defers all responses to her eldest daughter. The OT's service protocol requires documenting the client's own rehabilitation goals. Which action BEST demonstrates culturally safe practice?
questions.correct_rationale: Cultural safety requires the OT to recognize that collective, family-centered decision-making is a legitimate and valued practice in many Indigenous cultures, not an indicator of incapacity or communication difficulty. By actively welcoming the family into the goal-setting process rather than redirecting away from them, the OT honors the client's relational framework and avoids imposing a Western individualistic model of autonomous consent. The OT can still fulfill documentation requirements by facilitating dialogue within this inclusive structure — asking open questions to the group while leaving space for the client to speak — thereby capturing her authentic priorities without cultural coercion.
questions.core_concept: Cultural safety in occupational therapy practice means adapting the service encounter to fit the client's cultural context rather than requiring the client to conform to dominant-culture norms. Collectivist or family-mediated decision-making is a legitimate expression of client-centeredness, not a barrier to it, and practitioners must distinguish between a client exercising relational autonomy and a client who is being silenced or coerced.
questions.explain_differently: Think of "client-centered practice" not as "client alone in the room" but as "centered on what this specific client values." For this woman, her family is not an obstacle to goal-setting — they are part of how she makes decisions. Asking them to leave would be like removing someone's glasses before asking them to read: you have eliminated the very support through which they function best. The OT's job is to work inside the client's world, not to retrofit the client into the OT's workflow.
questions.topic: Cultural Safety and Indigenous Client-Centered Practice

options.label: A
options.text: Ask the family members to step outside so the client can discuss her goals privately with the OT.
options.incorrect_rationale: Excluding the family imposes a Western individualistic framework on the encounter and may be experienced as disrespectful or unsafe by a client whose cultural values center collective decision-making.

options.label: B
options.text: Document the daughter's stated goals as the client's goals, since the client has voluntarily chosen to defer to her family.
options.incorrect_rationale: Accepting the daughter's responses without further collaborative exploration risks silencing the client's own perspective and does not fulfill the OT's obligation to genuinely understand the client's priorities within her cultural context.

options.label: C
options.text: Acknowledge the family's involvement as consistent with the client's values and explore rehabilitation goals collaboratively with both the client and her family present.

options.label: D
options.text: Reschedule the session for a time when the client can meet one-on-one with the OT to ensure her individual goals are captured accurately.
options.incorrect_rationale: Rescheduling delays care and presupposes that individual sessions are superior, which reproduces a dominant-culture assumption rather than adapting the service model to fit the client's relational framework.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist is beginning intervention planning with a 58-year-old client who sustained a mild stroke three weeks ago and has returned home. The therapist wants to identify which occupational performance issues the client considers most important to address and to establish a baseline measure of the client's own perceived performance and satisfaction. Which assessment tool is BEST suited for this purpose?
questions.correct_rationale: The COPM is a standardized, client-centered semi-structured interview in which the client identifies and rates occupational performance problems across self-care, productivity, and leisure. The client scores each identified problem on two 10-point scales — perceived performance and satisfaction with performance — generating individualized baseline scores. This directly answers the therapist's need to uncover what the client values most and to establish a measurable starting point, consistent with client-centered practice and top-down assessment frameworks.
questions.core_concept: Client-centered assessment in OT begins by eliciting the client's own perceived occupational performance problems and priorities rather than imposing a clinician-determined task battery. The COPM operationalizes this principle by using a structured interview and numerical self-rating to place the client's voice at the center of goal-setting and outcome measurement.
questions.explain_differently: Think of the COPM as handing the steering wheel to the client: the therapist asks "what matters most to you?" and the client rates — in their own words and on their own scale — how well they are doing and how happy they are with that performance. Every other option listed has the clinician doing the observing and scoring, so the client's perspective never formally enters the data.
questions.topic: Client-Centered Occupational Performance Assessment

options.label: A
options.text: Barthel Index (BI)
options.incorrect_rationale: The Barthel Index measures functional independence in basic ADLs as rated by a clinician or observer, not the client's self-identified priorities or satisfaction with performance.

options.label: B
options.text: Functional Independence Measure (FIM)
options.incorrect_rationale: The FIM quantifies caregiver burden and level of assistance required across functional tasks; it is a clinician-rated scale and does not capture the client's perceived importance, performance, or satisfaction.

options.label: C
options.text: Kohlman Evaluation of Living Skills (KELS)
options.incorrect_rationale: The KELS screens basic and instrumental living skills through structured task performance and interview, but it does not systematically elicit or score the client's own occupational priorities or satisfaction ratings.

options.label: D
options.text: Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM)

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with a moderate traumatic brain injury is referred to outpatient occupational therapy. He lives alone and reports that forgetting to take his medications has become the primary barrier to maintaining his independent living situation. Evaluation reveals intact procedural memory, significantly impaired prospective memory (the ability to remember to perform an intended action at a future time), and functional literacy. He clearly states his goal is to manage his own medications without caregiver assistance. Which intervention is MOST appropriate to address this goal?
questions.correct_rationale: Habit stacking — anchoring the medication task to an already-automatic morning routine such as making coffee — leverages the client's intact procedural memory, bypassing the impaired prospective memory system entirely. The weekly pill organizer adds a low-tech, visible external cue that further reduces reliance on internal memory. Together, these compensatory strategies are occupation-centered, evidence-based for cognitive rehabilitation after TBI, and directly aligned with the client's independence goal.
questions.core_concept: When prospective memory is impaired following acquired brain injury, occupational therapists select compensatory strategies — external cues and habit-based routines — that reroute around the deficit rather than demanding the impaired system to perform. Matching intervention to the client's intact cognitive capacities (here, procedural memory) is a foundational principle of evidence-based cognitive rehabilitation in OT.
questions.explain_differently: Picture the brain as having two separate filing systems: a "to-do reminder" drawer (prospective memory, which is damaged) and a "how I do my routines" drawer (procedural memory, which still works fine). Option B stops trying to fix the broken drawer and instead slips the medication task into the working drawer — it becomes part of the morning routine automatically, like muscle memory. The pill organizer is a visible flag on the counter so the client can see at a glance whether he has already done it, removing the need to rely on internal reminders at all.
questions.topic: Cognitive rehabilitation — compensatory strategies for prospective memory impairment in traumatic brain injury

options.label: A
options.text: Pair medication taking with an established morning routine using habit stacking, and introduce a weekly pill organizer as a low-tech external aid
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct answer.

options.label: B
options.text: Train the client to use internal verbal rehearsal to mentally remind himself of scheduled medication times throughout the day
options.incorrect_rationale: Internal verbal rehearsal is a metacognitive strategy that depends on the prospective memory system, which is the client's primary deficit, making it an ineffective match for this cognitive profile.

options.label: C
options.text: Recommend a home health aide to supervise daily medication administration until the client's prospective memory improves sufficiently
options.incorrect_rationale: Recommending a caregiver directly contradicts the client's stated goal of independence, removes client agency, and does not build any functional strategy the client can use autonomously.

options.label: D
options.text: Immediately introduce a smartphone application with multiple timed medication alerts and a logging feature to track adherence
options.incorrect_rationale: A multi-feature smartphone application is a high-tech, high-complexity solution that still requires the client to respond to alerts prospectively; simpler, habit-anchored compensatory strategies should be established before advancing to complex technology.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist is ending a shift and must hand over the care of a client with a recent total hip replacement to a covering therapist. Which structured communication tool is MOST appropriate to ensure a safe and complete transfer of client information?
questions.correct_rationale: SBAR — Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation — is a standardized interprofessional communication framework specifically designed for structured handover in healthcare settings. It organizes critical client information into four predictable categories, reducing omissions, misinterpretations, and communication failures that can compromise client safety during care transitions.
questions.core_concept: SBAR is a structured handover communication tool (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) adopted across healthcare disciplines to standardize the transfer of critical client information between providers. Its predictable format reduces cognitive load and the risk of information loss during care transitions, which is a key interprofessional collaboration competency for occupational therapists.
questions.explain_differently: Imagine passing a baton in a relay race — if the hand-off is disorganized, the baton drops. SBAR gives both clinicians the same grip pattern every single time: what is happening right now, what led up to it, what the therapist thinks about it, and what needs to happen next. That shared script means the covering therapist hears everything in the same order and knows exactly what to act on, no matter who is doing the handing over.
questions.topic: Interprofessional Handover Communication

options.label: A
options.text: SOAP note
options.incorrect_rationale: A SOAP note is a written progress-note format used to document a single therapy session, not a tool designed to structure a verbal or written handover between providers.

options.label: B
options.text: SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation)
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct answer; SBAR is the structured handover tool purpose-built for safe interprofessional care transitions.

options.label: C
options.text: Discharge summary
options.incorrect_rationale: A discharge summary is completed at the conclusion of an entire episode of care to communicate outcomes to outpatient or community providers, not to hand over ongoing care between shift staff.

options.label: D
options.text: Activity configuration form
options.incorrect_rationale: An activity configuration form is an occupational therapy assessment tool used to map how a client occupies their time across a typical day; it has no role in clinical handover communication.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a core joint protection principle the occupational therapist should teach Margaret to reduce mechanical stress on her metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints during daily activities?
questions.correct_rationale: A foundational joint protection principle in RA is to redistribute mechanical load from vulnerable small distal joints (MCPs, PIPs) to larger, more stable proximal joints (wrists, elbows, shoulders). For example, using the forearm or palm to carry a pot rather than gripping the handle with the fingers reduces deforming forces on already compromised MCP joint structures.
questions.core_concept: Joint protection in RA involves deliberately redistributing mechanical forces away from vulnerable small joints toward larger proximal joints through modified movement patterns and adaptive techniques, preserving joint integrity while maintaining occupational participation.
questions.explain_differently: Think of joints as bridges: a small footbridge collapses under a heavy truck, but a large highway bridge handles the same load easily. Joint protection teaches people to route heavy mechanical loads over the big bridges — the shoulders, elbows, and palms — and off the small footbridges of the finger joints. It is smart load routing, not road closure.
questions.topic: Joint protection principles — foundational RA self-management education

options.label: A
options.text: Sustain a firm pinch grip when carrying objects in order to maintain muscle endurance around the joint.
options.incorrect_rationale: Sustained tight pinch grip concentrates compressive and shear forces directly at the MCP and IP joints — this is directly contraindicated in RA and opposes joint protection principles.

options.label: B
options.text: Perform all activities at a rapid pace to minimize the total duration that joints are under mechanical stress.
options.incorrect_rationale: Rapid pacing does not reduce joint stress and ignores energy conservation principles; it may increase fatigue, reduce movement accuracy, and lead to compensatory postures that increase deforming forces on vulnerable joints.

options.label: C
options.text: Distribute load across larger, proximal joints whenever possible rather than concentrating force through the small finger joints.

options.label: D
options.text: Permanently avoid all resistive activities to prevent any further joint loading throughout the course of the disease.
options.incorrect_rationale: Permanent avoidance of all resistive activity causes disuse atrophy, reduces periarticular muscle support, and leads to progressive functional decline — joint protection modifies how activities are performed, not whether they are performed.

questions.stem: During a morning treatment session, an occupational therapist notices that a client has become significantly less responsive and appears confused compared to yesterday. The OT needs to communicate this urgent change to the assigned nurse immediately. Which structured communication framework is most appropriate for this verbal report?
questions.correct_rationale: SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) is an evidence-based verbal communication framework developed for healthcare teams to convey urgent clinical concerns in a concise, organized manner. It prompts the clinician to state what is happening now (Situation), relevant context (Background), their clinical interpretation (Assessment), and what action is needed (Recommendation). This structure reduces communication errors during time-sensitive escalations and is endorsed by patient-safety organizations for interprofessional use. The other options — SOAP, PIE, and DAP — are written documentation formats, not verbal escalation tools.
questions.core_concept: SBAR is a standardized interprofessional communication tool for urgent verbal reporting. Unlike written charting frameworks (SOAP, PIE, DAP), SBAR is explicitly designed to organize spoken clinical information so that any team member can quickly understand the problem and act, supporting patient safety and effective collaboration.
questions.explain_differently: Think of SBAR as a script for a high-stakes phone call: you tell the nurse what is wrong right now, why you are worried (background), what you think is happening, and exactly what you need from them. SOAP and the others are more like filling out a form after the fact — they belong on paper in the chart, not in a hallway urgent report. When seconds matter, SBAR gives both people the same roadmap.
questions.topic: Interprofessional Communication — Urgent Escalation Frameworks

options.label: A
options.text: SOAP (Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan)
options.incorrect_rationale: SOAP is a written documentation format used in progress notes, not a verbal urgent-communication tool for interprofessional handover.

options.label: B
options.text: PIE (Problem, Intervention, Evaluation)
options.incorrect_rationale: PIE is a narrative charting framework for written clinical documentation, not designed for urgent verbal communication between team members.

options.label: C
options.text: DAP (Data, Assessment, Plan)
options.incorrect_rationale: DAP is a structured written progress-note format and does not serve as a verbal escalation or handover communication tool.

options.label: D
options.text: SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation)

questions.stem: An occupational therapist completes a home assessment for a 72-year-old First Nations elder who was recently discharged after a hip fracture repair. Based on the assessment, the OT recommends installation of grab bars in the bathroom as a fall-prevention measure. The elder responds, "That sounds reasonable, but a decision like this about my home is not mine alone to make — my daughter and our community health representative need to be part of this conversation." A follow-up appointment is available in one week. Which action should the OT take next?
questions.correct_rationale: Option C upholds cultural safety by honouring the elder's explicit identification of who constitutes their decision-making circle. Many Indigenous communities operate within relational, collectivist frameworks in which major decisions — including those affecting the home — are reached through family and community consensus rather than individual choice. The OT acts in a client-centred manner by restructuring the process to fit the client's values rather than expecting the client to conform to a dominant-culture clinical process. Preparing materials in advance demonstrates respect and maintains therapeutic momentum without bypassing the elder's agency.
questions.core_concept: Cultural safety in OT practice requires the practitioner to recognize that the dominant Western healthcare model assumes individual autonomous decision-making, and to actively adjust clinical processes when a client's cultural framework situates decision-making within family or community relationships. Failing to accommodate collective decision-making is itself a structural form of harm, not a neutral clinical default.
questions.explain_differently: Think of the OT's role as fitting the process around the person, not the person around the process. The elder did not say "no" — they said "not yet, and not alone." A culturally safe OT hears that as a cue to restructure the meeting, not to override or re-educate. Just as an OT would adapt a task for a physical limitation without arguing the client should do it the standard way, here the OT adapts the decision-making process to fit the client's relational world, because the "standard" individual-consent model is itself a cultural assumption, not a universal truth.
questions.topic: Cultural Safety and Collective Decision-Making in Indigenous Health

options.label: A
options.text: Collaborate with the elder to schedule the follow-up visit at a time when the daughter and community health representative can attend, and use the interim period to prepare visual materials the group can review together.

options.label: B
options.text: Arrange for the grab bars to be installed before the follow-up visit, given that fall prevention is a documented safety priority that cannot be deferred.
options.incorrect_rationale: Proceeding without consent from the elder's identified decision-making circle overrides collective autonomy, constitutes culturally unsafe practice, and violates the principle of informed consent regardless of clinical urgency.

options.label: C
options.text: Document that the elder declined the recommendation and refer back to the physician, noting non-compliance with the discharge safety plan.
options.incorrect_rationale: The elder did not refuse the intervention — they communicated a culturally grounded process for reaching a decision; labelling this as non-compliance reflects a misunderstanding of collective decision-making and imposes a Western individualistic framework.

options.label: D
options.text: Explain to the elder that home modification decisions are legally and clinically an individual right, and that the plan can move forward with the elder's signature alone.
options.incorrect_rationale: Instructing the elder that family and community involvement is unnecessary imposes a Western individualistic legal framework, dismisses a legitimate cultural value, and is a form of cultural imposition that undermines therapeutic alliance.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist is completing a SOAP note following a treatment session with a client recovering from a total knee replacement in an inpatient rehabilitation unit. During the session, the client states, "My knee still feels very stiff in the mornings." In which section of the SOAP note should this statement be recorded?
questions.correct_rationale: The Subjective (S) section of a SOAP note captures information reported by the client, family, or caregiver in their own words — including symptoms, complaints, feelings, and perceptions that cannot be independently verified by the clinician. The client's statement about morning stiffness is a self-report, making A the correct placement.
questions.core_concept: SOAP note structure is a foundational documentation framework in which each section serves a distinct purpose: Subjective = client-reported information; Objective = clinician-measured or observed data; Assessment = clinical interpretation; Plan = future intervention direction. Accurate placement of information ensures clear, legally defensible records and supports effective interprofessional communication.
questions.explain_differently: Think of the SOAP note like a courtroom distinction between a witness's testimony and a scientist's lab results. What the client tells you ("I feel stiff") is their testimony and goes in Subjective. What you measure with a goniometer or stopwatch is hard evidence and goes in Objective. The client's own words always belong in Subjective because the clinician cannot independently verify another person's internal experience.
questions.topic: SOAP Note Documentation Structure

options.label: A
options.text: Objective
options.incorrect_rationale: The Objective section contains measurable, observable data gathered by the clinician (e.g., goniometry readings, functional task performance times), not the client's self-reported experience.

options.label: B
options.text: Subjective

options.label: C
options.text: Assessment
options.incorrect_rationale: The Assessment section contains the clinician's professional interpretation and clinical reasoning about the client's status, not a direct client quote.

options.label: D
options.text: Plan
options.incorrect_rationale: The Plan section outlines upcoming intervention goals and strategies, not client-reported symptoms or statements from the current session.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist is going on a two-week leave and must transfer three active caseload clients to a colleague. Which action most effectively ensures safe continuity of care?
questions.correct_rationale: A comprehensive written summary covering functional status, active goals, upcoming appointments, and safety concerns creates a complete, accurate, and retrievable record the incoming therapist can consult at any time. This approach directly supports client safety, professional accountability, and the ethical obligation to maintain continuity of care during transitions in service delivery.
questions.core_concept: Structured handover communication is a core professional responsibility in occupational therapy. When transferring client care, written documentation of key clinical information — functional status, goals, pending actions, and safety concerns — is more reliable than verbal-only communication because it is accurate, retrievable, and reduces the risk of information loss at care transitions.
questions.explain_differently: Think of handing over a recipe versus describing a dish from memory. A written recipe (the handover summary) captures every detail exactly and can be re-read whenever needed, while verbal instructions depend on the listener's memory and can lose critical steps. In clinical care, those missing steps can be safety concerns or pending referrals — things a new therapist must know to protect the client.
questions.topic: Handover communication and continuity of care

options.label: A
options.text: Provide a brief verbal summary of each client to the colleague in the hallway between sessions
options.incorrect_rationale: Verbal-only handover is unreliable because information is easily forgotten or misremembered without a retrievable record to reference.

options.label: B
options.text: Email the colleague a list of client names and their primary diagnoses only
options.incorrect_rationale: Diagnosis alone omits the client's current functional status, active goals, scheduled appointments, and safety concerns that are essential for safe care delivery.

options.label: C
options.text: Prepare a written summary for each client that includes current functional status, active goals, upcoming appointments, and any safety concerns
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct answer and does not require a distractor rationale.

options.label: D
options.text: Instruct each client to explain their own therapy goals to the incoming occupational therapist at the next session
options.incorrect_rationale: Relying on the client to convey clinical information is inappropriate and unsafe because it places professional communication responsibility on the person receiving care, who may not retain or accurately report all clinically relevant details.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist is assigned to work with a First Nations client recently discharged from hospital. Before the first session, the therapist reflects on their own assumptions about Indigenous communities, acknowledges the limits of their cultural knowledge, and commits to learning from the client about what matters most in their daily life. This approach best describes which concept?
questions.correct_rationale: Cultural humility is defined by three ongoing commitments: lifelong self-reflection and critique of one's own biases, recognition and mitigation of power imbalances in the therapeutic relationship, and institutional accountability toward diverse populations. The stem depicts all three elements — self-reflection before the session, acknowledgment of knowledge limits, and centering the client's own definition of meaningful occupations — making cultural humility the single best match.
questions.core_concept: Cultural humility is an active, lifelong practice in which the clinician continuously examines their own cultural biases, acknowledges power differentials in the therapeutic relationship, and positions the client as the expert on their own cultural experience. It is distinct from cultural competence (a fixed endpoint) and from cultural awareness or sensitivity (which are necessary but less reflexive or structurally oriented).
questions.explain_differently: Think of cultural competence as a destination — "I have arrived, I know this culture" — whereas cultural humility is the journey itself, one that never ends. The therapist in the question is not claiming expertise; they are showing up as a curious student of the client's life. That perpetual learner stance, combined with honest self-examination about their own assumptions, is the hallmark of cultural humility.
questions.topic: Cultural Humility in Occupational Therapy Practice

options.label: A
options.text: Cultural competence
options.incorrect_rationale: Cultural competence implies a finite, achievable level of mastery over cultural knowledge, whereas the therapist's behaviour reflects an ongoing, humble, learner-centred process rather than a fixed endpoint.

options.label: B
options.text: Cultural awareness
options.incorrect_rationale: Cultural awareness is a surface-level recognition that cultural differences exist; it does not encompass the self-reflective examination of one's own bias, power, or commitment to a lifelong learning stance described in the stem.

options.label: C
options.text: Cultural sensitivity
options.incorrect_rationale: Cultural sensitivity refers to being attentive and respectful of cultural differences in interactions, but it does not capture the internal, reflexive, power-conscious practice described in the stem.

options.label: D
options.text: Cultural humility
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct answer.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist performs a home evaluation for a 74-year-old man with moderate Alzheimer's disease (Clinical Dementia Rating = 2) who lives with his spouse, the sole caregiver. The client ambulates independently without a device and has no significant physical impairments. He requires full assistance for bathing and moderate assistance for dressing. His spouse reports a 90-minute morning care routine marked by frequent episodes of behavioral resistance — verbal refusals and attempts to leave mid-task — and states she is "exhausted and cannot keep doing this." The OT's stated goal is to reduce caregiver burden while preserving the client's occupational participation. Which intervention strategy should the OT prioritize FIRST?
questions.correct_rationale: Behavioral resistance during personal care in moderate Alzheimer's disease is primarily driven by task complexity, unpredictability, and cognitive overload — not physical impairment or caregiver knowledge deficits about disease progression. Errorless learning eliminates trial-and-error processing that overtaxes a damaged memory system, while task simplification reduces the number of decisions and transitions the client must navigate. Breaking the 90-minute routine into shorter, cued steps with consistent environmental anchors (same sequence, same location, same verbal prompts) builds procedural memory — one of the last cognitive systems preserved in AD — directly reducing agitation and resistance. This is the mechanism by which OT-specific dementia programs such as the Tailored Activity Program (TAP) and Skills2Care demonstrably reduce both client distress and caregiver burden. Option A targets the actual cause of the caregiver strain within OT's distinct scope of practice.
questions.core_concept: In dementia-related ADL decline, behavioral resistance during care is primarily a cognitive-environmental mismatch, not a volitional problem. OT's unique contribution is restructuring the task and environment using evidence-based approaches — errorless learning, task simplification, and consistent cueing hierarchies — to reduce cognitive demand, decrease agitation, and thereby reduce caregiver burden. This is distinct from equipment provision (which targets physical barriers) or social service referrals (which are adjunctive, not primary).
questions.explain_differently: Think of it this way: the 90-minute struggle is not happening because the spouse needs a better shower chair or a social worker's phone number. It is happening because the morning routine is a cognitively overwhelming series of decisions for a brain that can no longer sequence or remember. OT's job is to redesign that routine so the client's intact procedural memory can carry him through it almost on autopilot — short steps, same cues, same order every day.
