options.label: C
options.text: Ask the client to attend the next case conference in person so the team can hear the discharge preference directly from the client, thereby resolving the disagreement.
options.incorrect_rationale: Bringing the client into an unresolved team conflict exposes them to a distressing dynamic, which conflicts with the duty to communicate in a manner that respects client dignity under the CAOT Code of Ethics, and does not address the professional disagreement itself.

options.label: D
options.text: Calmly and assertively restate the occupational therapy assessment findings, explicitly connecting them to the client's identified occupational goal of returning home, and invite the team to identify shared concerns so a collaborative discharge plan can be developed.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist is attending a discharge case conference at an urban acute care hospital for a 72-year-old client recovering from a right hemisphere stroke. The client, who has been assessed as having decision-making capacity, has clearly and consistently stated a wish to return home with community personal support services. The OT's comprehensive functional evaluation and home assessment support the feasibility of a safe discharge home, provided environmental modifications and a graduated personal support worker schedule are arranged. During the conference, the attending physician recommends transfer to a long-term care home citing "overall safety concerns," and the social worker concurs. The client becomes visibly distressed and looks toward the OT. What is the OT's most appropriate immediate course of action?
questions.correct_rationale: When a client with confirmed decision-making capacity expresses a clear, consistent preference that is supported by the OT's objective assessment evidence, the CAOT Code of Ethics (principles of autonomy and beneficence) and the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada (advocacy and interprofessional collaboration competencies) require the OT to surface that evidence at the case conference and advocate for the client's right to make an informed choice. Collaborative conflict resolution at the team level is the appropriate first step: presenting clinical findings clearly, naming the client-centred goal, and inviting structured problem-solving around the team's safety concerns — for example, referral to Home and Community Care Support Services, fall-prevention programming, or a community OT follow-up — before any escalation pathway is considered. This approach simultaneously upholds client self-determination and maintains respectful interprofessional relationships, consistent with Canadian OT practice standards.
questions.core_concept: Under the CAOT Code of Ethics and the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada, an OT holds a dual obligation: to advocate for a capable client's self-determination using objective assessment evidence, and to resolve interprofessional disagreement through transparent, collaborative dialogue at the earliest opportunity rather than through deference to professional hierarchy or premature escalation.
questions.explain_differently: Picture the OT as the person in the room whose assessment data is the bridge between what the client wants and what the team is worried about. When the physician and social worker are pointing toward a long-term care home and the client is pointing toward their front door, the OT's job is not to stay quiet to keep the peace — it is to calmly put the assessment on the table and say, "Here is what the functional evidence shows, and here is what this capable person has chosen; now let us work together to close the safety gaps." That is exactly what Canadian OT standards expect: advocacy and collaboration running at the same time, not one sacrificed for the other.
questions.topic: Interprofessional conflict resolution at a case conference

options.label: A
options.text: Present the functional and home assessment findings objectively, explicitly advocate for the client's capacity-based right to determine their discharge destination, and invite the team to collaboratively problem-solve the specific safety concerns that have been raised.
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct answer.

options.label: B
options.text: Align with the physician and social worker's recommendation to preserve team cohesion, and document the client's stated preferences in the medical record for potential revisiting at a future conference.
options.incorrect_rationale: Deferring to team hierarchy to avoid conflict constitutes an abandonment of the OT's professional advocacy obligation and directly contravenes the CAOT Code of Ethics principle of respect for client autonomy, particularly when the client has confirmed decision-making capacity.

options.label: C
options.text: Propose escalating the disagreement to the hospital ethics committee immediately, on the basis that conflict between the interprofessional team and a capable client constitutes an ethical dilemma exceeding the scope of the case conference.
options.incorrect_rationale: Ethics committee referral is premature; the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada expect the OT to attempt direct, evidence-based interprofessional conflict resolution at the team level first, as the scenario does not present an impasse that ordinary professional dialogue cannot address.

options.label: D
options.text: Recommend postponing the discharge decision to allow time for a formal capacity assessment by a designated capacity assessor, to confirm that the client fully appreciates the risks associated with returning home.
options.incorrect_rationale: Because the stem establishes that decision-making capacity has already been assessed, initiating a further formal capacity assessment without new clinical grounds is paternalistic, creates unwarranted delay, and misapplies provincial consent legislation such as Ontario's Health Care Consent Act.

questions.stem: During a case conference at a long-term care home in Ontario, an occupational therapist presents findings from a seating and positioning assessment for a 79-year-old resident with advanced dementia. The OT recommends a specialized pressure-relieving seating system to reduce the resident's risk of pressure injuries and to support her participation in recreational activities. The attending physician responds, "That's not a medical priority — we're moving on," and attempts to close the agenda item. Other team members remain silent. The OT believes the recommendation is clinically essential and that dismissing it without discussion places the resident at risk. What should the OT do FIRST?
questions.correct_rationale: The Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada (2021) and the CAOT Code of Ethics require OTs to advocate for client safety and occupational participation and to communicate assertively and respectfully within interprofessional teams. When a recommendation with direct safety implications is dismissed without discussion, the OT's first obligation is to use clear, evidence-informed, client-centred language to re-engage the team — naming specific risks, grounding the concern in assessment data, and requesting continued dialogue before the item is closed. This approach upholds the OT's professional accountability, models collaborative conflict resolution, and keeps the client's needs at the centre of team decision-making. Escalation or unilateral action is appropriate only after internal resolution has been genuinely attempted and failed.
questions.core_concept: Under the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada (2021) and the CAOT Code of Ethics, OTs have a professional obligation to communicate assertively and advocate for client safety within interprofessional teams. When a clinically grounded recommendation is dismissed at a case conference, the first and appropriate response is respectful, evidence-based re-engagement with the team — not silence, unilateral action, or premature escalation.
questions.explain_differently: Think of the OT as a skilled translator at the team table: if the physician has not yet heard the safety story in terms that land — specific risks, concrete assessment findings, occupational consequences — the OT's job is to tell it again, clearly and calmly, before the page turns. Leaving the room or going around the team is like a translator walking out of a negotiation; it doesn't serve the client and skips the very step that might resolve the disagreement.
questions.topic: Interprofessional conflict resolution at a case conference

options.label: A
options.text: Accept the physician's direction, document the team's decision in the resident's health record, and defer any further advocacy to a future care conference.
options.incorrect_rationale: Silently deferring fails the OT's ethical duty to advocate for client safety and does not constitute a genuine attempt at conflict resolution within the team process.

options.label: B
options.text: Calmly and assertively restate the key assessment findings, name the specific occupational performance and safety risks of not implementing the seating system, and ask the team to allow the item to remain open for discussion before moving on.

options.label: C
options.text: Contact the resident's substitute decision-maker privately after the conference to advocate for the seating recommendation without informing the interdisciplinary team.
options.incorrect_rationale: Approaching the substitute decision-maker without the team's knowledge undermines the collaborative care process, is not transparent, and bypasses the interprofessional conflict resolution step that must occur first.

options.label: D
options.text: File an immediate concern with the Ontario College of Occupational Therapists (COTO) regarding the physician's dismissal of the OT's recommendation.
options.incorrect_rationale: Regulatory colleges address conduct and competency concerns about OT registrants — not interprofessional team disagreements — and escalation to COTO is entirely premature before internal resolution mechanisms have been exhausted.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist (OT) is participating in a case conference in a rehabilitation unit at a regional hospital in British Columbia for a 74-year-old client recovering from a hip fracture. The OT's standardized functional assessment indicates the client requires a two-person assist for all transfers and is not yet safe for unsupported home discharge without environmental modifications and outpatient OT follow-up. The physiatrist leading the conference states the client is "medically optimized" and should be discharged home within 48 hours. The physiotherapist and social worker concur, citing pressure from bed management. The client's adult child — who holds a representation agreement under BC's Representation Agreement Act — is present and appears to accept the team's recommendation. The OT has briefly mentioned a safety concern but the team has moved on without acknowledging it. What is the MOST appropriate next action for the OT at this point in the conference?
questions.correct_rationale: The CAOT Code of Ethics and the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada obligate the OT to advocate for client safety using their domain-specific expertise. In an interprofessional conflict at a case conference, the first and most appropriate step is to explicitly re-present the assessment findings — with specific, evidence-linked reasoning — within the team forum rather than allowing the concern to be passed over. This respects collaborative practice norms while fulfilling the professional duty to advocate. If the team remains unresponsive, the OT must document the professional disagreement in the health record (creating a safety accountability trail) and initiate the facility's formal escalation process (e.g., department lead, risk management, or patient safety officer). This sequenced approach — advocate clearly, document, escalate internally — aligns with both the CAOT competency framework and standard organizational governance before any external regulatory avenue is considered.
questions.core_concept: Occupational therapists have a professional and ethical obligation to advocate for client safety using their unique assessment expertise, even when their position diverges from team consensus. When interprofessional conflict is unresolved at a case conference, the appropriate sequence under Canadian competency and ethical frameworks is: articulate the concern explicitly within the team forum, document the professional disagreement, and follow internal organizational escalation pathways before any external reporting is considered.
questions.explain_differently: Think of the OT's role like a structural engineer at a project meeting — even if the project manager declares the building ready to open, the engineer has a professional duty to formally put their safety concern on the table and on the record before anyone turns the key. Staying quiet is not acceptable, but calling the licensing board mid-meeting is not the first move either. You raise the flag clearly in the room, note it in the chart, and work up the internal chain — in that order.
questions.topic: Interprofessional conflict resolution at a case conference

options.label: A
options.text: Defer to the physiatrist's discharge decision, as the physician is the team lead and holds ultimate clinical authority over discharge planning.
options.incorrect_rationale: Deferring without voicing safety concerns contradicts the OT's professional obligation under the CAOT Code of Ethics and the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada to advocate for client safety and represent their unique scope of practice expertise; role hierarchy does not justify professional silence on a documented safety risk.

options.label: B
options.text: Step out during a break in the conference and contact the BC College of Occupational Therapists (BCOT) to report the team's decision as a breach of client safety obligations.
options.incorrect_rationale: Regulatory colleges address complaints about a registrant's professional conduct after the fact and are not a mechanism for resolving real-time clinical disagreements; contacting BCOT at this stage is a premature and inappropriate escalation that bypasses all internal organizational channels.

options.label: C
options.text: Re-engage the team by clearly presenting the specific functional assessment findings and articulating the concrete fall and injury risks associated with the proposed discharge plan; if the concern remains unaddressed, state that the OT will document the professional disagreement in the health record and follow the facility's escalation process.

options.label: D
options.text: Approach the client's adult child privately after the conference concludes to advise them to formally reject the discharge plan on the client's behalf.
options.incorrect_rationale: Privately coaching the substitute decision-maker outside the team forum to override the plan circumvents collaborative interprofessional decision-making, may constitute undue influence, and is not the appropriate escalation pathway when a professional disagreement remains unresolved.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist in an acute care hospital completes a discharge assessment for a 79-year-old woman with moderate Alzheimer's disease who lives alone in a second-floor apartment. The OT identifies significant impairments in meal preparation, medication management, and safety awareness, with a high fall risk. The interdisciplinary team considers twice-weekly homecare insufficient for safe discharge. During the discharge planning meeting, the client's son — who holds a continuing power of attorney for personal care — becomes defensive and says, "She's always managed fine. You don't know her like I do." What is the OT's BEST initial response?
questions.correct_rationale: Acknowledging the son's lived knowledge of his mother validates his role as substitute decision-maker (SDM) and de-escalates defensiveness before information is shared. Presenting objective, plain-language assessment findings — fall risk, medication errors, unsafe meal preparation — translates the OT's clinical evidence into terms the family can act on, fulfilling the duty to inform under provincial health care consent legislation (e.g., Ontario's Health Care Consent Act). Collaborative exploration of additional supports (e.g., increased homecare hours, personal support worker, day programme, assisted living transition) honours the SDM's authority while upholding the OT's professional obligation to promote client safety. This sequence — acknowledge, inform, collaborate — directly reflects the Communication and Collaboration competency domain in the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada (2021) and the CAOT Code of Ethics principle of acting in the client's best interests.
questions.core_concept: When a substitute decision-maker's preferred discharge plan poses a safety risk, the OT's primary obligation is to engage in transparent, person-centred communication — validating the family's perspective, presenting objective assessment evidence in accessible language, and jointly exploring options — before escalating to formal protective mechanisms. This reflects the Communication and Collaboration competency in the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada (2021) and the ethical duty under the CAOT Code of Ethics to act in the client's best interests while respecting the authority of legally appointed decision-makers.
questions.explain_differently: Think of it as navigating together rather than issuing a verdict. The son loves his mother and genuinely believes twice-weekly homecare is enough — and his lived knowledge of her matters. The OT's job at this moment is not to override him or immediately call in external authorities, but to put the assessment findings on the table in language he can actually hear ("When we asked her to take her medications, she missed three of five doses and couldn't recall taking them"), then problem-solve side by side. You would not skip to the fire alarm before first opening a window — collaborative communication is the first, most appropriate tool, and formal escalation only becomes appropriate if that process fails.
questions.topic: Difficult conversation with family about discharge safety risk

options.label: A
options.text: Document that the substitute decision-maker has been informed of the risks and proceed with discharge planning as requested, since the son holds legal authority to make personal care decisions on his mother's behalf.
options.incorrect_rationale: Simply documenting and deferring is premature — it abandons the OT's professional obligation to engage in collaborative problem-solving and advocate for a safe plan before accepting an outcome that places the client at serious risk.

options.label: B
options.text: Request a formal capacity assessment for the client before continuing the discharge meeting, as the degree of cognitive impairment must be formally confirmed before viable options can be discussed.
options.incorrect_rationale: A formal capacity assessment addresses the client's own decision-making ability, not the SDM's authority or the current communication impasse; requesting one at this moment sidesteps rather than resolves the conversation with the son.

options.label: C
options.text: Refer the matter to the provincial adult protection authority, as the son's insistence on a plan the team considers unsafe constitutes a failure to protect a vulnerable adult.
options.incorrect_rationale: Referral to a provincial adult protection authority is a last-resort measure reserved for situations where collaborative strategies have been genuinely exhausted; invoking it before meaningful dialogue has occurred is disproportionate and risks irreparably damaging the therapeutic relationship.

options.label: D
options.text: Acknowledge the son's knowledge of his mother, share specific functional assessment findings in plain language, and collaboratively explore what additional supports could reduce the identified safety risks and what might happen if they are not in place.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old woman with moderate dementia is recovering in an acute care hospital following a right hip fracture repair. An OT functional assessment documents that she requires two-person physical assist for all transfers, has significant executive function deficits that impair safety judgment, and cannot manage her medications independently. Her daughter, who holds a continuing power of attorney for personal care under provincial legislation, requests immediate discharge home and asserts she can provide all necessary care without additional supports. During the family meeting, when the OT begins to present the assessment findings, the daughter becomes tearful and accusatory, saying: "You are being paternalistic. I know my mother better than you ever will, and you are just stalling." Which of the following responses by the OT best reflects professional obligations under the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada?
questions.correct_rationale: Under the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada, OTs are obligated to communicate assessment findings clearly, transparently, and in a manner the recipient can understand, even — and especially — when the conversation is emotionally charged. A continuing power of attorney for personal care grants legal decision-making authority, but that authority is only meaningfully exercised when the substitute decision-maker (SDM) possesses a genuine, specific understanding of the identified risks. Simply "noting risks" without ensuring comprehension fails this standard. Option B fulfills the OT's duty by translating clinical findings into plain language, validating the daughter's role and emotional investment (reducing defensiveness without abandoning professional responsibility), and pivoting to collaborative problem-solving — which operationalizes both client-centred practice (CMOP-E) and the CAOT Code of Ethics principle of respect for persons. Escalation steps (capacity consultation, interprofessional escalation, documentation-only) become appropriate only after this foundational communication has occurred and proven insufficient.
questions.core_concept: Under the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada, OTs hold an autonomous duty to communicate occupational performance assessment findings clearly and transparently to substitute decision-makers, ensuring that legally authorized decision-making is genuinely informed. A continuing power of attorney for personal care confers authority, not dispensation from the need for full information; the OT's professional obligation to disclose specific, evidence-based risks is not satisfied by merely documenting that a concern exists.
questions.explain_differently: Think of the OT's role here the way a structural engineer advises a homeowner before renovation: the homeowner legally owns the house and can make whatever decision they want — but the engineer still has a professional duty to clearly explain exactly which load-bearing walls cannot be removed and why, before the homeowner picks up a sledgehammer. The daughter has every right to make the final discharge decision, but the OT's job is to make sure she is swinging with full knowledge of what is holding the structure up, not just a note in a file saying "concerns were raised."
questions.topic: Difficult discharge safety conversation with a substitute decision-maker holding a continuing power of attorney for personal care

options.label: A
options.text: Name each specific, evidence-based safety risk identified in the assessment using plain, non-judgmental language, explicitly acknowledge the daughter's caregiving commitment, and then collaboratively explore which community supports or environmental modifications could reduce identified risks and make a safer home discharge achievable.

options.label: B
options.text: Acknowledge the daughter's emotional distress and defer to her decision as the legally designated substitute decision-maker, documenting in the chart that safety risks were noted and the family elected to proceed.
options.incorrect_rationale: Documenting that risks were 'noted' without verifying that the SDM received and understood specific, evidence-based findings does not fulfill the OT's professional duty of transparent communication and leaves the daughter unable to exercise genuinely informed decision-making authority.

options.label: C
options.text: Advise the daughter that ongoing disagreement with the clinical team's recommendations will require a formal capacity assessment to evaluate whether she is exercising her substitute decision-maker authority in accordance with her mother's prior expressed wishes and best interests.
options.incorrect_rationale: A formal capacity assessment under provincial legislation evaluates the patient's decision-making capacity, not the SDM's conduct; invoking this mechanism in response to a family disagreement misapplies the process and would be ethically unjustifiable and premature before full information-sharing has been attempted.

options.label: D
options.text: Pause the family meeting and request that the attending physician join before proceeding, so that medical authority can reinforce the OT's safety concerns and present a unified clinical position to the daughter.
options.incorrect_rationale: Suspending OT-led communication pending physician presence misrepresents the OT's autonomous professional standing to communicate functional assessment findings and may inappropriately signal to the family that the OT's assessment conclusions require medical endorsement to be legitimate.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist (OT) working in acute care has assessed a 79-year-old woman with moderate dementia and bilateral lower extremity weakness following a stroke. The OT determines that the client lacks capacity to make discharge decisions. The client's son, who holds a continuing power of attorney for personal care, wants his mother discharged home to live alone with one daily home care visit. During the discharge planning meeting, when the OT begins to share concerns about fall risk and the client's inability to safely manage activities of daily living independently, the son becomes visibly distressed and says, "My mother would never want to go to a facility. You're being far too cautious — you don't know her like I do." What is the MOST appropriate initial response by the OT?
questions.correct_rationale: Acknowledging the son's emotional response and his intimate knowledge of his mother first establishes rapport and validates his substitute decision-maker role before introducing potentially distressing clinical information. Following this with a collaborative, evidence-based review of specific functional findings — such as timed mobility results, falls during assessment, and observed ADL deficits — fulfills the OT's professional duty of honest and transparent communication under the CAOT Code of Ethics (beneficence, honesty) and the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada (communication, collaboration domain). Provincial health care consent frameworks (e.g., Ontario's Health Care Consent Act) require that substitute decision makers receive adequate information to make a genuine decision; this approach ensures the son can exercise his role meaningfully while maintaining the therapeutic relationship needed to problem-solve together.
questions.core_concept: When delivering difficult discharge safety information to a substitute decision maker, OTs must first use therapeutic communication to validate the family member's perspective, then provide a clear, evidence-based disclosure of functional risks — fulfilling both the honesty principle of the CAOT Code of Ethics and the communication and collaboration competencies required under the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada, while enabling the substitute decision maker to exercise genuine informed consent under applicable provincial health care consent legislation.
questions.explain_differently: Think of the OT as a navigator who has spotted hazardous rocks ahead. Before doing anything else, the navigator says to the captain, "I know you've sailed this water for years and you know this ship better than anyone." That acknowledgment earns trust. Only then does the navigator spread the chart on the table and point to the exact rocks — the specific falls during assessment, the failed meal preparation task, the unsafe transfers — so both people are looking at the same evidence. You cannot safely chart a new course together if one person feels dismissed and the other is the only one who has seen the map.
questions.topic: Communication & Collaboration — Difficult conversations with family regarding discharge safety risk

options.label: A
options.text: Remind the son that as the continuing power of attorney for personal care, he has a legal obligation under provincial health care consent legislation to act in his mother's best interest as determined by the health care team.
options.incorrect_rationale: Leading with a legal obligation is adversarial and factually overstated — provincial consent legislation generally requires the substitute decision maker to act in the person's best interest, but the care team does not unilaterally define that standard; this approach escalates conflict rather than fostering the collaborative engagement needed first.

options.label: B
options.text: Acknowledge the son's distress and his knowledge of his mother, then collaboratively review the specific functional assessment findings so he has the information needed to make an informed decision as the continuing power of attorney for personal care.

options.label: C
options.text: Suggest the son speak directly with the attending physician to resolve the disagreement, and indicate that further OT involvement will resume once a consensus is reached by the family.
options.incorrect_rationale: Redirecting the family to the physician deflects the OT's professional communication responsibility; OTs are accountable under their regulatory college standards for communicating their own functional assessment findings and must not abdicate this role.

options.label: D
options.text: Document the son's concerns in the chart as an informed refusal of the recommended discharge plan and inform the interprofessional team that the family has declined the OT's recommendations.
options.incorrect_rationale: Recording an informed refusal is premature when collaborative engagement has not yet occurred; the son has expressed emotion, not a final decision, and closing communication at this point fails the OT's duty to clearly disclose risk and explore all options before accepting an outcome.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist in an acute care hospital has completed a comprehensive discharge assessment for Mrs. Okafor, a 78-year-old woman admitted following a right hemisphere stroke. Findings include severe anosognosia, moderate cognitive impairment, and near-total dependence in all self-care and home management tasks. The interprofessional team has determined she lacks capacity to make decisions about her discharge destination under provincial legislation. Her adult daughter — identified as the highest-ranking substitute decision-maker (SDM) under that legislation — states firmly, "My mother always said she would never go into a nursing home," and refuses to consider any long-term care home options or engage with the OT's safety concerns. Which action should the OT take first?
questions.correct_rationale: Under provincial legislation such as Ontario's Health Care Consent Act, an SDM for an incapable person must make decisions based on the person's prior capable expressed wishes and known values applied to the current circumstances; where no applicable prior wish exists or the circumstance was not anticipated, the SDM must act in the person's best interests, which explicitly includes safety. The OT's professional obligations under the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada require clear, honest communication of objective assessment findings and advocacy for the client's safety and well-being. Option B fulfils both duties: it validates the prior expressed wish as a legitimate and important consideration, while correcting the daughter's misunderstanding that a past general statement unconditionally binds the decision regardless of a dramatically changed functional status. Crucially, it distinguishes between the daughter's personal preference and her legal role as SDM, opening space for a fully informed conversation before any escalation pathway is considered.
questions.core_concept: When a client lacks capacity, a substitute decision-maker has a legislated obligation under provincial consent statutes such as the Health Care Consent Act to apply the client's prior expressed wishes to the current situation and to consider best interests — including safety — where no applicable wish was expressed. The OT's professional role is to ensure the SDM possesses complete, objective assessment information and understands this legal standard before any escalation to formal dispute mechanisms is pursued.
questions.explain_differently: Imagine the client gave the SDM an old travel itinerary saying "never go through town X," but the OT has just discovered the main bridge on the original route is out and town X is now the safest detour. The daughter is waving the old itinerary and refusing to look at the updated map. The OT's first job is not to grab the wheel or call a judge — it is to spread out the new map, explain what has changed on the road, and help the daughter understand that truly honouring her mother means applying the old preference to today's reality, not pretending the bridge is still standing.
questions.topic: Communication and Collaboration — Difficult Conversations with Family About Discharge Safety Risk

options.label: A
options.text: Proceed with arranging home discharge with the maximum available community supports, because the daughter, acting as SDM, is legally required to honour her mother's prior expressed wish to avoid long-term care.
options.incorrect_rationale: Prior expressed wishes are one input for the SDM, not an unconditional override; provincial legislation requires the SDM to apply those wishes to the current situation and, where safety is implicated, to weigh best interests, so proceeding to home discharge without ensuring the SDM has complete assessment information fails both the client and the legal standard.

options.label: B
options.text: Immediately refer the matter to the provincial Consent and Capacity Board or equivalent tribunal, as the family's refusal constitutes an obstruction of a safe discharge.
options.incorrect_rationale: Escalating to a formal adjudicative body is appropriate only after good-faith communication has been exhausted; bypassing further discussion with the daughter at this stage is premature and inconsistent with the OT's professional obligation to engage collaboratively with the SDM before seeking external resolution.

options.label: C
options.text: Acknowledge the significance of Mrs. Okafor's prior expressed wish, then clearly present the objective assessment findings and explain to the daughter that provincial consent legislation requires an SDM to apply the client's known wishes and values to the current situation and, where safety is implicated, to weigh her best interests — not to act solely on the SDM's own preferences or an isolated past statement.
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct answer.

options.label: D
options.text: Escalate directly to the interprofessional team to override the daughter's discharge preference on safety grounds, without further direct engagement with her.
options.incorrect_rationale: Seeking to override the SDM without first ensuring she fully understands the OT's assessment findings violates the collaborative, client- and family-centred practice principles in the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada and does not fulfil the OT's communication responsibilities before escalation is warranted.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist (OT) working in an acute care hospital assesses a 72-year-old client four days post-stroke. Using standardized functional assessments, the OT concludes the client presents significant safety risks for discharge home due to uncompensated unilateral neglect and unsafe transfers. The attending physician documents in the shared electronic health record (EHR) that the client is medically stable and ready for discharge in 48 hours. The OT raises concerns directly with the physician during rounds; the physician reviews the chart but maintains the discharge plan. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step for the OT regarding documentation in the shared interprofessional record?
questions.correct_rationale: The Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada (2021) — specifically the Communicator and Advocate competency domains — require OTs to articulate professional opinions clearly and to act in the client's best interest when safety is at risk. Provincial regulatory colleges (e.g., COTO in Ontario, ACOTRO member colleges across Canada) and their documentation standards mandate that a regulated health professional record all clinically relevant findings, the professional reasoning derived from those findings, and any steps taken to address identified risks. Entering this information in the shared EHR ensures the entire interprofessional team has access to the OT's safety analysis, creates a contemporaneous and verifiable record of advocacy, and fulfills the OT's duty of care. The note must use objective, non-judgmental language so it is defensible, collegial, and compliant with privacy legislation (e.g., PHIPA in Ontario) governing shared clinical records.
questions.core_concept: When an OT's professional assessment conflicts with a documented interprofessional plan, the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada and provincial regulatory college documentation standards require the OT to record objective findings, professional safety concerns, and communication efforts in the shared health record — fulfilling the dual obligations of client advocacy and transparent interprofessional communication while using factual, non-judgmental language.
questions.explain_differently: The shared health record functions as the team's official log of clinical decisions. If the OT's safety concerns do not appear in that log, it is professionally equivalent to never having raised them — the team cannot respond to information it cannot see, and the OT has no documented evidence of fulfilling their duty of care. Writing a clear, factual note about the disagreement is not a confrontational act; it is simply completing the OT's professional job, in the same way a fire-safety inspector would document a code violation even if the building owner disagreed.
questions.topic: Interprofessional documentation of clinical disagreement in a shared electronic health record

options.label: A
options.text: Refrain from entering any reference to the disagreement in the shared EHR and instead document concerns only in a private OT-specific chart note to preserve interprofessional relationships.
options.incorrect_rationale: Sequestering safety-critical clinical information away from the shared record defeats the purpose of an interprofessional record and means the team cannot act on information they cannot see, placing the client at risk and leaving the OT professionally exposed.

options.label: B
options.text: Document in the shared EHR that the physician's decision is clinically inappropriate and request that the note be formally flagged for review by the hospital's regulatory compliance office.
options.incorrect_rationale: The shared health record is a clinical communication tool, not a vehicle for professional complaints; characterizing a colleague's decision as inappropriate within it violates professional documentation standards and could constitute unprofessional conduct — concerns about a colleague's practice are addressed through the relevant regulatory college's formal complaints process.

options.label: C
options.text: Record only the raw assessment scores without narrative, as articulating a professional opinion that contradicts the physician's plan exceeds the OT's documentation scope in a shared medical record.
options.incorrect_rationale: Omitting professional interpretation from the record is an incomplete note that fails the OT's duty to advocate for client safety; OTs are fully authorized and professionally obligated to document clinical reasoning and professional opinions within a shared health record.

options.label: D
options.text: Document the objective functional assessment findings, the identified safety concerns, and the steps already taken to communicate those concerns to the team, using factual and professional language throughout the note.

questions.stem: A registered occupational therapist (OT) working on an inpatient rehabilitation unit completes a standardized functional assessment on a 74-year-old client who sustained a right hip fracture and lives alone in a second-floor apartment. The OT's findings indicate the client cannot safely negotiate stairs, requires standby assistance for transfers, and scores below the cut-off for safe unsupervised home management. The attending physician has already documented in the shared interprofessional electronic health record (EHR) that the client is "medically ready for discharge home tomorrow." The charge nurse informs the OT that the team is aligned with the physician's plan and that "stirring things up in the chart" could create conflict. Which action BEST reflects the OT's professional and documentation obligations under Canadian regulatory standards?
questions.correct_rationale: Under the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada (2021) — particularly the Communication and Collaboration competency domain — and provincial regulatory college documentation standards (e.g., COTO's Standards for Occupational Therapy Records), OTs are professionally accountable for documenting their clinical findings, reasoning, and recommendations accurately, completely, and in a timely manner. When an OT's functional assessment yields findings that are clinically significant and bear directly on client safety, omitting that information from the health record would constitute incomplete documentation and a failure of professional accountability. Documenting the assessment results and the OT's professional opinion — clearly attributed to the OT, factual in content, and professional in tone — fulfills the OT's duty regardless of what other team members have written. Each regulated health professional contributes their own discipline-specific perspective to the shared record; the presence of differing documented opinions is an expected feature of interprofessional care, not a breach of team norms. The CAOT Code of Ethics also obligates OTs to act in the client's best interest, which in this case requires that the safety concern be formally on record so that the team and, if necessary, the client or substitute decision-maker can make a fully informed decision.
questions.core_concept: Under the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada (2021) and provincial regulatory college documentation standards, OTs bear independent professional accountability for recording their clinical findings and opinions in the health record — including when those opinions diverge from other team members — because each discipline's entry constitutes that profession's accountable contribution to the shared record and to client safety.
questions.explain_differently: Picture the shared health record as each profession's sworn testimony about what they observed and concluded. If the OT examined the client and found real safety risks, not writing those findings down is like a witness staying silent at a crucial moment — the chart then tells an incomplete story and the team cannot make a truly informed decision. The OT's note does not "overrule" the physician's note; both entries coexist honestly, giving decision-makers the full clinical picture. Writing your professional truth clearly and respectfully is both a duty and a protection for the client.
questions.topic: Documentation of professional disagreement in a shared interprofessional health record

options.label: A
options.text: Document the standardized assessment results, the specific functional deficits identified, and the OT's professional opinion that the client does not currently meet criteria for safe independent discharge, ensuring the entry is clearly attributed to the OT, written in professional language, and entered in a timely manner.

options.label: B
options.text: Document only that "further interprofessional discussion regarding discharge planning is recommended," omitting explicit reference to the functional deficits or the OT's clinical opinion, to preserve team cohesion and avoid visible disagreement in the shared record.
options.incorrect_rationale: Vague language that obscures the OT's actual clinical findings fails to meet regulatory standards for complete and accurate documentation and leaves a critical client safety concern invisible in the record.

options.label: C
options.text: Refrain from adding any documentation that contradicts the physician's entry until the OT has first contacted the provincial regulatory college for written guidance on whether disagreement may be recorded in a shared health record.
options.incorrect_rationale: Delaying documentation to seek regulatory pre-approval is not standard practice; the OT already has clear obligations under existing regulatory college documentation standards, and withholding timely clinical findings would itself constitute a documentation failure.

options.label: D
options.text: Append a note directly beneath the physician's entry disputing its accuracy and formally requesting that the physician amend or retract the discharge-ready statement before any discharge planning proceeds.
options.incorrect_rationale: Each regulated professional is solely accountable for their own entries; the OT cannot alter, dispute the validity of, or demand retraction of another clinician's documentation, as this misrepresents how shared health records function under Canadian health record law and regulatory standards.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist (OT) working in an acute care hospital in Ontario completes a standardized functional assessment with a 74-year-old client who underwent a total hip arthroplasty four days ago. Using validated tools, the OT finds the client requires maximum assistance for transfers, is unable to safely navigate stairs, and lives alone in a two-storey home. The attending physician has documented a discharge plan for the following morning, noting the client is "medically stable and ready for home." The OT disagrees with this plan based on significant functional safety concerns. Regarding documentation in the shared interprofessional electronic health record, what is the MOST appropriate action for the OT to take?
questions.correct_rationale: The Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada (2021) establish that OTs must communicate their professional opinion clearly and advocate for client safety, including through accurate and timely documentation. Provincial regulatory colleges such as COTO reinforce that each regulated health professional documents their own assessment findings and clinical recommendations independently and contemporaneously. When an OT's functional assessment reveals a safety risk that differs from another provider's conclusion, the professionally appropriate response is to record objective findings, validated scores, and a clearly reasoned recommendation in the shared record. This fulfils the OT's duty to the client, creates a traceable professional record of the safety concern, and supports interprofessional decision-making by ensuring all team members can see the full clinical picture. It does not require disparaging a colleague's note — it requires the OT to stand behind their own scope-appropriate assessment.
questions.core_concept: Occupational therapists have an independent professional obligation, grounded in the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada and enforced by provincial regulatory colleges, to document their clinical findings and reasoned recommendations accurately and contemporaneously — including when those findings differ from another team member's assessment. Professional disagreement is expressed through objective evidence and transparent reasoning, never through editorial criticism of a colleague.
questions.explain_differently: Picture the shared health record as a table at which every discipline places their own evidence. The physician places "medically stable" on the table; the OT places "requires maximum assist for transfers, cannot manage stairs, lives alone." Neither note cancels the other — together they give the team and the client a complete picture. The OT's job is not to argue with what the physician wrote, but to make sure their own chair at that table is fully occupied with their scope-specific findings. Leaving the chair empty (no OT note) or filling it with criticism of the physician's chair both fail the client; a clear, objective functional summary fulfils the OT's professional duty and gives the discharge decision the safety data it needs.
questions.topic: COMM_COLLAB

options.label: A
options.text: Omit the disagreement from the shared record and raise the concern verbally with the physician and team at the next rounds, to avoid creating conflict in the written chart.
options.incorrect_rationale: Relying solely on verbal communication without contemporaneous written documentation fails to fulfill the OT's professional documentation obligation and leaves no record of the safety concern if an adverse event occurs.

options.label: B
options.text: Document the OT's functional assessment findings, standardized tool scores, and a clearly reasoned professional recommendation that the client requires a short-term rehabilitation placement before home discharge is safe.
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct answer.

options.label: C
options.text: Document in the shared record that the physician's discharge plan is clinically premature and exposes the client to an unacceptable risk of harm.
options.incorrect_rationale: This language editorializes about a colleague's clinical judgment rather than reporting objective OT findings; such commentary is unprofessional, potentially defamatory, and inconsistent with provincial regulatory college documentation standards.

options.label: D
options.text: Withhold any chart entry until the interprofessional team reaches consensus on the discharge plan, so the record reflects an agreed-upon decision.
options.incorrect_rationale: Delaying documentation until consensus is achieved is not required and conflicts with the principle of contemporaneous, accurate charting; it also suppresses the OT's independent clinical findings, which the record must capture to support informed decision-making.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist working on a rehabilitation unit at a community hospital completes a standardized home safety assessment and determines that a patient with moderate stroke-related cognitive and physical impairments cannot safely return to living alone, as originally planned. The attending physician and the social worker have already documented in the shared electronic health record (EHR) that the patient is medically cleared for discharge home independently within 48 hours. The OT's assessment findings directly contradict this conclusion. The OT raises the concern verbally with the social worker, who says the team has already discussed it and supports the discharge plan. Which action should the OT take next?
questions.correct_rationale: Under the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada and provincial regulatory college standards (e.g., COTO's documentation practice standards), each regulated professional is independently accountable for documenting their own assessment findings and clinical opinions. The shared health record is a legal document and a primary vehicle for interprofessional communication. When an OT's professional assessment reveals a patient safety concern that contradicts the current care plan, the OT has an ethical obligation — grounded in the CAOT Code of Ethics (beneficence, non-maleficence) — to enter that finding in the shared record promptly and transparently, regardless of whether it aligns with the team consensus. Documenting the disagreement formally also activates a traceable escalation pathway, ensuring the concern is visible to all regulated members of the team and to the patient's substitute decision-maker if applicable. Professional documentation of a dissenting clinical opinion does not invalidate other clinicians' entries; it adds the OT's independent professional perspective, which is precisely what interprofessional documentation is designed to accommodate.
questions.core_concept: Regulated occupational therapists hold independent professional accountability for documenting their clinical findings and opinions in the shared health record; under the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada and provincial regulatory college documentation standards, a professionally identified safety concern must be recorded transparently and promptly in the shared record even when it conflicts with the documented consensus of other team members.
questions.explain_differently: Think of the shared health record as a written professional roundtable — every regulated clinician has both the right and the duty to add their own voice. An OT does not need the team's permission to speak in writing, and staying silent in the record when a patient may be harmed is legally and ethically the same as not raising the concern at all. A dissenting entry does not erase what others have written; it ensures the full clinical picture is preserved, escalation pathways are activated, and the OT's professional registration is protected if questions arise later.
questions.topic: Interprofessional documentation — recording clinical disagreement in a shared health record

options.label: A
options.text: Contact the attending physician directly and request that the discharge documentation be amended before entering any conflicting entry into the shared record, so the record reflects a unified team position.
options.incorrect_rationale: Requiring another regulated professional to amend their documentation before the OT records their own findings is not appropriate; each regulated professional documents their independent clinical opinion, and withholding an OT's safety-critical findings until others comply delays necessary communication and subordinates professional accountability to interpersonal convenience.

options.label: B
options.text: Record the safety concerns only in a confidential OT-specific progress note that is not visible to the broader interprofessional team, to preserve collegial relationships while maintaining a personal professional record.
options.incorrect_rationale: A note that is invisible to the care team defeats the communicative purpose of the health record and means that physicians, nurses, and the patient's family cannot act on the OT's safety concern, leaving the client unprotected and the OT's professional obligation unfulfilled.

options.label: C
options.text: Document the standardized assessment findings, the specific functional safety concerns identified, and the OT's professional recommendation against independent discharge in the shared health record, and formally flag the interprofessional disagreement for urgent team review.

options.label: D
options.text: Defer any documentation of the disagreement until the next scheduled interprofessional team meeting so that a consensus-based plan can be recorded, avoiding contradictory entries in the shared record.
options.incorrect_rationale: When discharge is planned within 48 hours, deferring documentation of a serious safety concern to a future meeting allows a potentially unsafe discharge to proceed undocumented, violating the OT's duty to act promptly on client safety matters and their regulatory college's standards for timely, accurate documentation.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist (OT) working on an inpatient rehabilitation unit completes verbal handover to a covering OT at the end of their shift. While driving home, the OT realizes they failed to communicate that the orthopedic surgeon updated a patient's weight-bearing status from "weight-bearing as tolerated" (WBAT) to "non-weight-bearing" (NWB) earlier that afternoon following a post-operative complication from a left total knee arthroplasty. The covering OT is scheduled to conduct a transfer assessment with this patient first thing the following morning. What is the OT's most appropriate immediate action?
questions.correct_rationale: Under the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada (2021), OTs are accountable for the completeness and accuracy of care transition communications. A weight-bearing status change from WBAT to NWB is a safety-critical, time-sensitive clinical parameter: if not corrected before the assessment, it exposes the patient to a risk of implant failure or re-injury. Direct person-to-person contact with the receiving clinician is the most reliable mechanism to close a broken communication loop — it confirms receipt, allows the covering OT to ask clarifying questions, and is aligned with the CAOT Code of Ethics duty to act in the client's best interest. Correcting the chart is a necessary concurrent step, but it does not substitute for confirmed direct communication with the clinician responsible for the patient's upcoming care.
questions.core_concept: The Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada establish that OTs are professionally accountable for the accuracy and completeness of information exchanged during care transitions. When an OT identifies a safety-critical omission from handover, the duty to protect client safety requires immediate corrective action through direct, confirmed communication with the receiving clinician — not deferred or indirect notification.
questions.explain_differently: Imagine handover as physically passing a sealed envelope containing the patient's care plan. If you realize halfway home that you handed over an envelope with the wrong instructions inside, you do not slip a correction under the door later and hope it is found in time — you call the person who received it immediately to make sure the right instructions are in their hands before any action is taken. The OT's professional obligation works the same way: close the loop directly, and close it now.
questions.topic: Handover communication breakdown and patient safety in inpatient rehabilitation

options.label: A
options.text: Log in to the electronic health record remotely to update the documentation, trusting that the covering OT will review the chart prior to conducting the assessment.
options.incorrect_rationale: Updating documentation is necessary but insufficient on its own; documentation review is not guaranteed before a scheduled assessment, and this approach does not confirm the covering OT has received the safety-critical information.

options.label: B
options.text: Call the unit charge nurse and ask them to relay the updated weight-bearing precaution to the covering OT on the OT's behalf.
options.incorrect_rationale: Routing safety-critical clinical information through an intermediary adds an unnecessary link in the communication chain, increasing the likelihood of message loss, delay, or distortion before it reaches the responsible clinician.

options.label: C
options.text: Arrive at the unit early the next morning before the assessment to verbally correct the omission in person at that time.
options.incorrect_rationale: This approach is contingent on the OT arriving before the assessment begins and assumes no unexpected change in the schedule overnight, leaving the patient exposed to an avoidable safety risk for the entire intervening period.

options.label: D
options.text: Contact the covering OT directly by phone to communicate the updated NWB precaution and confirm it is documented accurately in the patient's chart before the assessment occurs.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist (OT) working on an inpatient orthopaedic rehabilitation unit begins the morning shift and reviews the written handover notes for Mrs. Lavoie (72 years old), who is on post-operative day 3 following a right total hip arthroplasty. The handover notes document her mobility status as "full weight-bearing (FWB) with walker, supervised assist of one." During a brief check-in, Mrs. Lavoie — who is alert and oriented — tells the OT that the physiotherapist assessed her at 16:00 h the previous day and changed her status to touchdown weight-bearing (TDWB) due to an intraoperative finding reviewed with the orthopaedic surgeon. She says, "The physio told me not to put full weight on it — I assumed everyone knew." The nursing staff and personal support workers (PSWs) are actively preparing to assist Mrs. Lavoie with morning care, including a bed-to-wheelchair transfer, which will begin in the next few minutes. Which action should the OT take FIRST?
questions.correct_rationale: Mrs. Lavoie is a competent, alert adult whose account of a clinician-ordered precaution change constitutes sufficient grounds to halt a potentially harmful procedure. The Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada (2021) identify patient safety and interprofessional communication as core OT responsibilities. When a handover breakdown creates an imminent safety risk — here, a FWB transfer on a limb that may be TDWB — the OT must interrupt the unsafe care process and escalate to the charge nurse immediately, before completing documentation or personally verifying the order. This approach preserves patient safety while simultaneously enabling the charge nurse to initiate parallel verification with the physiotherapist, avoiding both delay and unilateral action outside the OT's scope. Prioritizing the alert over documentation or personal verification reflects the hierarchy of obligations when the cost of inaction (potential dislocation, fracture, or fall) outweighs the cost of a brief care pause.
questions.core_concept: When a handover communication breakdown creates an imminent patient safety risk, an occupational therapist's primary obligation — consistent with the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada (2021) and Canadian patient safety principles — is to interrupt the unsafe care process and alert the responsible team immediately, recognizing that safety supersedes documentation and that verification of orders may proceed through parallel interprofessional channels rather than sequentially.
questions.explain_differently: Picture a colleague about to pour what might be the wrong medication into a cup — you shout "Hold on" first and ask questions second. You do not stop to update the chart, and you do not personally phone the pharmacy before saying a word; you stop the pour, then sort out the details. The OT's role in a handover breakdown is the same: break the chain of the unsafe action the moment it is identified, then let the charge nurse orchestrate confirmation through the proper channels.
questions.topic: Interprofessional Communication — Handover Breakdown and Patient Safety

options.label: A
options.text: Immediately interrupt morning care, alert the charge nurse and bedside PSW to hold all weight-bearing mobility, and communicate the reported weight-bearing change to the team pending confirmation with the physiotherapist.
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct answer.

options.label: B
options.text: Update Mrs. Lavoie's care plan and post a weight-bearing precaution alert at the bedside so all team members have accurate written documentation of the change.
options.incorrect_rationale: Updating documentation is important but takes time and does not prevent an unsafe transfer from occurring in the next few minutes; addressing the record after the fact does not protect the client from imminent harm.

options.label: C
options.text: Contact the physiotherapist directly to verify the weight-bearing status change before advising any other team member, to ensure only confirmed information is communicated.
options.incorrect_rationale: Waiting to personally verify with the physiotherapist before alerting bedside staff introduces a dangerous delay during which a harmful transfer could occur; confirmation can be sought in parallel by the charge nurse while the OT prevents the transfer.

options.label: D
options.text: Conduct a focused OT functional mobility re-assessment of Mrs. Lavoie and then communicate findings to the team based on the OT's own clinical observations.
options.incorrect_rationale: Re-assessing functional mobility before notifying the team is inappropriate because the OT does not hold authority to reinterpret or override a surgeon-sanctioned physiotherapy weight-bearing precaution, and the time required creates an unacceptable window for harm.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist (OT) working on an inpatient rehabilitation unit at a hospital in Ontario completes a verbal handover to a colleague who will cover afternoon sessions. The outgoing OT communicates that Mr. Okafor, a 72-year-old client who is two days post-total hip arthroplasty, has been cleared for supervised ambulation with a quad cane. She does not mention that a physician note entered earlier that morning has changed his weight-bearing status to toe-touch weight-bearing only following an intraoperative complication identified at morning rounds. Twenty minutes after leaving the unit, the outgoing OT realizes the omission. What is the MOST appropriate immediate action?
questions.correct_rationale: When a clinician identifies a critical handover omission that poses an imminent patient safety risk, the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada (Communication and Collaboration domain) and the CAOT Code of Ethics (Principle of Beneficence/Non-Maleficence) require that the OT act immediately to prevent harm. Direct, real-time verbal contact with the covering OT is the fastest, most reliable method of closing the communication gap before an unsafe transfer is attempted. Documentation updates and incident reporting are necessary follow-up steps but cannot substitute for urgent direct communication when a client's physical safety is at stake in the immediate moment.
questions.core_concept: When a handover omission creates an imminent patient safety risk, the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada (Communication and Collaboration domain) and the CAOT Code of Ethics obligate the identifying OT to prioritize direct, real-time communication with the receiving clinician above documentation or administrative processes. Structured handover practices (such as SBAR) exist to prevent such gaps, but when a gap is discovered, the hierarchy of action is: prevent harm first, document and report second.
questions.explain_differently: Imagine handing someone your car keys and then realizing the brakes are faulty. You would not send them a text message or file a maintenance report first — you would run after them and stop them before they drive away. The principle is the same: the fastest, most direct route to the person who can act on the information always takes priority when harm is imminent. Everything else — the chart note, the incident form, the manager conversation — comes once the person is safe.
questions.topic: COMM_COLLAB — Communication Breakdown During Handover and Patient Safety

options.label: A
options.text: Update Mr. Okafor's electronic health record immediately with the correct weight-bearing status, trusting the covering OT will review his chart before initiating treatment.
options.incorrect_rationale: Updating the record is a necessary subsequent step, but it is not reliable as an immediate safety measure because the covering OT may have already begun treatment before checking for new entries.

options.label: B
options.text: Directly contact the covering OT by phone or in person to communicate the weight-bearing restriction before any ambulation is attempted.

options.label: C
options.text: Notify the unit manager and complete a critical incident report to formally document the handover communication error.
options.incorrect_rationale: Incident reporting and managerial notification are appropriate accountability steps after the immediate safety threat is addressed, not before direct harm-prevention action is taken.

options.label: D
options.text: Return to the unit to independently reassess Mr. Okafor's weight-bearing tolerance before discussing the situation with the covering OT.
options.incorrect_rationale: Conducting an independent reassessment before alerting the covering OT delays the critical warning and may cause the covering OT to initiate ambulation before the OT can return, worsening the safety risk.

questions.stem: A covering occupational therapist (OT) on an inpatient rehabilitation unit reviews a client's chart before a morning ADL session. The client is a 74-year-old Cree woman recovering from a total hip replacement. The verbal handover received from the departing OT noted she was "independent with a walker on level surfaces." However, the chart contains a physiotherapy entry from the previous afternoon documenting a change to two-person assist for all transfers following a near-fall, along with a nursing note indicating increased pain and fatigue overnight. This information was not communicated verbally or in any written handover summary. The client is in her room, expecting her ADL session. What is the MOST appropriate FIRST action for the covering OT?
questions.correct_rationale: The Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada (2021) require OTs to communicate safety-critical information across the interprofessional team and to prioritize client safety when risks are identified. The handover gap here is not merely an OT-to-OT issue: nursing staff, rehabilitation assistants, and any other provider assisting with mobility are at risk of transferring this client using an unsafe approach because the two-person assist precaution was never team-wide. The covering OT's first obligation is therefore to halt a potentially unsafe interaction AND correct the information deficit across all relevant team members — not just internally adjust their own practice. Only after the full team is aligned on current precautions can a safe, collaborative reassessment of the client's goals and session readiness occur. This sequence reflects the duty of care, the interprofessional collaboration competency, and the CAOT Code of Ethics principle of beneficence and non-maleficence.
questions.core_concept: When an OT identifies a safety-critical handover omission, professional accountability under the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada requires immediate interprofessional disclosure — not isolated correction — because a communication breakdown affecting mobility precautions creates team-wide risk, not just a dyadic clinical gap between two OTs.
questions.explain_differently: Think of a handover failure like a dropped relay baton that everyone on the track missed seeing. One runner quietly picking it up and adjusting their stride does not help the three other runners still sprinting on the assumption the baton is in the original position. The right move is to stop the race, signal the entire field, and confirm everyone has the same picture before resuming — because the hazard belongs to the whole team, not just the runner who spotted it.
questions.topic: COMM_COLLAB — Communication breakdown during handover and patient safety

options.label: A
options.text: Proceed with the ADL session using the updated two-person assist status, as the physiotherapy note in the chart provides sufficient clinical information to safely modify the intervention approach.
options.incorrect_rationale: Acting on the updated information in isolation does not address the team-wide gap; nursing staff and other providers interacting with this client may remain unaware of the revised precautions, leaving the client at continued risk of harm from unsupported transfers by others.

options.label: B
options.text: Postpone the client's session, file an incident report regarding the handover omission, and contact the departing OT to conduct a retrospective verbal handover before initiating any intervention.
options.incorrect_rationale: While incident reporting is eventually appropriate, delaying all action to pursue the departing OT subordinates immediate client safety to administrative process, and the covering OT holds independent professional accountability to act on identified safety risks without awaiting the original clinician's guidance.

options.label: C
options.text: Before initiating the ADL session, immediately inform the nursing staff and the most responsible provider of the identified discrepancy to ensure updated mobility precautions are communicated across the interprofessional team, then collaboratively reassess the client's goals and readiness before proceeding.

options.label: D
options.text: Conduct a brief independent functional reassessment of the client's current transfer status during the session, then update the care plan and document a revised baseline to inform the team going forward.
options.incorrect_rationale: Proceeding to reassess the client independently without first alerting the team perpetuates the safety gap — nursing and other staff remain uninformed and may transfer the client without the required two-person assist — and places the OT in the position of managing a systemic communication failure unilaterally rather than through accountable interprofessional channels.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist (OT) working on an inpatient orthopaedic rehabilitation unit in Ontario returns from a day off to find that the physiotherapist (PT) has completed a home environment assessment for a mutual client recovering from a total hip replacement. The PT's discharge summary already includes specific recommendations for a raised toilet seat, grab bars, and a shower bench — interventions the OT had planned to address. The OT believes this encroaches on OT scope of practice as defined by the College of Occupational Therapists of Ontario (COTO). What is the OT's most appropriate initial action?
questions.correct_rationale: Under the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada (2021), OTs enact both the Collaborator and Professional roles by asserting their distinct scope through respectful, direct dialogue before escalating. Home environment assessment and adaptive equipment recommendations to support independent occupational performance are core OT competencies recognized by COTO. Speaking privately with the PT first honours professional courtesy, gives the colleague an opportunity to understand the boundary, and opens a constructive conversation about role delineation — mirroring the CAOT Code of Ethics principle of acting with integrity in interprofessional relationships. If the concern is not resolved through direct dialogue, escalating to a team leader or manager is the appropriate next step, and only if harm or repeated disregard for scope occurs would a regulatory pathway become relevant.
questions.core_concept: OTs have a professional and ethical obligation to advocate for the occupational therapy scope of practice — including home environment assessment and adaptive equipment prescription — through direct, constructive interprofessional communication before escalating, as outlined in the Collaborator and Professional competency roles in the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada (2021) and the CAOT Code of Ethics.
questions.explain_differently: Think of scope advocacy like a property boundary dispute between neighbours: the right first move is a calm, direct conversation over the fence — not calling a lawyer. The OT knocks on the PT's door, explains which part of the yard belongs to OT practice (home assessment, occupation-focused equipment), and they agree on where the fence should sit for future clients. Only if the neighbour keeps crossing the line does it make sense to involve the strata council (team lead) or the municipality (regulatory college).
questions.topic: Advocating for OT scope of practice in interprofessional settings

options.label: A
options.text: File a formal complaint with COTO against the PT for practising outside their regulated scope of practice.
options.incorrect_rationale: Filing a regulatory complaint is a measure of last resort reserved for serious or repeated harm; bypassing direct communication is disproportionate and inconsistent with the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada, which require OTs to first attempt collegial resolution.

options.label: B
options.text: Complete a separate, independent home assessment and submit a second set of recommendations to the team without addressing the overlap with the PT.
options.incorrect_rationale: Duplicating the assessment without communication creates conflicting advice that can confuse the client and care team, and fails to advocate for the OT role or resolve the underlying scope issue.

options.label: C
options.text: Raise the scope concern at the next interprofessional team meeting without first approaching the PT privately.
options.incorrect_rationale: Raising the issue publicly before attempting a direct conversation can embarrass the PT, damage the therapeutic relationship, and escalates the conflict prematurely — contravening the professional communication standards in the CAOT Code of Ethics.

options.label: D
options.text: Speak directly and promptly with the PT to explain how home environment assessment and adaptive equipment recommendation fall within OT scope, and collaboratively establish a clear process for role delineation on future similar cases.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist (OT) is employed on an inpatient acquired brain injury rehabilitation unit at a hospital in Ontario. In response to growing wait-list pressures, the unit manager — with the support of the OT's direct supervisor — has instructed the physiotherapy team to complete self-care performance assessments and make adaptive equipment recommendations for all newly admitted patients prior to OT involvement. The physiotherapists are acting in good faith under this directive. The College of Occupational Therapists of Ontario (COTO) explicitly identifies the assessment of self-care occupations and recommendation of adaptive equipment as core OT competencies. The OT is concerned that this arrangement compromises patient care quality and misrepresents professional scopes of practice. What is the OT's BEST initial course of action?
questions.correct_rationale: Option B reflects the graduated, evidence-based advocacy pathway that the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada (Competency 7: Advocacy) and the CAOT Code of Ethics require.
