options.text: Explore the client's specific concerns about the prosthesis (e.g., socket fit, weight, terminal device design) and collaboratively develop a modified prosthetic training plan that targets his foreman occupational roles.
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct answer and does not require an incorrect rationale.

options.label: B
options.text: Document the client's refusal and refer immediately to the WSIB case manager to explore non-prosthetic workplace accommodations for return to work.
options.incorrect_rationale: Escalating to the WSIB case manager before identifying and addressing modifiable prosthetic barriers bypasses the OT's professional role in rehabilitation and prematurely forecloses device-based options without adequate assessment.

options.label: C
options.text: Inform the client that WSIB rehabilitation guidelines require demonstrated prosthetic competency before clearance to return to the construction worksite.
options.incorrect_rationale: This overstates WSIB requirements and is coercive; WSIB-funded rehabilitation is guided by functional and occupational goals rather than a mandated obligation to use a specific device, and this approach violates the CAOT Code of Ethics principle of respecting client autonomy.

options.label: D
options.text: Discharge the client from prosthetic training and initiate a referral for vocational retraining toward a sedentary occupation.
options.incorrect_rationale: Recommending vocational retraining at 9 weeks post-amputation, before exhausting strategies to address prosthetic barriers, is premature and inconsistent with the OT's duty to maximize the client's occupational potential within his identified role.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old right-hand-dominant man sustained a traumatic right transradial amputation while operating machinery at an Ontario manufacturing plant. He is 8 weeks post-amputation, has received a myoelectric prosthetic fitting, and has completed basic prosthetic training at an inpatient rehabilitation centre. His WSIB case manager has requested a functional capacity evaluation (FCE) within two weeks to support return-to-work planning for his pre-injury machinist role. During the OT session, the client reports he can don and doff the prosthesis independently, but describes unreliable grip force control when manipulating small metal components. He also discloses phantom limb pain rated 7/10 that worsens significantly with prolonged prosthetic wear, limiting his training sessions to under 30 minutes before he must remove the device. He states: "I just want my old life back — I need to get back to work." Using the Canadian Practice Process Framework (CPPF), what is the OT's PRIORITY action at this stage of intervention?
questions.correct_rationale: The CPPF directs OTs to identify and prioritize the root occupational performance barriers before implementing enabling strategies. Here, phantom limb pain rated 7/10 that limits prosthetic wear to under 30 minutes is the primary barrier that will undermine every downstream goal: advanced myoelectric training cannot be adequately practised, an FCE conducted under these conditions would underestimate the client's true capacity and produce a misleading WSIB report, and any return-to-work plan would be built on an inaccurate functional picture. By collaborating with the physician to optimize pain management — through evidence-based strategies such as graded motor imagery, mirror therapy, transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS), or pharmacological adjustment — the OT addresses the person dimension of the CMOP-E (physical and affective components) before progressing to occupation-focused goals. Communicating transparently with the WSIB case manager about this clinical rationale upholds both client-centred practice and professional accountability under the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada.
questions.core_concept: In upper-limb prosthetic rehabilitation, uncontrolled phantom limb pain is a primary occupational performance barrier that must be systematically addressed before advancing prosthetic skill training or conducting functional evaluations. The CPPF and CMOP-E direct OTs to resolve foundational person-level barriers (physical, affective) that gate meaningful occupational engagement, rather than progressing through a rehabilitation sequence that the barrier renders ineffective.
questions.explain_differently: Imagine trying to assess someone's ability to run a race while they have an untreated broken foot — the result tells you nothing useful about their actual running capacity, and training them harder will only cause harm. Phantom limb pain limiting prosthetic wear to 30 minutes is that broken foot: you must treat the underlying problem first, or every evaluation and training session built on top of it is invalid and potentially harmful. Fixing the pain is not a detour from return-to-work — it is the fastest route to an accurate picture of what this client can actually do.
questions.topic: Upper-limb prosthetic rehabilitation and occupational reintegration (transradial amputation, myoelectric prosthesis, WSIB return-to-work, phantom limb pain)

options.label: A
options.text: Proceed with the FCE within the WSIB case manager's requested timeline to document the client's current functional capacity and avoid jeopardizing his return-to-work benefits.
options.incorrect_rationale: Conducting an FCE while phantom limb pain limits prosthetic wear to under 30 minutes would produce an artificially low and unreliable functional baseline, potentially underestimating the client's true capacity and leading to an inaccurate WSIB recommendation.

options.label: B
options.text: Collaborate with the client and his treating physician to address phantom limb pain management strategies (e.g., graded motor imagery, mirror therapy, pharmacological review) as the foundational step before advancing prosthetic training or scheduling the FCE.

options.label: C
options.text: Prioritize intensive myoelectric grip-force control training targeting small-object manipulation tasks to prepare the client for the specific demands of his machinist role before the FCE.
options.incorrect_rationale: Intensive grip-force training is not feasible when pain already limits prosthetic wear to under 30 minutes and may worsen sensitization; the primary barrier of uncontrolled pain must be resolved before skill-refinement training can be effective.

options.label: D
options.text: Recommend a graduated return-to-work plan to the WSIB case manager that begins immediately with modified duties at the plant while prosthetic training continues on a parallel track.
options.incorrect_rationale: Recommending a return-to-work plan is premature without first resolving the primary barrier of phantom limb pain and without a valid FCE to inform the safe parameters of any modified duties.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist working in an outpatient burn rehabilitation clinic in Ontario is treating a client who sustained partial-thickness burns to the dominant hand eight weeks ago. The wounds are fully healed. The therapist observes raised, erythematous, firm scar tissue over the volar surface that limits composite finger flexion. The client's primary goal is to return to independent dressing. Which intervention best addresses both hypertrophic scar management and ADL retraining?
questions.correct_rationale: Healed burn scar tissue remains biologically active and responsive to mechanical forces during the remodeling phase (typically 6-24 months). Grading meaningful dressing tasks so that the client progressively moves their fingers through increasing ranges of flexion applies controlled tensile stress to the scar, stimulating collagen realignment and elongation. Simultaneously, a custom compression glove delivers sustained pressure (ideally 15-25 mmHg) that flattens and softens hypertrophic scar tissue by reducing local blood flow and collagen synthesis. This combined approach is consistent with CMOP-E, which positions the client's occupational goal (dressing) as both the therapeutic medium and the desired outcome, addressing the physical component of the person while restoring engagement in self-care occupation.
questions.core_concept: In burn rehabilitation, OTs concurrently use pressure therapy (compression garments) and graded functional activity to promote scar remodeling and restore occupational performance. These interventions are complementary: compression modulates collagen formation, while active movement through meaningful tasks elongates the scar and rebuilds motor patterns, reflecting CMOP-E's integration of person, occupation, and environment.
questions.explain_differently: Healing scar tissue behaves like stiff modelling clay — it must be worked gently while still pliable, or it hardens in a shortened position. Practicing dressing is the working: each button done up gives the scar an active stretch at just the right moment. The compression glove is the press and hold: constant gentle pressure between sessions prevents the scar from heaping up again. Waiting for the scar to settle on its own before starting activities is like putting the clay on a shelf and hoping it reshapes itself — the window closes and the opportunity is lost.
questions.topic: Burn Rehabilitation: Scar Management and ADL Retraining

options.label: A
options.text: Apply silicone gel sheeting exclusively during nighttime hours and defer ADL practice until the scar softens.
options.incorrect_rationale: Restricting silicone use to nighttime provides insufficient pressure duration, and deferring functional practice delays scar elongation through active movement, narrowing the optimal remodeling window.

options.label: B
options.text: Provide adaptive equipment (e.g., button hook, zipper pull) as the primary strategy to restore independent dressing.
options.incorrect_rationale: Adaptive equipment compensates for lost hand function but does not address the underlying hypertrophic scar or scar contracture; used in isolation, it foregoes the impairment-level intervention that can restore native function.

options.label: C
options.text: Grade dressing practice tasks to progressively incorporate active finger flexion through the scar while prescribing a custom compression glove to be worn between sessions.
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct answer.

options.label: D
options.text: Position the hand in a volar resting splint worn continuously until scar maturation is complete at approximately two years post-injury.
options.incorrect_rationale: Continuous immobilization prevents the active joint motion needed to elongate maturing scar tissue and delays occupational retraining, worsening long-term functional outcomes.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man sustained partial-thickness burns to his dominant right hand and wrist in a workplace fire 10 weeks ago. He has been referred to outpatient occupational therapy by his plastic surgeon. Assessment reveals hypertrophic scarring across the dorsal hand and wrist, composite finger flexion limited to 50°, and wrist extension of 25°. He reports significant difficulty with grooming, meal preparation, and fastening clothing. He is wearing a compression glove but removes it frequently due to discomfort and fit concerns. The scar remains erythematous and raised. His WSIB file is open and return to modified duties is a goal within the next two months. Which intervention approach BEST addresses both scar management and ADL retraining at this stage of healing?
questions.correct_rationale: At 10 weeks post-burn, the wound is in the proliferative phase, during which hypertrophic scar tissue is still biologically responsive to mechanical input. The combination of properly fitted compression therapy and silicone gel sheeting represents the highest-evidence conservative approach to reducing scar height, erythema, and pliability. A dorsal anti-contracture splint worn at night maintains wrist extension and MCP flexion, counteracting the contractile forces of maturing scar tissue and preserving the range gained during therapy. Crucially, scar management and ADL retraining are not sequential — they must occur concurrently. Graded ADL tasks using adapted equipment (e.g., button hooks, built-up handles, non-slip mats) address the client's immediate occupational priorities, support engagement in meaningful activity, and provide purposeful active motion that reinforces range-of-motion gains. This integrated approach aligns with the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada (enabling occupation through client-centred, evidence-based practice) and is consistent with WSIB rehabilitation expectations for timely, function-focused intervention.
questions.core_concept: During the proliferative phase of burn healing, occupational therapists integrate multimodal scar management (compression, silicone, anti-contracture splinting) simultaneously with graded ADL retraining and adaptive equipment to prevent contracture-related disability and restore occupational performance — these two streams are concurrent, not sequential.
questions.explain_differently: Picture burn scar management and ADL retraining as two construction crews working on the same building at the same time, not one after the other. While one crew is actively shaping and softening the scar with compression and silicone (the scar is still "wet cement" at 10 weeks and can be molded), the other crew is teaching the client how to button his shirt with a button hook today — not two years from now when the cement has hardened. Waiting for the scar to mature before addressing function would mean months of unnecessary dependency, and the scar would harden in whatever position it wants rather than the functional position you helped establish.
questions.topic: Burn Rehabilitation: Scar Management and ADL Retraining

options.label: A
options.text: Discontinue the compression glove given the client's poor tolerance, and shift focus entirely to active range-of-motion exercises and compensatory ADL strategies using the non-dominant hand.
options.incorrect_rationale: Discontinuing compression during the active proliferative phase removes a primary evidence-based intervention for hypertrophic scar control; tolerance issues should be addressed through glove modification or adjustment, not discontinuation.

options.label: B
options.text: Refer the client back to the plastic surgeon immediately to discuss surgical scar release, as the functional deficits at 10 weeks indicate conservative management has been insufficient.
options.incorrect_rationale: Surgical scar revision is generally deferred for 12 to 24 months to allow full scar maturation; recommending surgery at 10 weeks bypasses the established conservative management window.

options.label: C
options.text: Prioritize a structured sensory desensitization program and defer formal ADL retraining until the scar has fully matured to avoid disrupting the healing tissue.
options.incorrect_rationale: Deferring ADL retraining until scar maturity imposes unnecessary functional disability and occupational deprivation; active ADL engagement, supported by adaptive equipment and graded activity, is safe and therapeutically beneficial during the proliferative phase.

options.label: D
options.text: Adjust and troubleshoot the compression glove fit, add silicone gel sheeting under the glove, fabricate a dorsal anti-contracture splint for nighttime positioning, and concurrently grade ADL tasks using adapted equipment to restore occupational performance.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman sustained full-thickness burns covering 40% TBSA (bilateral upper extremities and anterior trunk) in a workplace incident. She is 12 weeks post-skin grafting and has worn custom compression garments for six weeks. At her outpatient OT appointment, she reports wearing the garments only 12–14 hours daily because of significant difficulty performing meal preparation and personal care while wearing them. On assessment, the OT observes a developing hypertrophic scar band across the right antecubital fossa with active elbow extension limited to –20° (20° extension lag). Her priority goal is to return to her job as an office administrator. Which of the following should the OT prioritize FIRST?
questions.correct_rationale: At 12 weeks post-grafting, hypertrophic scar tissue is still in the active remodelling phase and highly responsive to mechanical intervention. A –20° elbow extension lag with a visible scar band signals an early contracture that, if unchecked, will become permanent and severely limit the client's return-to-work goal. The OT must act on two interconnected problems simultaneously: (1) fabricate a volar elbow extension splint worn during rest and at night to apply a sustained low-load stretch and counteract the contracture force; and (2) address the root cause of garment non-adherence—ADL difficulty—by introducing adaptive equipment (e.g., built-up handles, loop scissors, dycem), joint-protection techniques, and garment donning/doffing strategies so the client can sustain the recommended wear time (~23 hours/day) without sacrificing occupational performance. This dual approach aligns with the CMOP-E by simultaneously addressing the physical component (scar contracture) and occupational performance (ADL retraining), and reflects the CPPF principle of collaborating with the client to remove participation barriers rather than simply directing behaviour.
questions.core_concept: In burn scar rehabilitation, the OT must concurrently address hypertrophic scar contracture prevention through splinting and sustained pressure garment adherence, and occupational performance barriers through adaptive strategies — because these goals are interdependent: a contracture worsens when garments are removed, and garments are removed when ADLs cannot be performed with them on. Effective intervention targets both problems in the same treatment plan rather than sequencing them.
questions.explain_differently: Imagine trying to rehabilitate a torn knee ligament while the brace is so uncomfortable the patient keeps removing it. Simply telling the patient "wear it more" does nothing if the brace prevents them from walking to the bathroom. And letting them go brace-free so they can walk normally defeats the whole healing purpose. The smart move is to re-fit the brace AND teach them how to move safely with it on — both at the same time. This OT scenario is identical: fix the garment-adherence problem by teaching ADL workarounds, and simultaneously prevent the contracture from solidifying with a night splint. One without the other fails.
questions.topic: Burn Rehabilitation: Scar Management and ADL Retraining

options.label: A
options.text: Fabricate a volar elbow extension splint for nighttime and rest periods to address the developing antecubital contracture, and collaboratively identify adaptive equipment and techniques that allow the client to perform ADLs while wearing the compression garments.

options.label: B
options.text: Provide targeted education emphasizing the critical importance of 23-hour daily compression garment wear and encourage the client to adhere to the full schedule before the next appointment.
options.incorrect_rationale: Education alone does not resolve the functional barrier causing non-adherence, and it entirely ignores the developing –20° elbow extension contracture that requires immediate mechanical intervention.

options.label: C
options.text: Schedule structured garment-free ADL practice sessions to rebuild occupational performance and confidence, with a plan to reintroduce full garment wear once ADL independence is re-established.
options.incorrect_rationale: Removing compression garments during ADL practice eliminates the mechanical pressure critical during the active scar-remodelling phase, accelerating hypertrophic scar maturation and worsening the contracture the OT is trying to prevent.

options.label: D
options.text: Refer the client urgently back to the plastic surgery or burn surgery team to assess the need for surgical scar release of the antecubital contracture before proceeding with further OT intervention.
options.incorrect_rationale: Surgical scar release is indicated only after conservative measures (sustained splinting, pressure, silicone) have failed over 12–18 months; referring at 12 weeks bypasses first-line OT interventions that are highly likely to resolve an early contracture.

questions.stem: An OT is providing home-based rehabilitation to a 71-year-old woman with moderate chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). She reports increasing shortness of breath and fatigue when preparing her daily meals and asks for strategies to remain independent in the kitchen. Which energy conservation recommendation should the OT prioritize FIRST?
questions.correct_rationale: Option B applies three of the foundational energy conservation principles (the "4 Ps") simultaneously. Sitting on a high stool reduces postural muscle energy expenditure relative to standing, directly lowering cardiac and pulmonary demand during the task. Pre-organizing all supplies eliminates unnecessary trips and movement, applying the Plan and Prioritize principles. Scheduled rest breaks implement Pacing, preventing the client from reaching the point of exhaustion before the task is complete. Together these strategies allow the client to maintain independence in a meaningful IADL while operating within her cardiopulmonary tolerance — a client-centred outcome aligned with the CMOP-E occupational performance framework.
questions.core_concept: Energy conservation in cardiopulmonary rehabilitation is guided by the "4 Ps": Plan (organize the task in advance), Prioritize (decide what matters most), Pace (alternate activity with rest), and Position (use seated or supported postures to reduce metabolic load). OTs apply these principles to grade activity demands so clients can sustain meaningful occupations within their physiological tolerance.
questions.explain_differently: Think of the client's available energy like a phone battery that charges slowly. Sitting down is like turning the screen brightness down — the phone still works but uses less power. Laying out everything before you start is like loading all your apps before you leave Wi-Fi — no wasted searching mid-task. Planned rest breaks are like plugging in for a quick charge before the battery hits zero. The goal is to keep the phone running all day, not to avoid using it.
questions.topic: Cardiac/Pulmonary Rehabilitation — Energy Conservation and Graded Activity

options.label: A
options.text: Complete all meal preparation tasks while standing at the counter to maintain upright posture and promote lung expansion.
options.incorrect_rationale: Although an upright posture supports diaphragmatic breathing, standing significantly increases metabolic demand compared with sitting, exacerbating dyspnea and fatigue.

options.label: B
options.text: Sit on a high stool at the counter, organize all required supplies before beginning, and schedule planned rest breaks throughout the task.

options.label: C
options.text: Work through meal preparation as quickly as possible to complete the task before fatigue and breathlessness onset.
options.incorrect_rationale: Rushing increases cardiopulmonary demand and hastens symptom onset; pacing is the opposite of rushing and is a foundational energy conservation principle.

options.label: D
options.text: Discontinue meal preparation and arrange a permanent Meals on Wheels referral until respiratory symptoms improve.
options.incorrect_rationale: Eliminating a meaningful occupation is inconsistent with the OT goal of optimizing participation and independence; COPD is a chronic condition that benefits from graded activity and adaptive strategies, not avoidance.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man was discharged home three weeks ago following a myocardial infarction and is now attending Phase II outpatient cardiac rehabilitation at a hospital in Manitoba. He reports that showering leaves him exhausted and he must rest for 90 minutes afterward before he can dress. His resting heart rate is 72 bpm and his cardiologist has cleared him for light activity. He rates his fatigue as 7/10 immediately after showering. Which intervention should the occupational therapist implement first?
questions.correct_rationale: The client is medically stable and cleared for light activity, so OT intervention is appropriate. The presenting concern is occupational performance disruption caused by excessive energy expenditure during a specific ADL — showering. Energy conservation strategies (seated positioning to reduce postural work, adaptive equipment to minimize reaching, and planned rest breaks between tasks) directly reduce the metabolic cost of the activity without eliminating it, enabling the client to complete morning self-care within his current cardiac capacity. This is the priority first-line OT intervention because it immediately addresses the identified occupational performance barrier, aligns with the client's functional goal of independent morning routines, and is within OT scope of practice under the Phase II cardiac rehab framework.
questions.core_concept: In cardiac and pulmonary rehabilitation, occupational therapists apply energy conservation principles — task modification, adaptive positioning, strategic rest pacing, and equipment use — to reduce the metabolic demand of meaningful occupations so clients can perform ADLs safely within their current physiological limits. This is distinct from graded activity, which is a longer-term strategy for progressively building endurance.
questions.explain_differently: Think of the client's daily energy like a modest daily bank account after a heart attack — the balance is smaller than it used to be and cannot be instantly replenished. Energy conservation is not about depositing more money; it is about spending less on each transaction. Sitting during a shower costs far fewer "dollars" than standing, so the client has enough left to get dressed, eat breakfast, and still feel human — rather than spending everything in the shower and going bankrupt before 9 a.m.
questions.topic: Cardiac/Pulmonary Rehabilitation — Energy Conservation and Graded Activity

options.label: A
options.text: Introduce a graded walking program beginning with 5-minute walks, increasing by 2 minutes each week, to build overall cardiac endurance before addressing morning self-care.
options.incorrect_rationale: A walking program targets global endurance over weeks and does not address the immediate ADL performance barrier; the OT should first modify the fatiguing task, not defer self-care intervention.

options.label: B
options.text: Advise the client to shower every other day and consolidate all morning ADLs on the alternate day to reduce his total weekly cardiovascular demand.
options.incorrect_rationale: Reducing bathing frequency is avoidance rather than energy conservation; consolidating all ADLs into one session on alternating days would actually cluster metabolic demands and increase, not decrease, cardiovascular strain on those days.

options.label: C
options.text: Teach energy conservation strategies for showering: use a shower chair, a long-handled sponge, and schedule a seated rest break between showering and dressing.

options.label: D
options.text: Refer the client back to his cardiologist for further reassessment prior to initiating any self-care intervention, given his high post-activity fatigue rating.
options.incorrect_rationale: The client has an existing medical clearance for light activity, so deferring OT intervention pending another medical review is unnecessary and delays appropriate rehabilitation; post-activity fatigue is an expected finding that OT is specifically trained to address through energy conservation.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man is attending outpatient cardiac rehabilitation at a community hospital in British Columbia, 8 weeks post-coronary artery bypass graft (CABG). His cardiologist has cleared him for occupational activities up to 5 METs. He reports feeling "fully recovered" and is eager to resume splitting firewood and pushing his gas lawn mower — activities estimated at 6 to 7 METs. During a supervised 6-minute walk test, his heart rate reaches 128 bpm and his perceived exertion is 16 on the Borg RPE scale, indicating a current sustained functional capacity of approximately 3 to 4 METs. When the occupational therapist raises the issue of pacing, he becomes defensive and states he "knows his own body better than any chart." Which of the following represents the MOST appropriate OT approach at this stage of intervention?
questions.correct_rationale: Option B is best because it integrates three interdependent principles of cardiac OT practice: (1) graded activity — the client's current sustained capacity (3–4 METs) must serve as the starting point, with incremental advances of approximately 1 MET per week, not a direct progression to the 5-MET ceiling; (2) client-centred practice aligned with the CMOP-E and CPPF — collaborative goal-setting around the client's own occupational priorities (yard work, home maintenance) addresses his defensiveness more effectively than prescriptive restriction; and (3) energy conservation education — structured teaching on warning signs (angina, dyspnea, dizziness, diaphoresis) and the physiological rationale for pacing builds the client's self-monitoring capacity, which is essential when the OT is not present. The medically cleared ceiling of 5 METs defines the outer boundary of safe activity, not the immediate target; the OT's expertise lies in charting the graded occupational path between the client's present capacity and that ceiling.
questions.core_concept: In cardiac rehabilitation, occupational therapists apply graded activity by incrementally advancing occupational demands from the client's current functional capacity — not directly to the medically cleared maximum — using approximately 1-MET steps per week as tolerated. Client-centred collaborative goal-setting (CMOP-E/CPPF) and structured energy conservation education are the cornerstones of this approach, balancing autonomy with safe physiological progression.
questions.explain_differently: Imagine the cardiologist's 5-MET clearance as the speed limit on a highway — it tells you how fast you are legally permitted to go, but it does not mean you accelerate from a standstill straight to 100 km/h. The OT's role is to be the driving instructor who maps out a series of on-ramps: meaningful activities at today's safe speed, then slightly faster next week, and so on — while teaching the driver what the warning lights on the dashboard actually mean so he can manage the journey independently.
questions.topic: Cardiac/Pulmonary Rehabilitation — Energy Conservation and Graded Activity

options.label: A
options.text: Affirm the client's self-knowledge, introduce a symptom diary, and allow him to trial light yard work beginning with raking (approximately 3.5 to 4 METs) this week, monitoring for cardiac warning signs as the primary safeguard.
options.incorrect_rationale: Proceeding immediately to the upper boundary of current functional capacity — without a structured incremental progression plan or formal education — bypasses graded activity principles and creates unnecessary cardiac risk, even though raking falls within the cleared ceiling.

options.label: B
options.text: Advise the client to defer all yard work and home maintenance until the full 12-week cardiac rehabilitation program is complete, then conduct a formal exercise stress test before establishing any occupational goals.
options.incorrect_rationale: Withholding all goal-directed occupational engagement for weeks is unnecessarily restrictive, contradicts current evidence supporting early graded activity post-CABG, and is incongruent with the client-centred approach required by the CPPF and CMOP-E.

options.label: C
options.text: Refer the client immediately back to his cardiologist to obtain a revised MET prescription before proceeding with any occupational goal-setting, as initiating activity programming without updated medical clearance may exceed OT scope of practice in British Columbia.
options.incorrect_rationale: Valid medical clearance (up to 5 METs) already exists; deferring all goal-setting pending a new prescription misrepresents OT scope of practice and unnecessarily delays an evidence-based intervention the OT is qualified and expected to provide.

options.label: D
options.text: Collaborate with the client to identify meaningful short-term occupational goals within his current 3 to 4 MET capacity, structure a graded activity program with incremental MET advances (approximately 1 MET per week as tolerated), and provide explicit education on cardiac warning signs and the physiological rationale for progressive load advancement.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist working in a community oncology survivorship program sees a 58-year-old woman who completed chemotherapy and radiation for non-Hodgkin lymphoma nine months ago. She reports that persistent cancer-related fatigue (CRF) limits her to completing either her morning hygiene routine or preparing lunch — but not both — before needing several hours of rest. She is motivated to regain independence and manage her own schedule. Which intervention should the OT introduce FIRST?
questions.correct_rationale: Activity pacing — strategically scheduling tasks with deliberate rest breaks rather than pushing to exhaustion — is the foundational, first-line OT self-management strategy for cancer-related fatigue in survivorship. It directly addresses the client's stated occupational performance barrier (inability to complete both morning hygiene and meal preparation in the same morning) by matching energy expenditure to available capacity. Canadian occupational therapy practice, grounded in the CMOP-E, prioritizes enabling meaningful occupation through client-centred energy management education before introducing equipment or interdisciplinary referrals.
questions.core_concept: Cancer-related fatigue (CRF) is one of the most prevalent and disabling sequelae in oncology survivorship; the occupational therapist's primary, evidence-based role is teaching activity pacing and energy conservation strategies to enable clients to engage in valued occupations within their available energy envelope.
questions.explain_differently: Think of the client's daily energy like a bank account with a limited daily deposit. Right now she spends everything on one transaction (hygiene) and has nothing left for a second (meal prep). Activity pacing teaches her to make smaller withdrawals spread across the day — short task, planned rest, next task — so the account never hits zero before noon. That is the OT's job to teach first, before handing out equipment or sending her elsewhere.
questions.topic: Oncology and fatigue management in survivorship

options.label: A
options.text: Teach activity pacing by helping the client distribute valued tasks across the day with planned rest intervals between them.

options.label: B
options.text: Advise the client to rest completely on high-fatigue days and attempt tasks only when she feels fully recovered.
options.incorrect_rationale: Complete rest is contraindicated for CRF; current evidence shows that activity avoidance leads to deconditioning that worsens fatigue, creating a downward cycle rather than restoring function.

options.label: C
options.text: Provide a shower chair and long-handled bath sponge to reduce the physical effort required for morning hygiene.
options.incorrect_rationale: Assistive devices are appropriate adjuncts but address physical effort mechanically rather than teaching the client transferable self-management strategies; they would follow, not replace, pacing education.

options.label: D
options.text: Refer the client to physiotherapy for a graduated aerobic conditioning program to address deconditioning.
options.incorrect_rationale: Although exercise is evidence-supported for CRF management, a referral to physiotherapy is not the OT's first step; the OT's distinct role is occupational performance and energy conservation education, which should be initiated before interdisciplinary referral.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman was referred to an outpatient OT clinic by her oncologist eight months after completing chemotherapy and radiation for stage II breast cancer. She reports persistent cancer-related fatigue (CRF) rated 7/10, which prevents her from returning to her role as a part-time dental receptionist and from managing her household as she did before treatment. She states, "My doctor said treatment went well, so I keep pushing through my to-do list when I have energy, then I crash and spend two days in bed." The OT has completed an occupational performance assessment using the Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM) and identified fatigue management as the primary priority area. Which intervention approach should the OT implement first?
questions.correct_rationale: Current evidence consistently shows that cancer-related fatigue in survivorship is best addressed through an energy conservation and activity management approach that integrates two complementary strategies: pacing and activity scheduling (to break the push-crash cycle this client describes) alongside a graded, progressively increasing low-to-moderate aerobic activity program (which counteracts deconditioning and directly reduces CRF severity). OT is the regulated health professional with the occupational performance expertise to operationalize these strategies within the client's specific roles — receptionist work and home management — using a CMOP-E lens. Initiating ECAM aligns with CAOT competency expectations to apply evidence-based intervention at the occupational performance level and respects the client's self-identified priorities as captured by the COPM.
questions.core_concept: Cancer-related fatigue (CRF) in oncology survivorship is a distinct, evidence-based OT practice area. The recommended OT approach combines energy conservation and activity management (ECAM) — including pacing and occupational prioritization — with a graded physical activity program, rather than rest alone. OTs apply this within Canadian occupational performance frameworks (CMOP-E/CPPF) to restore engagement in valued roles.
questions.explain_differently: Think of CRF like a bank account that is chronically overdrawn: the client is making large, irregular withdrawals (pushing through), then the account empties completely (crash). ECAM teaches her to make small, predictable withdrawals every day while also slowly growing the account's balance through gentle exercise — so that over weeks, the account gets larger and the crashes stop happening. The OT's job is to map those withdrawals onto her actual roles (work, home) so the strategy fits her real life, not just a generic pamphlet.
questions.topic: Oncology and fatigue management in survivorship

options.label: A
options.text: Instruct the client to rest whenever fatigue is felt and defer all household and work activities until her energy levels stabilize naturally over the next several months.
options.incorrect_rationale: Extended rest and activity avoidance perpetuate the deconditioning cycle, worsen CRF over time, and directly contradict the evidence base for survivorship fatigue management.

options.label: B
options.text: Introduce an energy conservation and activity management (ECAM) program that combines activity pacing, prioritization of valued occupations, and a gradually graded low-to-moderate physical activity plan.

options.label: C
options.text: Advise the client to return immediately to her full work schedule and household routine, as resuming normal activity is the fastest way to rebuild stamina after cancer treatment.
options.incorrect_rationale: Abrupt return to full activity without pacing replicates the push-crash pattern the client already experiences, risks symptom exacerbation, and ignores the occupational analysis required for safe graded return.

options.label: D
options.text: Refer the client to a psychologist for cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) and defer all OT fatigue intervention until the psychological assessment is complete.
options.incorrect_rationale: While CBT has evidence for CRF and interprofessional referral may be appropriate, deferring OT intervention is unnecessary — OT can address occupational performance and fatigue management concurrently with psychological support, and delaying increases occupational role loss.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist working in an outpatient cancer survivorship clinic is assessing a 61-year-old woman who completed adjuvant chemotherapy for ovarian cancer 16 months ago. She scores 6.2 out of 10 on the Brief Fatigue Inventory, indicating severe cancer-related fatigue (CRF). She has withdrawn from her roles as a community choir director and part-time bookkeeper and now spends most waking hours resting. Her oncologist has provided written medical clearance for physical activity with no restrictions. During the OT interview she states, "I have learned that if I push myself I feel terrible the next day, so I rest as much as possible." The Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM) confirms large performance and satisfaction deficits across productivity and leisure. Her priority goal is to resume directing the choir rehearsals. Which of the following represents the MOST evidence-based and occupation-centred initial OT approach to managing her CRF?
questions.correct_rationale: Current high-quality evidence (including systematic reviews and CAOT-endorsed clinical practice guidelines) establishes that graded physical activity — not rest, not energy conservation alone — is the most effective intervention for persistent CRF in cancer survivorship. The client's avoidance of activity has created a deconditioning-fatigue spiral: inactivity worsens deconditioning, which lowers activity tolerance, which amplifies perceived fatigue. An OT applying CMOP-E targets the interaction among the person (reduced physical capacity, maladaptive illness beliefs), occupation (choir direction), and environment (survivorship context). Addressing the client's erroneous rest-equals-recovery belief through evidence-informed education is essential before she will engage in a graded program. Occupation-based goal-setting — anchoring progressions to choir rehearsal demands — ensures the activity grading is meaningful, motivating, and directly linked to her COPM priority, consistent with the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada (Practice domain: Evidence-Informed Practice; Occupational Enabling domain). Medical clearance has already been obtained, so no referral or deferral is required before initiating the program.
questions.core_concept: In cancer-related fatigue survivorship, the highest-evidence OT intervention is graded physical activity integrated with occupation-based goal-setting, not rest or energy conservation alone. OTs must recognize and correct the deconditioning-fatigue cycle and align the activity progression with the client's meaningful occupational goals, consistent with CMOP-E and the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada.
questions.explain_differently: Think of CRF like a muscle that atrophies from disuse: the client's instinct to rest feels logical, but it is like refusing to walk on a sprained ankle long after it has healed — the prolonged rest creates its own weakness. The OT's role is to act like a rehabilitation coach who designs a gradual return-to-play plan, starting small and building systematically toward the full activity, while also convincing the client that gentle progressive movement — not the bench — is the path back. Teaching energy conservation without this graded challenge is like giving the athlete a cane permanently instead of a rehabilitation plan.
questions.topic: Oncology and fatigue management in survivorship

options.label: A
options.text: Implement a comprehensive energy conservation and activity pacing program, teaching the client to distribute effort evenly throughout the day, use assistive devices, and simplify choir-directing tasks to reduce symptom burden.
options.incorrect_rationale: Energy conservation and pacing alone do not reverse the deconditioning that perpetuates CRF in survivorship; without graded activity, this approach risks reinforcing the avoidance cycle the client has already established.

options.label: B
options.text: Refer the client to physiotherapy for a formal exercise program first, and defer occupation-based OT intervention until physical reconditioning is established, to ensure safety before task-specific practice.
options.incorrect_rationale: Graded activity programming for CRF falls within OT scope of practice; sequential rather than concurrent service provision unnecessarily delays occupation-centred intervention and is inconsistent with interprofessional survivorship care standards.

options.label: C
options.text: Initiate a graded physical activity program integrated with occupation-based goal-setting, explicitly address the client's belief that rest reduces fatigue, and progressively build activity tolerance toward resumed choir direction using principles from the CMOP-E.
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct answer and does not require a distractor rationale.

options.label: D
options.text: Educate the client on sleep hygiene strategies, introduce a structured daytime rest schedule with planned nap periods, and prioritize high-value occupations for her peak-energy morning window to conserve reserves for choir rehearsal.
options.incorrect_rationale: Structured rest and sleep hygiene address sleep disturbance as a contributing factor but do not constitute a primary CRF intervention; building a rest-based schedule as the primary strategy reinforces behavioural deconditioning and contradicts current survivorship evidence.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist begins an initial assessment at a community mental health outpatient program. The client's referral documentation lists the legal name "Daniel." Upon introducing themselves, the client says, "I go by Maya and use she/her pronouns." What is the MOST appropriate immediate response by the occupational therapist?
questions.correct_rationale: Using the client's chosen name and correct pronouns immediately honours the client's autonomy and dignity, which are foundational obligations under the CAOT Code of Ethics (principles of respect for persons and justice) and the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada (client-centred, equity-informed practice). Affirmation does not require legal documentation; the client's self-identification is sufficient. Where clinical records allow a preferred-name field separate from the legal-name field — as many provincial electronic health record systems do — the OT should populate both, ensuring billing and legal fields remain accurate while day-to-day communication and clinical notes use Maya/she/her. This reflects both regulatory college expectations (e.g., COTO standards for respectful, non-discriminatory practice) and 2SLGBTQ+ affirming care frameworks endorsed by CAOT.
questions.core_concept: Affirming and client-centred practice for 2SLGBTQ+ clients requires that occupational therapists use a client's chosen name and correct pronouns from the first interaction, without requiring legal proof of identity change. This obligation flows from the CAOT Code of Ethics principles of respect for persons, non-discrimination, and justice, and from the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada emphasis on equity and cultural safety.
questions.explain_differently: Think of it like this: if a client told you they preferred to be called "Pat" rather than "Patricia," you would simply start using "Pat." A transgender or non-binary client sharing their name and pronouns is exactly the same kind of basic courtesy — it costs nothing, it is immediately within the OT's control, and getting it right from the first moment signals that the therapeutic space is safe and respectful.
questions.topic: 2SLGBTQ+ affirming and inclusive occupational therapy practice

options.label: A
options.text: Continue using the legal name Daniel in both verbal communication and all documentation until the client provides proof of a legal name change.
options.incorrect_rationale: Requiring legal documentation before using a client's chosen name is unnecessarily burdensome, violates client dignity, and is inconsistent with person-centred and 2SLGBTQ+ affirming practice under the CAOT Code of Ethics.

options.label: B
options.text: Use the legal name Daniel in all verbal interactions to avoid confusion with other team members who have already seen the referral.
options.incorrect_rationale: Prioritizing administrative convenience over the client's stated identity is a form of misgendering that undermines therapeutic alliance and contradicts the OT's duty to provide respectful, inclusive care.

options.label: C
options.text: Defer the decision about which name and pronouns to use until consulting with the interdisciplinary team so that all providers communicate consistently.
options.incorrect_rationale: Deferring affirmation of a client's stated identity to a team process is unnecessary and risks immediate harm; the OT can use correct name and pronouns right away while coordinating team communication as a secondary step.

options.label: D
options.text: Address the client as Maya using she/her pronouns immediately, and update the working documentation to reflect this name and pronouns going forward.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist is conducting a functional mobility assessment with a 16-year-old transgender adolescent (he/him pronouns) admitted to a pediatric rehabilitation unit following orthopedic surgery. The client's parent is present and consistently addresses the client using his birth name and she/her pronouns throughout the session. The client becomes visibly withdrawn, stops responding to prompts, and disengages from the assessment tasks. Which action by the OT is most consistent with 2SLGBTQ+ affirming practice and the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada?
questions.correct_rationale: In most Canadian provinces, adolescents who demonstrate capacity — including under the mature minor doctrine and, in Ontario, under the Health Care Consent Act — hold the right to direct the use and disclosure of their own health information, including gender identity. The OT's fiduciary and ethical obligations under the CAOT Code of Ethics (respect for autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence) run primarily to the client, not the family. Checking in privately accomplishes three things: it restores a safe therapeutic environment so occupational engagement can resume; it allows the OT to use affirming language in all subsequent interactions; and it ensures any disclosure to the parent occurs only with the client's informed direction, consistent with provincial privacy legislation such as PHIPA in Ontario. This approach is also aligned with the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada, which require culturally safe, client-centred, and equity-oriented practice.
questions.core_concept: 2SLGBTQ+ affirming OT practice requires centring client autonomy over disclosure of gender identity. A capable adolescent client controls who receives information about their gender identity; the OT's role is to establish a safe therapeutic space and act on the client's direction — not to disclose without consent, not to collude with misgendering, and not to pathologize the resulting occupational disengagement.
questions.explain_differently: Think of gender identity disclosure the way you would any sensitive clinical finding: you would never share a patient's diagnosis with their family without the patient's consent, even if it would make team communication easier. The same rule applies here. The OT's job is to step back, create a private moment, and ask the client what he wants — then follow his lead. The parent's presence in the room does not override the client's right to decide who learns what about his identity.
questions.topic: 2SLGBTQ+ affirming and inclusive occupational therapy practice

options.label: A
options.text: Pause the assessment, find a moment to speak privately with the client, ask how he wishes to be addressed during therapy, and clarify whether he consents to his parent being informed of his gender identity before the next session.
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct answer and is not a distractor.

options.label: B
options.text: Continue using the parent's preferred name and pronouns for the remainder of the session to preserve the therapeutic relationship with the family unit.
options.incorrect_rationale: Prioritizing the parent's preferences over the client's gender identity mirrors the harm being done and abandons the OT's primary ethical obligation to the client.

options.label: C
options.text: Immediately inform the parent that the client uses he/him pronouns and a different name, explaining this information is clinically necessary for the rehabilitation team to use consistently.
options.incorrect_rationale: Disclosing a client's gender identity to a third party without the client's consent constitutes outing, removes the client's autonomy over sensitive personal information, and may create safety risks at home.

options.label: D
options.text: Document the client's withdrawal as decreased participation and submit a social work referral to address underlying family conflict.
options.incorrect_rationale: Attributing the client's disengagement to family conflict rather than to the relational barriers caused by misgendering fails to identify the actual cause of occupational disruption and delays affirming care.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist (OT) works in a long-term care home (LTCH) in Ontario. A 78-year-old resident — a transgender woman named Maria who transitioned 15 years ago and uses she/her pronouns — has mild cognitive impairment but retains decision-making capacity for personal care. Maria has told the OT that being addressed by her correct name and pronouns is central to her sense of self, her engagement in daily occupations, and her emotional well-being. Her adult son, who is listed only as an emergency contact and has not been designated her substitute decision maker, approaches the OT and demands that all staff revert to Maria's birth name and he/him pronouns, citing the family's religious and cultural values. He threatens to escalate to the facility administrator if the OT does not comply. What is the OT's MOST appropriate response?
questions.correct_rationale: Maria retains decision-making capacity for personal care; therefore she — not her son — holds the right to determine how she is addressed. Under Ontario's Health Care Consent Act, emergency contact status confers no authority over personal care decisions for a capable person: only a lawfully designated substitute decision maker may act on another's behalf, and only when capacity is absent. The CAOT Code of Ethics obligates OTs to respect client autonomy and human dignity, and 2SLGBTQ+ affirming practice recognizes that correct name and pronoun use is not a preference but a clinical and ethical imperative with direct links to occupational engagement and mental health. The OT explains these professional and legal parameters respectfully to the son — an educational response that may reduce future conflict — continues services without interruption to avoid occupational harm, and documents the interaction and clinical reasoning, fulfilling the accountability expectations of the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada.
questions.core_concept: When a 2SLGBTQ+ client retains decision-making capacity, affirming their gender identity (including preferred name and pronouns) is a professional and ethical obligation under the CAOT Code of Ethics; an emergency contact has no substitute decision-making authority under provincial law (e.g., Ontario's Health Care Consent Act), so family preferences cannot override a capable client's right to self-determination in personal care.
questions.explain_differently: Think of Maria's preferred name and pronouns the same way you would think of her right to choose what she eats or whether she participates in a group activity — because she has capacity, those are her decisions, full stop. Her son being listed as an emergency contact is like being the person called if she falls: it does not give him a vote in how she lives her daily life. The OT's job is to hold that boundary clearly and kindly, keep providing care, and write down exactly why.
questions.topic: 2SLGBTQ+ affirming and inclusive occupational therapy practice — capacity, substitute decision-making authority, and client autonomy in long-term care

options.label: A
options.text: Temporarily defer to the son's request to preserve family engagement while arranging an urgent social work referral, documenting that the family raised cultural and religious concerns.
options.incorrect_rationale: Deferring to an emergency contact who holds no substitute decision-making authority directly violates Maria's legally protected autonomy and constitutes a failure of 2SLGBTQ+ affirming practice, regardless of family motivation.

options.label: B
options.text: Continue using Maria's preferred name and pronouns in all care contexts, explain to the son that Maria retains decision-making capacity and therefore has the right to self-identify, and document the conversation, the OT's professional reasoning, and Maria's expressed occupational priorities.

options.label: C
options.text: Suspend all occupational therapy services and escalate immediately to the facility administrator and ethics committee, as a family conflict of this nature exceeds the OT's scope of practice to resolve independently.
options.incorrect_rationale: Suspending services causes direct occupational harm to Maria without justification; the OT has sufficient ethical and regulatory grounding — including the CAOT Code of Ethics and the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada — to act without first withdrawing care.

options.label: D
options.text: Use Maria's preferred name and pronouns only in private one-on-one sessions to affirm her identity, while accommodating the son's request in group and family-facing settings to respect cultural and religious values.
options.incorrect_rationale: Applying inconsistent practices across care settings is not affirming care; it exposes Maria to predictable misgendering harm, undermines her dignity in communal occupation, and compromises the OT's professional accountability and integrity.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist in a community health centre is beginning an initial session with a 38-year-old woman referred following recent separation from an abusive partner. The client appears guarded, avoids eye contact, and says she is unsure whether she wants to participate in any programs. Which of the following responses BEST reflects trauma-informed care principles?
questions.correct_rationale: Option B reflects the foundational trauma-informed care principles of safety, trustworthiness, and empowerment. Intimate partner violence frequently involves systematic coercive control that strips survivors of agency; restoring a sense of choice and transparency—even over something as small as what is discussed today—begins to rebuild psychological safety. The Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada (2021) emphasize collaborative, person-centred practice in which the client directs goal-setting. Offering explicit choice about pace and content signals that the therapeutic relationship is fundamentally different from the abusive one, making genuine engagement possible.
questions.core_concept: Trauma-informed care for IPV survivors prioritizes re-establishing physical and psychological safety and restoring the client's sense of control and autonomy before advancing any occupational therapy process. This aligns with both the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada (person-centred, collaborative practice) and the CAOT Code of Ethics (respect for autonomy; non-maleficence).
questions.explain_differently: Imagine someone who has spent years living in a house where every decision was made for them and every room had a lock they could not open. On day one with the OT, the most powerful thing you can do is hand them the keys—let them choose which door to open, or whether to open any at all. Getting paperwork or assessments done can wait; giving back a sense of control cannot.
questions.topic: Trauma-informed care for survivors of intimate partner violence

options.label: A
options.text: Administer a standardized occupational performance measure to establish a baseline before addressing the client's hesitation.
options.incorrect_rationale: Proceeding directly to formal assessment without first establishing safety and trust can feel controlling and retraumatizing for an IPV survivor, and it prioritizes OT data-gathering over the client's immediate emotional needs.

options.label: B
options.text: Encourage the client to share details of the abusive relationship so the occupational therapist can fully understand the impact on her daily occupations.
options.incorrect_rationale: Prompting an IPV survivor to recount trauma details early in the relationship risks retraumatization, violates the principle of safety, and exceeds what is necessary at an initial contact.

options.label: C
options.text: Acknowledge the client's hesitation, clearly explain that she can set the pace and decline any question, and ask what—if anything—she would find helpful today.

options.label: D
options.text: Explain that occupational therapy can only begin once the client is ready to commit to a full intervention plan and attend all scheduled sessions.
options.incorrect_rationale: Placing conditions on participation undermines client autonomy and mirrors the coercive control pattern the client has already experienced, directly contradicting trauma-informed and person-centred practice.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist (OT) working in a community mental health clinic in Ontario is conducting the third session with a 34-year-old woman referred for low mood and significantly reduced occupational engagement. The client discloses that her partner has been physically assaulting her at home. She asks the OT to keep this private, explains she is not yet ready to leave the relationship, and expresses fear that involving authorities would escalate the danger. The client is oriented, communicates clearly, and demonstrates capacity to make decisions about her care. What is the OT's BEST initial response?
questions.correct_rationale: Trauma-informed care for survivors of intimate partner violence (IPV) is grounded in the core principles of safety, trustworthiness, choice, collaboration, and empowerment — all reflected in the CAOT Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada (Practice Domain: Occupational Therapy Process; Enabling Occupation). Because this client has demonstrated decision-making capacity and has clearly expressed her preferences and fears, the OT is ethically obligated to respect her autonomy and right to self-determination (CAOT Code of Ethics). Forcing action — arranging a shelter, contacting police, or sharing information without consent — without the client's agreement can increase her immediate danger (abusers often escalate when they sense loss of control), rupture the therapeutic alliance, and re-traumatize the survivor. The trauma-informed approach requires the OT to validate the disclosure non-judgmentally, explore what matters most to this client occupationally and personally, and offer information about safety planning and community resources in a collaborative, unhurried way, so that any steps taken are ones she chooses and is prepared for.
questions.core_concept: Trauma-informed occupational therapy practice with IPV survivors requires centering the five principles of safety, trustworthiness, choice, collaboration, and empowerment (aligned with CAOT Competencies and the CMOP-E's focus on person-environment-occupation fit). For a competent adult, the OT's ethical duty to respect autonomy and self-determination (CAOT Code of Ethics) takes precedence over paternalistic action; sustainable safety planning emerges when the client, not the clinician, directs the pace and nature of change.
questions.explain_differently: Picture the OT as a knowledgeable guide standing at a crossroads with a client who has just shared something terrifying. A trauma-informed guide does not grab the client's arm and pull her down one path — that can make her stumble or run back to what feels familiar. Instead, the guide stands beside her, names the paths clearly, holds a lantern so she can see the options, and then walks whichever direction she chooses, at her speed. That collaborative, non-coercive stance is what keeps her safer over time, because it builds trust and preserves the relationship through which real change becomes possible.
questions.topic: Trauma-informed care and intimate partner violence — client autonomy, confidentiality, and scope of mandatory reporting in Canadian community practice

options.label: A
options.text: Contact the local women's shelter immediately and arrange emergency housing on the client's behalf, as her physical safety is the overriding clinical concern.
options.incorrect_rationale: Arranging housing without the client's consent is paternalistic, overrides the autonomy of a capable adult, and can paradoxically increase danger by triggering the abuser; trauma-informed practice requires following the survivor's lead rather than imposing action.

options.label: B
options.text: Inform the client that Ontario law requires you to report the abuse to police, because intimate partner violence constitutes a criminal offence.
options.incorrect_rationale: No Ontario statute (nor any Canadian provincial or territorial law) imposes a mandatory reporting duty on health professionals for intimate partner violence disclosed by a competent adult; mandatory reporting obligations apply to children under the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017, and to residents of long-term care homes under the Long-Term Care Homes Act, 2007 — not to competent adults in community settings.

options.label: C
options.text: Document the disclosure in the health record and notify the supervising physician without delay, as they hold ultimate responsibility for the client's safety plan.
options.incorrect_rationale: Sharing the client's personal health information with the physician without her consent would breach confidentiality under PHIPA; while PHIPA does permit discretionary disclosure without consent when there is a risk of serious bodily harm, this is a carefully considered professional judgment — not an automatic notification triggered by any IPV disclosure — and it does not override the OT's primary obligation to respond in a trauma-informed, client-centred manner.

options.label: D
options.text: Acknowledge the disclosure with compassion, affirm the client's courage in sharing, and collaboratively explore her goals, priorities, and safety options at a pace she leads.

questions.stem: An OT employed by a community health centre in Ontario is conducting a home visit with Aisha, a 34-year-old survivor of intimate partner violence who recently relocated to a subsidized apartment after leaving a shelter. Aisha discloses that her former partner has obtained her new address and she is now too frightened to leave her unit, severely limiting her occupational participation. Before the visit notes are entered, Aisha explicitly requests that her address not be recorded in the centre's electronic health record (EHR), stating she fears her former partner may access it through unofficial channels. The OT knows that COTO requires accurate and complete client records and that PHIPA mandates privacy safeguards on the EHR. Which response BEST reflects a trauma-informed approach while upholding professional obligations?
questions.correct_rationale: Trauma-informed care with IPV survivors requires validating the client's safety concern as clinically legitimate rather than subordinating it to administrative routine. Restricted-access or sensitivity flags are available in many Canadian EHR systems and allow location information to be shielded from broader staff access while preserving a record for clinical continuity — a mechanism that simultaneously honours PHIPA's principle of proportionate privacy protection and COTO's documentation standards. Consulting the privacy officer operationalizes this institutional tool and demonstrates the trustworthiness central to trauma-informed practice. Documenting the safety rationale for any deviation fulfills COTO's accountability requirements. Critically, the OT involves Aisha in every decision step, reinforcing her agency — a core therapeutic goal in IPV recovery under a trauma-informed, CMOP-E–aligned framework that treats the compromised physical environment (safety in the home) as a direct barrier to occupational performance.
questions.core_concept: In trauma-informed OT practice with IPV survivors, a client's safety concerns about documentation and disclosure carry clinical and ethical weight and must be addressed through collaborative use of available institutional privacy mechanisms — such as restricted-access record flags and privacy officer consultation — rather than forcing a binary choice between full standard documentation and omission. COTO documentation obligations and client physical safety are not inherently in conflict when the OT actively engages organizational tools and transparently documents clinical rationale for any adaptation.
questions.explain_differently: Imagine a hospital applying a sensitivity flag to a patient's chart so that only the direct care team — not every clerk in the building — can see the address. Trauma-informed OT uses exactly that logic: the OT does not tear up the chart (omit everything) or ignore the fear (just document and move on). Instead, they find the dial between 'fully open record' and 'no record at all' by activating privacy controls the system already provides, looping in the privacy officer who knows those controls best, and keeping Aisha in the driver's seat at every step. Her sense of control over who knows where she lives is not a bureaucratic inconvenience — it is a direct occupational therapy intervention, because regaining control over personal information is part of recovery from intimate partner violence.
questions.topic: Trauma-informed documentation and privacy decision-making for survivors of intimate partner violence in Canadian community OT practice

options.label: A
options.text: Acknowledge Aisha's concern as clinically valid, collaborate with her to determine whether the EHR supports a restricted-access flag on location information, consult the centre's privacy officer before entering any identifying address, and document the safety rationale for any departure from standard practice.

options.label: B
options.text: Reassure Aisha that the EHR is secured under PHIPA, document her full address as required by COTO standards, and explain that incomplete records could compromise continuity of care.
options.incorrect_rationale: Citing existing system security without exploring enhanced protections dismisses a specific, credible safety threat and violates the trauma-informed principle of trustworthiness, which requires transparent, client-centred problem-solving rather than institutional reassurance.

options.label: C
options.text: Omit the address from the EHR entirely, record only 'address withheld at client request,' and proceed with the visit without further discussion of the documentation concern.
options.incorrect_rationale: Unilaterally omitting required documentation without consulting the privacy officer or exploring available alternatives fails COTO's accuracy standards and resolves the tension without collaborative problem-solving, undermining the trauma-informed principle of shared decision-making.

options.label: D
options.text: Defer recording the address until Aisha has obtained a court-issued peace bond or protection order, then complete the documentation once a formal legal safety measure is in place.
options.incorrect_rationale: Conditioning documentation on the client securing legal relief creates an indeterminate and burdensome delay, shifts institutional responsibility onto the survivor, and fails to address the immediate safety and documentation concern through available clinical and organizational channels.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist working at a community settlement agency is seeing a recently arrived Eritrean refugee who reports feeling unable to participate in local programs and social groups because all written program information is available only in English and no interpretation services are offered. Which action BEST reflects the occupational therapist's role in addressing the occupational justice dimensions of this situation?
questions.correct_rationale: The Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada (2021) explicitly identify advocacy as a core OT competency, and the CAOT Code of Ethics directs OTs to promote equitable access to occupational participation. Within the CMOP-E, the absence of language-accessible information and interpretation represents an institutional environmental barrier preventing occupational engagement. Advocating for translated materials and interpretation services directly targets this barrier, enabling the client to participate in meaningful social and community occupations — an occupational justice imperative when a systemic, not a personal, factor is the primary obstacle.
questions.core_concept: Occupational justice requires OTs to identify and address environmental — particularly institutional — barriers that prevent equitable occupational participation. Per the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada (2021) and the CAOT Code of Ethics, advocacy at the program or systems level is a legitimate and expected OT role, especially when newcomers or refugees face language-based exclusion from community life.
questions.explain_differently: Think of language access as the equivalent of a wheelchair ramp: if a building has no ramp, the correct response is not to tell the wheelchair user to come back when they can manage stairs — it is to advocate for the ramp to be built. For a newcomer, translated materials and interpretation services are that ramp. The OT's job is to help build access, not to wait for the client to overcome a systemic obstacle on her own.
questions.topic: Newcomer and refugee occupational adaptation and access barriers

options.label: A
options.text: Advise the client to delay program participation until she has developed sufficient English proficiency.
options.incorrect_rationale: This places the burden of adaptation entirely on the client rather than addressing the institutional barrier, which contradicts occupational justice and enablement principles.

options.label: B
options.text: Advocate with program administrators for translated materials and trained interpretation services to enable equitable access to programs.

options.label: C
options.text: Refer the client to a social worker, as systemic access barriers fall outside the scope of occupational therapy practice.
options.incorrect_rationale: Advocacy to reduce environmental barriers to occupational participation is explicitly within OT scope per the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada; it is not solely a social-work function.

options.label: D
options.text: Document the language barrier as a contraindication to occupational therapy service at this time and close the file.
options.incorrect_rationale: A language barrier is not a contraindication to OT service; it signals a need for enabling supports such as interpretation, and closing the file would abandon the client unjustifiably.

questions.stem: An OT working in a community health centre is providing services to a 38-year-old woman who arrived in Canada as a government-assisted refugee from Somalia ten months ago. She has limited English proficiency. The OT has conducted two sessions using a telephone interpreter service; during both sessions the client became visibly tense when discussing daily roles and family routines, offering only brief, vague responses. She has since cancelled two follow-up appointments, citing "family obligations." Which action BEST addresses the occupational participation barriers this client is experiencing?
questions.correct_rationale: The CMOP-E situates occupational performance at the intersection of person, occupation, and environment; institutional and cultural environmental factors — including the format and perceived safety of interpreter services — directly shape whether a client can engage in the therapeutic process. The CPPF requires the OT to analyse contextual enablers and barriers at each practice process point, not only at assessment. For refugee clients, telephone interpreter services routed through community networks raise legitimate concerns about confidentiality given lived experiences of surveillance and persecution; these concerns produce the observable tension and withdrawal. An accredited language service with a certified confidentiality protocol, combined with a flexible location (home visit or community site), directly removes two identified institutional barriers. This approach reflects the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada (2021) expectations under Practice Management and Leadership — specifically, advocating for conditions that enable equitable access — and the CAOT Code of Ethics principle of justice, which requires OTs to reduce inequitable barriers to participation.
questions.core_concept: Under the CMOP-E and the CPPF, the OT is responsible for identifying and modifying environmental (cultural, social, and institutional) factors that restrict occupational engagement. For newcomer and refugee clients, culturally safe and confidentiality-assured interpreter services are an environmental enabler, not an optional accommodation; addressing this barrier is a prerequisite to any meaningful occupational assessment or intervention.
questions.explain_differently: Imagine trying to have a private medical conversation in a crowded room where you suspect a neighbour might be listening. You would not open up — not because you do not want help, but because the room itself feels unsafe. The telephone interpreter line is that crowded room for this client. Changing the interpreter arrangement and the physical setting changes the room, making it possible for the client to speak freely. The OT's job here is to fix the environment before expecting the person to perform differently within it.
questions.topic: Newcomer and Refugee Occupational Adaptation and Access Barriers

options.label: A
options.text: Switch to standardized, non-verbal assessment tools so that language is no longer a barrier to completing the occupational profile.
