Leading the meeting without confirming this framework risks either wrongfully overriding a capable client's autonomy or inadvertently bypassing the designated SDM, both of which breach the OT's ethical and professional obligations under the CAOT Code of Ethics and the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada (2021), which require OTs to uphold clients' rights and navigate interprofessional and family dynamics within the applicable legal and ethical framework.
questions.core_concept: When facilitating discharge planning for a client with cognitive impairment, the OT must determine decision-making capacity for the specific decision at hand before proceeding, because provincial health care consent legislation (e.g., the Health Care Consent Act) governs whether the client or a substitute decision-maker — such as a holder of a continuing power of attorney for personal care — holds legal authority to consent. This determination is the ethical and legal foundation on which all subsequent collaborative planning rests, consistent with the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada (2021).
questions.explain_differently: Imagine you are about to negotiate the terms of a contract but no one has checked whose name is authorized to sign it. If you start presenting risk data, weighing family opinions, or even honouring the client's stated wishes without knowing whether she or her daughter holds legal decision-making authority for this choice, you are building the entire plan on an unstable foundation. The capacity question is the keystone of the arch — everything else (whose voice governs, how risk is framed, what consent looks like) depends on getting that one structural piece right before laying anything else on top of it.
questions.topic: COMM_COLLAB — Leading a family meeting about a high-risk discharge

options.label: A
options.text: Clarify and confirm whether the patient has been formally determined to lack decision-making capacity for this specific discharge decision, and explicitly establish the substitute decision-maker's role and obligations before any planning proceeds.

options.label: B
options.text: Invite the patient to open the meeting by sharing her discharge goals and describing what daily life at home would look like for her.
options.incorrect_rationale: Privileging the patient's narrative is client-centred and ultimately important, but proceeding without first establishing capacity and legal decision-making authority risks conducting the entire meeting on the wrong governance framework.

options.label: C
options.text: Present the OT's home assessment findings — including fall hazards and unmet care needs — so all participants have a shared factual foundation before discussion begins.
options.incorrect_rationale: Sharing objective assessment findings is necessary but premature as the opening move; who holds authority to act on those findings depends entirely on the capacity determination that has not yet been confirmed.

options.label: D
options.text: Facilitate an open family discussion between the daughter and son to identify areas of agreement and work toward a consensus position on discharge destination.
options.incorrect_rationale: Brokering sibling consensus is inappropriate because discharge consent is not a family vote; if the patient lacks capacity, the continuing power of attorney for personal care confers legal authority on the daughter alone, making consensus-building secondary to clarifying that framework.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist employed at a long-term care home completes a handwritten progress note in the paper-based health record following a dressing-skills session with a resident. The following morning, while preparing for team rounds, she reviews the chart and notices she recorded June 10 as the session date when the session actually took place on June 11. Which of the following is the most appropriate action to correct this documentation error?
questions.correct_rationale: Drawing a single line through the error — while keeping the original entry legible — and adding the corrected date, the author's initials, and the date of correction is the universally accepted method for amending errors in paper-based health records in Canadian practice. This approach satisfies two concurrent obligations: (1) it preserves the unaltered original entry, demonstrating transparency and preventing any appearance of falsification, which is required under provincial health records legislation and the standards of practice of regulatory colleges such as COTO; and (2) it creates a clear, attributable audit trail that shows precisely what was changed, by whom, and when. The note therefore remains legally defensible and the chain of custody of the record is unbroken.
questions.core_concept: Canadian regulatory college standards (e.g., COTO, ACOTRO member colleges) and provincial health records legislation require that errors in paper health records be corrected by striking through with a single line, preserving legibility of the original, and adding the correction with the author's initials and date — thereby maintaining a transparent, unbroken, and legally defensible record of care.
questions.explain_differently: Think of correcting a health record the same way a bank teller corrects a signed cheque: you never cover the mistake, you cross it out neatly so anyone can still read what was originally written, write the right information next to it, and sign and date it. That way, if the record is ever reviewed in a legal or regulatory proceeding, it is absolutely clear that nothing was hidden — only honestly corrected.
questions.topic: Documentation standards and defensible progress note correction in Canadian OT practice

options.label: A
options.text: Apply correction fluid (White-Out) over the incorrect date, write June 11 above it, and proceed with rounds.
options.incorrect_rationale: Using correction fluid is never acceptable in health record documentation because it permanently conceals the original entry, making the record potentially fraudulent and undermining its legal integrity under provincial health records standards.

options.label: B
options.text: Draw a single line through the incorrect date so it remains legible, write June 11 beside the correction, then add her initials and the current date.

options.label: C
options.text: Remove the page containing the error from the chart and rewrite the entire progress note with the correct date on a new page.
options.incorrect_rationale: Removing or destroying a page from an official health record constitutes falsification or destruction of a legal document, which violates provincial health records legislation and a regulatory college's professional conduct requirements.

options.label: D
options.text: Write a late entry on today's date, note that the session occurred on June 11, and cross-reference the original note without altering it.
options.incorrect_rationale: A late entry is the appropriate mechanism when an entire note was omitted at the time of care, not when correcting a minor transcription error within an existing note; using it here leaves the incorrect date uncorrected in the original entry and creates unnecessary redundancy.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist (OT) working in an inpatient rehabilitation unit completes a session with a 72-year-old client recovering from a right hip arthroplasty. The client demonstrates improved sit-to-stand transfers but declines the OT's recommendation to use a raised toilet seat at home upon discharge, stating, "I've managed without gadgets my whole life." The OT reviews the clinical rationale and associated risks with the client, who acknowledges understanding but maintains their decision. Which progress note entry BEST satisfies provincial regulatory college documentation standards for a record that is accurate, complete, and defensible?
questions.correct_rationale: Option B satisfies provincial regulatory college standards for a defensible progress note on five counts: (1) it records objective, quantifiable functional performance (assist level, specific cue type); (2) it names the precise recommendation and its clinical rationale, establishing the OT's professional reasoning; (3) it captures the client's verbatim words — a direct quote that documents the exercise of autonomous decision-making and is far more defensible than a paraphrase; (4) it confirms the client demonstrated understanding of the disclosed risks, satisfying the informed refusal standard upheld under provincial health care consent legislation (e.g., Ontario's Health Care Consent Act); and (5) it states a clear forward plan, including team communication and reassessment. Each element contributes to a record that is accurate, complete, and protects both client rights and OT accountability should the entry ever be reviewed by the regulatory college, a coroner, or a court.
questions.core_concept: Canadian provincial regulatory colleges (e.g., COTO, COTNS, COTBC) require progress notes to be accurate, complete, timely, and objective. When a client exercises their right to refuse a recommendation, documentation must capture the specific intervention offered, the clinical rationale, the client's own words where possible, evidence that risks were disclosed and understood, and the OT's response — fulfilling both the duty to inform under provincial consent law and the professional accountability standard of the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada (Enabling Practice domain).
questions.explain_differently: Picture the progress note as your sworn witness statement, written at the time of the event, to be read aloud at a regulatory college hearing two years from now when no one can ask you questions. The note has to tell the whole story on its own: what you saw the client do (with a number attached), what you recommended and exactly why, what the client said back to you in their own words, that they understood what could go wrong, and what you did next. Option B is the only entry that tells that complete story — every other option leaves a gap a lawyer or investigator could walk through.
questions.topic: COMM_COLLAB — Documentation Standards and Defensible Progress Notes

options.label: A
options.text: Client educated on benefits of raised toilet seat post-hip arthroplasty. Client non-compliant with equipment recommendations. Discharge planning ongoing. Risks discussed.
options.incorrect_rationale: The term 'non-compliant' is stigmatizing and discouraged by Canadian regulatory colleges, and the entry omits objective functional data, the client's direct words, and any documented evidence of informed decision-making.

options.label: B
options.text: Client progressing with mobility. Equipment needs discussed. Client verbalized understanding of discharge recommendations. Follow-up planned to address outstanding goals.
options.incorrect_rationale: This entry is vague, omits documentation of the client's refusal of a specific recommendation, and could be read as implying the client agreed to the plan — constituting an incomplete and potentially misleading record.

options.label: C
options.text: Client performed sit-to-stand from standard-height chair with supervision and 1 verbal cue for hip precautions. Raised toilet seat recommended; rationale reviewed with client (hip dislocation risk, fall risk given standard toilet height post-arthroplasty). Client declined, stating, 'I've managed without gadgets my whole life.' Client verbalized understanding of associated risks and maintained preference. Discharge team informed of client's decision. OT to reassess prior to discharge.

options.label: D
options.text: Discussed adaptive equipment needs with client. Client expressed reluctance regarding toilet seat recommendation. Safety concerns noted. Informed consent obtained for discharge plan. Discharge planning in progress.
options.incorrect_rationale: Stating 'informed consent obtained' is factually inaccurate — the client declined the recommendation — making this entry legally and ethically problematic and potentially misleading to other team members.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist (OT) works on an inpatient stroke rehabilitation unit in Ontario. Using the Canadian Practice Process Framework (CPPF), the OT completed a thorough assessment and identified the client's top priorities as returning to meal preparation and grocery shopping. At the weekly interprofessional team meeting, the physiotherapist states that a cooking goal is "not realistic for this admission" and recommends the team focus exclusively on achieving 200-metre ambulation before discharge. The client, who is present, reaffirms that cooking independently is essential to his quality of life. The OT respectfully disagrees with deferring the occupational goal. What is the most appropriate action for the OT to take at this point?
questions.correct_rationale: The Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada (2021) position interprofessional collaboration and client-centred practice as foundational competencies. When a goal conflict arises, the OT's professional obligation is to advocate for the client's identified occupational priorities while engaging constructively with team members — not to capitulate, bypass, or escalate prematurely. Facilitating a transparent, structured discussion that places the client's voice alongside each discipline's clinical reasoning is consistent with shared decision-making: it honours the client's autonomy, draws on each team member's expertise, and produces a plan the whole team can commit to. This approach also reflects the CAOT Code of Ethics principle of beneficence, ensuring that occupationally meaningful goals are not silently discarded without deliberation.
questions.core_concept: Interprofessional shared decision-making requires OTs to transparently advocate for the client's occupational priorities and to engage other team members in collaborative dialogue — rather than deferring, escalating prematurely, or acting unilaterally — in order to reach a consensus plan that is both clinically sound and client-centred, as outlined in the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada (2021) and the CAOT Code of Ethics.
questions.explain_differently: Think of the interprofessional team as a roundtable, not a hierarchy. When two disciplines see the same client differently, the first move is to pull everyone — including the client — to the table, lay all the cards face-up, and negotiate a plan together. The OT's job is to make sure the client's occupational card stays visible in that negotiation, not to fold quietly or call in a referee before the conversation has even happened.
questions.topic: Resolving an interprofessional disagreement on goals via shared decision-making

options.label: A
options.text: Defer to the physiotherapist's clinical opinion and agree to remove the cooking goal from the team plan for this admission.
options.incorrect_rationale: Deferring without discussion abandons the OT's professional duty to advocate for client-identified occupational goals and silences the client's expressed priorities, which contradicts both client-centred practice and the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada.

options.label: B
options.text: Escalate the disagreement to the unit manager immediately so that leadership can determine which discipline's goals will take precedence.
options.incorrect_rationale: Immediate escalation to management bypasses the collaborative conflict-resolution process that interprofessional practice standards expect team members to attempt first, and it positions the disagreement as a hierarchical power issue rather than a clinical dialogue.

options.label: C
options.text: Document the occupational therapy goals independently in the client record and proceed with cooking-focused intervention without further team discussion.
options.incorrect_rationale: Proceeding unilaterally without resolving the team disagreement undermines coordinated care, risks conflicting messages to the client, and does not fulfil the OT's obligation to collaborate within the interprofessional team.

options.label: D
options.text: Facilitate a structured team discussion that transparently presents the client's occupational priorities alongside the physiotherapy findings, inviting all team members and the client to co-develop a shared, realistic plan.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist (OT) on an inpatient rehabilitation unit has completed a comprehensive assessment of Mr. Bernard Tremblay, a 72-year-old francophone client recovering from a left hemisphere stroke. Using the Canadian Practice Process Framework (CPPF), the OT identifies that Mr. Tremblay's primary occupational priority is returning home to resume meal preparation independently. At the weekly interprofessional team meeting, the physiatrist proposes that independent safe ambulation on household surfaces is the sole discharge criterion and declines to include instrumental activities of daily living (IADLs) in the rehabilitation goals, stating that ADL function "can be addressed in the community." Mr. Tremblay has told the OT he feels excluded from decisions about his care. Which action BEST reflects the OT's professional responsibility to resolve this interprofessional disagreement?
questions.correct_rationale: The Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada (2021) identify Collaborative Practice and Client-Centred Practice as foundational competencies, requiring OTs to actively incorporate the client's voice and occupational evidence into interprofessional goal-setting rather than yielding or acting unilaterally. The CPPF operationalizes shared decision-making as a structured, iterative process in which the client is a primary participant — not a passive recipient of team decisions. By inviting Mr. Tremblay to participate directly and presenting objective assessment evidence, the OT fulfills dual obligations: advocating for occupational participation as a health outcome and modelling accountable, evidence-informed interprofessional collaboration. This approach addresses the disagreement at the earliest appropriate venue (the team meeting) without bypassing dialogue or fragmenting care.
questions.core_concept: The Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada (2021) establish that OTs must exercise accountable, evidence-informed advocacy within interprofessional teams by centering the client's occupational priorities and engaging in structured shared decision-making — not deferring silently, working in isolation, or escalating prematurely. The CPPF frames goal-setting as a collaborative, client-inclusive process in which the OT's unique contribution is translating occupational performance evidence into team-level decision-making.
questions.explain_differently: Picture the OT as Mr. Tremblay's occupational translator at the team table. Rather than losing an argument with the physiatrist or going around them, the OT pulls Mr. Tremblay's chair right up to the table — literally or by formally relaying his documented priorities — then lays the assessment data on the table to show the team that cooking and walking are not competing goals but complementary ones. That is collaborative influence: using evidence and the client's voice together, at the right time and place, rather than capitulating or freelancing.
questions.topic: Interprofessional Collaboration and Shared Decision-Making

options.label: A
options.text: Invite Mr. Tremblay to attend or formally contribute to the team meeting, present the OT assessment findings including his stated occupational priorities as evidence, and facilitate a structured shared decision-making discussion to integrate occupational participation goals alongside the safety goals.

options.label: B
options.text: Defer to the physiatrist's goal-setting authority as the most responsible provider, align OT interventions with the ambulation target, and address IADL goals informally with the client outside team planning.
options.incorrect_rationale: Deferring without advocacy abandons the OT's professional accountability under the CAOT Code of Ethics (client autonomy, beneficence) and the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada, and silently excludes occupational participation from the formal care plan.

options.label: C
options.text: Escalate the disagreement to the rehabilitation program director before the next team meeting so that the OT's perspective is formally represented and the client's occupational needs receive appropriate priority.
options.incorrect_rationale: Escalating to the program director is premature; the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada require OTs to first attempt direct collaborative resolution within the team before engaging administrative channels, which should be reserved for unresolved conflicts or safety risks.

options.label: D
options.text: Document the interprofessional disagreement and Mr. Tremblay's expressed priorities in the health record, then proceed with IADL-focused interventions independently within OT scope while awaiting team consensus.
options.incorrect_rationale: Proceeding with parallel, uncoordinated goals fragments the care plan, undermines interprofessional collaboration, and does not resolve the conflict or ensure Mr. Tremblay's priorities are incorporated into a unified, team-endorsed rehabilitation plan.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist working at a community-based supported employment program completes a standardized cognitive-functional assessment with a client who has an acquired brain injury. The non-OT program manager asks for a verbal summary of the findings to inform a pending decision about the client's suitability for a modified-duties work placement. The client has provided written consent for their information to be shared with program staff for service-planning purposes. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate action for the occupational therapist?
questions.correct_rationale: The Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada (2021) require OTs to tailor communication of assessment findings to the knowledge base and decision-making needs of the audience. A non-OT program manager cannot meaningfully act on raw test scores or clinical terminology. By framing findings in functional, occupation-focused language — for example, describing whether the client can reliably follow multi-step instructions, manage task-switching, or self-monitor errors during modified-duties work — the OT bridges the gap between clinical assessment and practical workforce decision-making. This approach also aligns with the Canadian Model of Occupational Performance and Engagement (CMOP-E), which situates performance within meaningful occupational contexts, and honours client-centred practice by ensuring the shared information directly serves the client's service-planning goals. Because written consent is in place, sharing is ethically and legally appropriate under applicable provincial privacy legislation (e.g., PHIPA in Ontario).
questions.core_concept: The Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada require OTs to communicate assessment findings in audience-appropriate, occupation-focused language so that non-OT stakeholders can make informed, evidence-based decisions — while the OT retains professional accountability for interpreting and contextualizing those findings.
questions.explain_differently: Think of the OT as a skilled translator at an intersectoral meeting: the assessment is written in clinical shorthand, but the manager's decision-making language is "Can this person do the job safely and reliably?" The OT's role is not simply to hand over the raw manuscript but to render it into the currency the decision-maker actually uses — practical functional capabilities tied directly to the modified-duties tasks at hand.
questions.topic: Communication and Collaboration — Communicating OT Assessment Findings to a Non-OT Manager

options.label: A
options.text: Provide the manager with the standardized test scores and numerical cutoff data so the manager can independently determine the client's eligibility for the placement.
options.incorrect_rationale: Raw psychometric scores carry no practical meaning for a non-OT manager and risk misinterpretation; the OT retains professional accountability to present findings in a contextually meaningful format.

options.label: B
options.text: Translate the assessment findings into functional, occupation-focused language that describes the client's specific cognitive strengths and limitations in relation to the demands of the modified-duties tasks.

options.label: C
options.text: Decline to share any findings verbally and direct the manager to wait for the formal written report before proceeding with the placement decision.
options.incorrect_rationale: Refusing all verbal communication when valid consent is in place and a time-sensitive decision is needed is unnecessarily restrictive and undermines the interprofessional collaboration expected under the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada.

options.label: D
options.text: Advise the manager that all clinical assessment findings are medical information and should be obtained directly from the client's neurologist or family physician.
options.incorrect_rationale: Deferring to the physician inappropriately transfers the OT's professional accountability; communicating the outcomes of a cognitive-functional assessment falls squarely within occupational therapy scope of practice.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist (OT) employed by a private rehabilitation company completes a functional capacity evaluation (FCE) for a worker with a musculoskeletal injury, funded through the Workplace Safety and Insurance Board (WSIB). The OT's findings clearly document that the client cannot safely return to full pre-injury duties and requires modified work with specific load and postural restrictions. Before submission, the non-OT rehabilitation program manager reviews the report and instructs the OT to "reframe the conclusions to emphasize what the worker can do" and to remove explicit language about ongoing restrictions, explaining that a more positive tone will help maintain the employer's future contract with the company. What is the MOST appropriate response by the OT?
questions.correct_rationale: An FCE report submitted to WSIB is a professional clinical document for which the OT bears sole regulatory accountability to their provincial college (e.g., COTO, ACOTRO member colleges). Under the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada (2021), the Communicator and Professional roles require the OT to convey accurate, evidence-based findings to all stakeholders, including those without clinical training. The CAOT Code of Ethics obligates integrity and honesty in all professional communications. Altering documented clinical findings to serve organizational business interests constitutes a misrepresentation that could harm the worker (e.g., precipitating re-injury through premature unrestricted return) and violates the OT's duty to the client and to WSIB as a funder. The OT's most important action is to transparently explain these non-negotiable professional obligations to the manager using plain language appropriate to the manager's role, firmly decline to misrepresent findings, and document the exchange in writing to create an accountable record — demonstrating both professional communication and self-protection within the regulatory framework.
questions.core_concept: OTs retain autonomous professional and regulatory accountability for the accuracy of their clinical documentation, including third-party reports to funders such as WSIB; this accountability originates with the provincial regulatory college and the CAOT Code of Ethics (integrity, client welfare) and cannot be delegated to or overridden by a non-OT manager's organizational authority. Effective communication with a non-OT manager includes explaining these obligations in accessible terms while firmly maintaining professional boundaries.
questions.explain_differently: Think of the OT's FCE report like a signed professional declaration — comparable to an accountant's audit opinion. Just as an auditor cannot adjust financial conclusions because a company's sales manager wants a better-looking report, an OT cannot remove clinical restrictions because a program manager wants to preserve a business contract. The OT's signature on the document signals accountability to the regulatory college first, and the manager's authority simply does not extend into that professional space. The OT's job in this moment is to translate that boundary into language the manager can understand: "My college holds me accountable for every word in this report — if I document something inaccurate, I face professional consequences, and more importantly, this worker could be hurt."
questions.topic: Professional accountability and ethical communication of assessment findings to non-OT managers

options.label: A
options.text: Revise the report as directed, since the manager holds organizational authority over program deliverables and client contract outcomes fall within the manager's scope of responsibility.
options.incorrect_rationale: Organizational authority is bounded by the OT's regulatory obligations; complying with a directive to misrepresent clinical findings would constitute professional misconduct reportable to the OT's regulatory college, regardless of employment hierarchy.

options.label: B
options.text: Submit the original unaltered report directly to WSIB without notifying the manager, in order to protect the client from the potential harm of a modified report.
options.incorrect_rationale: Bypassing the manager without first attempting transparent communication about professional obligations is premature and may breach workplace protocols; clear explanation of accountability to the manager is the required first step before escalation.

options.label: C
options.text: Decline to alter the findings, explain clearly to the manager the professional and regulatory accountability attached to the FCE as a clinical document, and create a written record of the manager's request and the OT's response.

options.label: D
options.text: Contact the employer directly to discuss the findings before deciding whether adjustments to the report's conclusions are clinically warranted given the employer's return-to-work goals.
options.incorrect_rationale: Soliciting employer input on whether to modify objective clinical conclusions introduces an unacceptable conflict of interest, further compromising the OT's impartiality and the validity of the FCE as an independent assessment.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist (OT) in a long-term care home is completing an initial assessment with Mrs. L., a 72-year-old woman with moderate left hemiplegia following a stroke three weeks ago. Her decision-making capacity is intact. When the OT invites her to share her goals for therapy, Mrs. L. crosses her arms and says, "I don't really have any goals. You're the professional — you decide what I need to work on." What is the BEST initial response by the OT?
questions.correct_rationale: The Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada and the Canadian Practice Process Framework (CPPF) position client-centred practice as a foundational mandate: the client — not the clinician or the team — is the primary author of occupational goals. When a client with intact capacity defers to the OT, this typically reflects unfamiliarity with the collaborative process, anxiety, or a sense of powerlessness rather than a genuine wish to opt out. The OT's professional obligation is to facilitate meaningful participation by first naming and normalizing the hesitation, then drawing out the client's values, roles, and occupational identity through open-ended, occupation-focused questions (e.g., "What did a typical Tuesday look like before your stroke?" or "What are you most hoping to be able to do again?"). This approach honours client autonomy and aligns with the CAOT Code of Ethics principle of respect for persons.
questions.core_concept: Client-centred practice, as framed by the CMOP-E and CPPF, requires OTs to actively facilitate a capacitated client's participation in occupational goal-setting rather than defaulting to clinician- or team-directed goals. Deferral by the client signals a need for skilled facilitation — not permission to bypass the client's voice.
questions.explain_differently: Think of the OT's role here like a skilled travel agent working with someone who has never taken a holiday and feels overwhelmed: the agent does not simply book what they think is best, nor hand over a catalogue and walk away. Instead, they ask warm, curious questions — "What kind of weather do you enjoy? Do you like busy cities or quiet beaches? What would make this trip feel worth it?" — until the traveller's real wishes surface and the two can plan together. The OT's open-ended, occupation-focused questions do exactly this: they transform "you decide" into a genuine conversation about what matters most to Mrs. L.
questions.topic: Client-centred goal negotiation with a hesitant client

options.label: A
options.text: Accept Mrs. L.'s preference, proceed to set goals based on the clinical assessment and the interprofessional team's rehabilitation plan, and share them with her for signature.
options.incorrect_rationale: Accepting initial reluctance at face value and reverting to OT-directed goal-setting without attempting to engage a capacitated client violates the client-centred mandate in the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada and reduces Mrs. L. to a passive recipient of care.

options.label: B
options.text: Provide Mrs. L. with a printed checklist of common post-stroke occupational goals and ask her to circle those she would like to work toward.
options.incorrect_rationale: A pre-set checklist constrains Mrs. L.'s responses to OT-defined categories and risks missing her most meaningful occupational priorities, reducing genuine client-centred collaboration to a superficial consumer-choice exercise.

options.label: C
options.text: Arrange a family meeting to gather information about Mrs. L.'s pre-stroke routines and priorities so that meaningful goals can be established on her behalf.
options.incorrect_rationale: Turning to family before fully attempting to engage a capacitated client as the primary source of her own goals bypasses client autonomy and is only appropriate as a supplementary strategy or when capacity is impaired.

options.label: D
options.text: Validate Mrs. L.'s hesitation, then use open-ended questions about her typical day, meaningful roles, and what she is hoping to return to, in order to collaboratively identify occupational priorities.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist (OT) is working with a 58-year-old man admitted to an inpatient rehabilitation unit following a left hemisphere stroke. He has been formally assessed as having decision-making capacity. When the OT initiates goal-setting, he says, "I used to coach my son's hockey team every weekend — I can barely hold a pen now. There is no point in setting goals." His wife, who is present, interjects and tells the OT she wants him "back to 100 percent" and proposes goals focused on returning to his previous job as a licensed electrician. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate initial response by the OT?
questions.correct_rationale: Under the Canadian Practice Process Framework (CPPF), the OT's role following initial assessment is to collaboratively explore the client's occupational performance concerns and priorities before negotiating goals. This client has capacity, so his perspective is legally and ethically primary — his wife's goals cannot substitute for his. Critically, expressing "no point" signals grief over occupational loss (coaching, skilled trade identity), not an informed refusal of intervention. The CAOT Code of Ethics and the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada both require the OT to engage the client as an active partner: by first validating the emotional experience of loss and then exploring what roles and activities carry meaning, the OT creates the conditions under which the client can authentically participate in negotiating achievable, occupation-focused goals. Skipping this step to deliver information (Option D), defer to the family (Option C), or disengage prematurely (Option B) each undermine client autonomy and the therapeutic alliance that makes goal negotiation possible.
questions.core_concept: The Canadian Practice Process Framework (CPPF) requires the OT to explore and validate a client's subjective occupational experience before negotiating goals; when a client with decision-making capacity expresses hesitancy rather than refusal, the OT's professional obligation — grounded in the CAOT Code of Ethics and the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada — is to facilitate meaningful participation in goal-setting through collaborative inquiry into occupational values, not to defer to substitute decision-makers or disengage.
questions.explain_differently: Think of hesitancy as a door that appears stuck rather than locked. The client is not refusing to enter the room — he is standing at the threshold, grieving that it looks different than he expected. A skilled OT does not force the door open (impose goals), leave and return later (defer reassessment), hand the key to someone else (accept the wife's goals), or slide information under the door (educate first). Instead, the OT stands at the threshold with the client, acknowledges what he sees, and asks what he valued about what was inside — because that conversation is what eventually allows both of them to step through together and decide, collaboratively, what the room should look like from here.
questions.topic: Client-centred goal negotiation with a hesitant client

options.label: A
options.text: Acknowledge the client's experience of loss, then collaboratively explore what aspects of coaching, his trade work, or other daily activities hold meaning for him as a foundation for negotiating realistic goals.
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct answer.

options.label: B
options.text: Document the client's statement as a refusal of goal-setting and schedule a reassessment in two weeks to allow him time to reconsider.
options.incorrect_rationale: The client's expression of hopelessness is not an informed refusal of services; treating it as such prematurely abandons the therapeutic relationship and misrepresents the clinical encounter in the health record.

options.label: C
options.text: Accept the wife's proposed goals around return to electrical work as the primary rehabilitation focus, since the client has not offered alternatives and the goals reflect a meaningful occupational role.
options.incorrect_rationale: Even when a family member's goals appear clinically reasonable, substituting a spouse's priorities for those of a client who has decision-making capacity directly violates the principle of client-centred practice under the CAOT Code of Ethics and the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada.

options.label: D
options.text: Provide the client with standardized information about realistic post-stroke recovery trajectories to correct his pessimistic expectations before attempting goal-setting.
options.incorrect_rationale: Offering factual information before validating the client's emotional experience of occupational loss risks being perceived as dismissive and paternalistic, and is likely to further disengage a hesitant client rather than open space for collaborative negotiation.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist in Ontario is conducting a scheduled video visit with a 72-year-old client who is recovering from a left-hemisphere stroke and lives alone in a two-storey home. The client has mild word-finding difficulties but is cognitively intact and is the sole decision-maker for her care. Over the course of the 45-minute session, the OT has reviewed grab bar placement in the bathroom, a tub-transfer technique, and three kitchen safety strategies. The connection has been stable throughout. The OT is preparing to close the session. Which action BEST reflects virtual-care best practice for confirming the client's comprehension of the home safety plan?
questions.correct_rationale: The teach-back method — asking the client to restate key information in her own words — is the evidence-informed gold standard for confirming health literacy and comprehension in any care setting, including virtual care. In a video visit, the OT cannot rely on nonverbal cues readily available in person (e.g., observing a client attempt a transfer), making an active, spoken demonstration of understanding even more critical. Asking the client to identify two or three priority actions is appropriately scoped, respects her autonomy as the sole decision-maker, occurs in real time before the session closes, and aligns with the Communicator and Collaborator competency roles in the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada (2021). It also accommodates mild word-finding difficulties by inviting open narrative rather than precise recall.
questions.core_concept: The Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada (2021) require OTs to use communication strategies that actively confirm client understanding, not merely offer the opportunity to ask questions. In virtual care, where sensory and environmental cues are reduced, real-time teach-back is the preferred method for verifying comprehension and ensuring informed, safe follow-through on therapeutic recommendations.
questions.explain_differently: Think of teach-back like a flight attendant asking you to point to the nearest exit rather than asking "Did you watch the safety video?" One checks whether the message actually landed; the other only checks whether you heard it. In a video visit, where the OT cannot watch the client practice the tub transfer before leaving the screen, asking her to narrate the plan back is the closest equivalent to hands-on confirmation — it surfaces misunderstandings while the OT is still present and can address them on the spot.
questions.topic: Virtual-care etiquette and remote comprehension verification

options.label: A
options.text: Ask the client, "Do you have any questions about everything we went over today?" and wait for her response before ending the call.
options.incorrect_rationale: A closed yes/no question does not actively elicit demonstration of understanding and is unreliable for clients who may not recognize gaps in their own comprehension.

options.label: B
options.text: Use a teach-back approach by asking the client to describe, in her own words, the two or three most important changes she plans to make at home before the next visit.
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct answer.

options.label: C
options.text: Email a written summary of all recommendations immediately after the session and instruct the client to call the clinic if anything is unclear.
options.incorrect_rationale: A post-session written summary does not verify comprehension in real time and places the burden on the client to self-identify confusion, which is especially problematic for clients with communication impairments.

options.label: D
options.text: Contact the client's daughter after the session to confirm the client understood the home safety plan and can follow through on the recommendations.
options.incorrect_rationale: Disclosing care information to a family member without the client's explicit consent violates confidentiality obligations under PHIPA and undermines the client's autonomous decision-making role, as the daughter has not been identified as a substitute decision-maker.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist employed by a home and community care organization in Manitoba is conducting a scheduled video-based session with a 71-year-old client recovering from hip replacement surgery. The purpose of the session is to review home safety recommendations and adaptive equipment use, including a raised toilet seat and grab bars. Midway through the session, the OT notices an unidentified person briefly visible in the background; the client has not acknowledged their presence or introduced them. Throughout the OT's explanations, the client responds with brief affirmations such as "sure" and "okay." The OT is approaching the end of the allocated session time. Which action BEST addresses both virtual-care etiquette and effective comprehension verification at this point?
questions.correct_rationale: Option A correctly sequences two distinct professional obligations. First, virtual-care etiquette requires the OT to address the unidentified third party before continuing to discuss confidential health information — an obligation grounded in PHIPA (and Manitoba's equivalent, PHIA) and the CAOT Code of Ethics principle of confidentiality. Continuing to share clinical information without knowing who else is present constitutes a potential privacy breach. Second, once the environment is confirmed private, the teach-back method — asking the client to explain the transfer technique in their own words — is the evidence-informed gold standard for comprehension verification and is especially critical in virtual care where non-verbal cues are reduced and brief affirmations ("sure," "okay") are unreliable proxies for understanding. Sequencing the etiquette concern before the comprehension check is important because disclosing additional clinical detail before privacy is confirmed would compound any existing breach.
questions.core_concept: Under PHIPA and provincial equivalents (e.g., Manitoba's PHIA), and consistent with the CAOT Code of Ethics principle of confidentiality, OTs providing virtual care must verify that the session environment is private before disclosing or continuing to discuss personal health information. Genuine comprehension verification in virtual care requires the teach-back method — asking the client to articulate or demonstrate understanding in their own words — rather than closed-ended questions that can be answered affirmatively without true understanding.
questions.explain_differently: Think of it like confirming the door is closed before a sensitive hallway conversation, then checking the other person really heard you by asking them to replay it back. In virtual care, you first make sure the "room" is private (identify who else is on the call), and only then do you test whether the message landed — not by asking "got it?" but by asking the client to teach it back to you. A client who truly understands a safe toilet transfer can describe it; one who is just being polite cannot.
questions.topic: Virtual-care etiquette and comprehension verification in home and community OT practice

options.label: A
options.text: Proceed with the closing summary and send a written follow-up email that recaps all recommendations, noting in the clinical record that comprehension could not be fully confirmed during the session.
options.incorrect_rationale: Deferring comprehension verification to a written follow-up fails to address both the immediate privacy concern of the unidentified third party and the real-time safety obligation to confirm the client can perform the transfers correctly before discharge from the session.

options.label: B
options.text: Immediately end the video session to protect the client's privacy, then telephone the client afterward to re-explain all home safety recommendations without the video connection.
options.incorrect_rationale: Abruptly ending the session is a disproportionate response to an unconfirmed privacy concern; the appropriate action is to clarify who is present rather than terminate, and a subsequent telephone call cannot substitute for verified comprehension of physical transfer techniques.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask the client to confirm who else is in the room and, once the session environment is verified as private, use the teach-back method by asking the client to explain in their own words how they will safely transfer on and off the raised toilet seat before concluding the session.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask the client a series of closed-ended yes/no questions about each recommendation to efficiently confirm understanding before the scheduled session time expires.
options.incorrect_rationale: Closed-ended yes/no questions are not a valid comprehension-verification strategy because they allow the client to respond affirmatively without demonstrating actual understanding, and they do not address the unresolved virtual-care etiquette concern of the unidentified person in the background.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist employed at a community mental health program in Ontario joins a private Facebook group for provincial OTs seeking peer support. Wanting advice on a complex case, she posts a detailed description of a client including the client's approximate age, primary diagnosis, neighbourhood, and type of employment. She does not include the client's name or photograph. Within an hour, a colleague from a different organization comments: "This sounds like someone from my community — I think I know exactly who this is." The OT's MOST appropriate next step is to:
questions.correct_rationale: Under Ontario's Personal Health Information Protection Act (PHIPA) and the CAOT Code of Ethics, the OT's duty is twofold: first, limit ongoing harm by removing the post, and second, follow the organization's breach management protocol by notifying the privacy officer. Omitting a client's name does not protect confidentiality when a combination of quasi-identifiers — age, diagnosis, neighbourhood, occupation — is sufficient for someone familiar with the community to identify the individual (the "mosaic effect"). A colleague's public comment that she recognizes the client is strong evidence a re-identification risk has materialized. PHIPA imposes notification obligations on health information custodians when a breach of personal health information occurs; the privacy officer is positioned to conduct the required breach risk assessment and determine whether the client and/or the Information and Privacy Commissioner of Ontario must be notified. Deleting the post without that consultation would be incomplete; consulting without deleting first would allow further exposure. Option A is the only choice that addresses both the immediate harm-limitation and the regulatory accountability obligation.
questions.core_concept: Client confidentiality under PHIPA and the CAOT Code of Ethics extends to any combination of details that could enable re-identification, even without a name; when an OT suspects a privacy breach has occurred on social media, professional and regulatory accountability requires both immediate harm-limitation and reporting through the organization's privacy breach protocol.
questions.explain_differently: Imagine describing a neighbour without ever saying her name — if you mention her age, her rare medical condition, her street, and her unusual job, everyone in the room still knows exactly who you mean. Omitting the name did not protect her privacy. The moment the OT realizes someone in that Facebook group has connected the dots, the ethical and legal response is to pull the post right away (stop the leak) and then call the privacy officer (assess the damage and follow the rules about reporting it) — not patch it, not dig deeper, not ask the client's permission after the fact.
questions.topic: Social media, client confidentiality, and privacy breach management under PHIPA

options.label: A
options.text: Edit the post to remove the neighbourhood and employment details, then continue seeking peer input within the group.
options.incorrect_rationale: Editing the post does not undo the exposure already seen by group members; the potentially identifiable information has already been disclosed and a breach may have occurred, so remediation rather than continuation is required.

options.label: B
options.text: Send a private message to the commenting colleague to confirm whether the client is who she suspects, so the colleague can provide more targeted advice.
options.incorrect_rationale: Confirming the client's identity to a third party without consent would constitute a further unauthorized disclosure, compounding rather than remedying the privacy breach.

options.label: C
options.text: Obtain the client's retroactive consent to the disclosure and document this in the health record to remedy the situation.
options.incorrect_rationale: Retroactive consent cannot undo a disclosure that has already occurred; PHIPA does not permit after-the-fact consent to remedy an unauthorized release of personal health information, and this approach bypasses the organization's mandatory breach response process.

options.label: D
options.text: Delete the post immediately and consult her organization's privacy officer to determine whether a reportable breach has occurred under PHIPA.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist (OT) employed at a community mental health centre in Ontario photographs the sensory room she designed for a group session. She posts the image on her personal Instagram account with the caption "So proud of the space I created for my clients today!" and the hashtags #MentalHealth and #CommunityOT. The photo inadvertently shows a whiteboard in the background listing a client's first name and the date of the client's next appointment. The OT is not concerned because no faces are visible and she considers a first name alone insufficient to identify anyone. Which of the following actions BEST reflects the OT's professional and legal obligations at this point?
questions.correct_rationale: Under PHIPA, personal health information (PHI) is defined broadly to include any information that can reasonably identify an individual in the context of receiving health services. A client's first name combined with an appointment date, the mental health centre context implied by the hashtags, and the geographic and institutional setting constitutes information that could reasonably identify that individual — it is not limited to names paired with diagnoses. The moment the post was published, a privacy breach occurred regardless of the OT's intent. PHIPA imposes obligations on health information custodians (and their agents) to manage breaches, which includes: (1) containing the breach by removing the disclosure, (2) documenting what occurred, (3) assessing the risk of harm, and (4) notifying affected individuals where warranted. COTO's standards on professional boundaries and social media, and the CAOT Code of Ethics principle of confidentiality, further reinforce that OTs must take active steps — not merely delete the post — when client information is disclosed without authorization. Both the removal and the breach reporting obligation arise simultaneously and are non-optional.
questions.core_concept: Under PHIPA (Ontario) and equivalent provincial health privacy legislation across Canada, PHI encompasses any combination of information that can reasonably identify an individual receiving health services — context matters as much as the specific data elements. When an OT inadvertently discloses PHI through a digital or social media channel, both immediate containment (removing the content) and formal organizational breach management (documentation, risk assessment, and potential client notification) are mandatory obligations that arise at the same time.
questions.explain_differently: Imagine you accidentally dropped a client's paper chart out of your bag on a busy public street. Picking it up quickly (removing the post) is the right first move — but that alone does not end your responsibility. You must still tell your manager, write up what happened, figure out who may have seen it, and consider whether the client needs to be told. Deleting an Instagram post works exactly the same way: the breach already happened the moment it was live, so the delete button is only step one of a formal process, not a complete fix.
questions.topic: Social media and professionalism — client confidentiality online

options.label: A
options.text: Remove the post immediately, document the incident, and report it through the organization's privacy breach protocol as required under Ontario's Personal Health Information Protection Act (PHIPA).

options.label: B
options.text: Retroactively edit the image to crop out the whiteboard and add a caption disclaimer stating that no client information was intentionally shared.
options.incorrect_rationale: Editing the post after publication does not undo the breach — the original image was already publicly accessible — and does not fulfil the mandatory breach reporting and documentation obligations under PHIPA.

options.label: C
options.text: Leave the post as published, because a first name alone is insufficient to identify an individual and no clinical diagnosis or treatment details were disclosed.
options.incorrect_rationale: PHIPA's definition of PHI is contextual, not limited to full names or diagnoses; a first name paired with an appointment date in a clearly identified mental health context can reasonably identify a client and therefore constitutes PHI.

options.label: D
options.text: Contact the client whose name appears on the whiteboard to obtain retroactive consent before taking any further action regarding the post.
options.incorrect_rationale: Retroactive consent does not nullify a privacy breach that has already occurred, and breach management obligations under PHIPA — including containment and reporting — arise independently of and prior to any consent discussion.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist holds registration with the College of Occupational Therapists of Ontario (COTO) and has been working entirely from her Toronto home office. She has been providing virtual home modification assessments and energy conservation counselling to a 68-year-old retired man for the past four months. The client has now permanently relocated to British Columbia and asks the OT to continue the same virtual services from his new home in Kelowna. The OT values the established therapeutic relationship and is confident she can deliver safe, effective care. What is the OT's most appropriate first action?
questions.correct_rationale: In Canada, occupational therapy is regulated at the provincial and territorial level, and jurisdiction is determined by where the client receives the service — not where the OT is physically located or initially registered. When the client relocated permanently to BC, the site of service delivery shifted to British Columbia, placing the practice squarely under COTBC's jurisdiction. The OT's COTO registration confers no legal authority to practice OT in BC. Before resuming any clinical activity — including virtual assessment or counselling — the OT must determine COTBC's registration pathway for interprovincial practitioners and obtain the required registration. Proceeding without BC registration would constitute unauthorized practice, regardless of the established relationship or the virtual nature of care.
questions.core_concept: In Canada, provincial regulatory colleges govern OT practice within their respective borders, and virtual care does not dissolve those boundaries. When a client receives occupational therapy services in a province other than the one in which the OT holds registration, the OT must be registered with the regulatory college of the province where the client is located before any services are provided.
questions.explain_differently: Think of provincial OT registration like a driver's licence valid only in the province that issued it: if the road you are driving on moves into a different province permanently, an Ontario licence no longer covers you there. The virtual camera does not erase the provincial border — it simply shifts where the "driving" is happening. The OT must get a BC licence before she can drive on BC roads, even from her Toronto living room.
questions.topic: Virtual care across provincial boundaries and regulatory college registration requirements

options.label: A
options.text: Continue virtual services without interruption, because the therapeutic relationship and care plan were established while the client lived in Ontario, and COTO registration authorizes ongoing virtual care with existing clients regardless of where they subsequently relocate.
options.incorrect_rationale: Provincial registration authorizes practice within that province's jurisdiction; a pre-existing therapeutic relationship does not extend a regulatory college's authority into another province.

options.label: B
options.text: Pause services, contact the College of Occupational Therapists of British Columbia (COTBC) to determine registration requirements for interprovincial virtual practice, and obtain BC registration before resuming any services with the client.
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct answer.

options.label: C
options.text: Provide one further virtual session solely to ensure a safe transition and referral to a BC-based OT, relying on a continuity-of-care exception that permits brief cross-provincial contact under existing COTO registration.
options.incorrect_rationale: No broadly recognized continuity-of-care exception in Canadian provincial regulatory frameworks permits an OT to practice in another province — even briefly — without holding registration in that province.

options.label: D
options.text: Document the cross-provincial arrangement thoroughly in the client record and send written notification to COTO before continuing services, as transparency with the home regulatory college fulfils the OT's professional obligations.
options.incorrect_rationale: Notifying COTO and documenting the arrangement addresses the OT's accountability to her home college but does not authorize practice in British Columbia, which requires independent registration with COTBC.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist (OT) holds active registration with the College of Occupational Therapists of Ontario (COTO) and has provided community mental health OT services via a secure video platform to a client for 14 months. The client has now permanently relocated to Winnipeg, Manitoba. The OT is not registered with the College of Occupational Therapists of Manitoba (COTM). The client wishes to continue the same virtual sessions. Which action BEST reflects the OT's professional and regulatory obligations?
questions.correct_rationale: Option C is best because it correctly addresses every layer of the competing obligations. First, regulatory: provincial regulatory colleges govern the practice of OT within their borders based on where the client is located. A client residing in Manitoba is receiving a service in Manitoba; therefore the OT must hold COTM registration to practise lawfully, irrespective of where the OT sits. COTO jurisdiction ends at Ontario's border. Second, ethical: the CAOT Code of Ethics (beneficence, non-maleficence, justice) requires the OT to avoid both unauthorized practice AND client abandonment. Simply ceasing contact without a plan could cause serious harm to a client with a mental health condition and a disrupted therapeutic relationship. Third, professional accountability: the OT must be transparent with the client about the situation, which respects the client's autonomy and enables informed decision-making about interim options (e.g., referral to a Manitoba OT, or a brief safety-monitoring pause while registration is processed). Applying for COTM registration immediately, communicating openly, and co-creating a continuity or transition plan balances all these obligations proportionately.
questions.core_concept: When an OT provides virtual care to a client, the province where the client is physically located determines regulatory jurisdiction — not the province where the OT's office is situated. The OT must therefore hold registration with the regulatory college of the province in which the client resides, and must balance this legal requirement against the ethical duty to avoid client abandonment through careful transition planning.
questions.explain_differently: Think of it like a driver's licence: an Ontario licence lets you drive in Ontario, but the moment you permanently move to Manitoba you need a Manitoba licence — it does not matter that the car was bought in Ontario. The same logic applies here: the "road" is Manitoba (where the client is), so the OT needs a Manitoba "licence" (COTM registration). But unlike a driver who can simply pull over, the OT also has a client whose mental health could be destabilized by a sudden cut-off, so the ethical move is to keep the client informed, apply for the Manitoba licence right away, and make a safe plan for the gap — not just slam on the brakes.
questions.topic: Virtual care across provincial boundaries and regulatory implications

options.label: A
options.text: Continue virtual services without change, because the OT practices from an Ontario office and COTO registration governs services delivered from that location.
options.incorrect_rationale: Provincial regulatory jurisdiction is determined by where the client receives the service, not where the OT is physically located, so COTO registration does not authorize practice with a client residing in Manitoba.

options.label: B
options.text: Immediately cease all clinical contact with the client until COTM registration is confirmed, to avoid any risk of unauthorized practice.
options.incorrect_rationale: Abrupt termination without a transition plan constitutes abandonment, which violates CAOT Code of Ethics obligations of beneficence and non-maleficence, and causes foreseeable harm to a vulnerable client.

options.label: C
options.text: Apply for registration with COTM, transparently inform the client of the regulatory requirement and the realistic timeline, and collaboratively develop a safe-continuity or transition-of-care plan in the interim.

options.label: D
options.text: Obtain the client's written informed consent explicitly acknowledging the cross-provincial, unregistered nature of the arrangement, and then continue sessions pending COTM registration.
options.incorrect_rationale: Client consent, however informed, cannot override a statutory registration requirement; the OT would remain in unauthorized practice regardless of the client's agreement.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist (OT) at a rehabilitation centre in Ontario is providing constraint-induced movement therapy (CIMT) to a client recovering from stroke. The programme coordinator informs the OT that the centre's Research Ethics Board (REB) has approved a study measuring CIMT outcomes, and asks the OT to begin entering this client's session data into the research database. The client signed a standard consent form for occupational therapy services on admission. The OT has not yet discussed the study with the client. What is the OT's most appropriate next step?
questions.correct_rationale: Under the Tri-Council Policy Statement: Ethical Conduct for Research Involving Humans (TCPS2), any individual asked to contribute data to a research study must provide free, informed, and ongoing consent specifically for that research, separate from any consent given for clinical care. The CAOT Code of Ethics (2021) reinforces client autonomy and the duty to avoid therapeutic misconception — the risk that clients assume research participation is simply part of their treatment. Clients must be explicitly told that refusing or withdrawing from the study will not compromise their clinical care. This information must be communicated before any research data are collected, and the consent process must allow for genuine voluntary choice, which is particularly important given the inherent power differential between a treating therapist and a vulnerable rehabilitation client. REB approval is a necessary condition for the study but does not replace individual participant consent.
questions.core_concept: When an OT simultaneously provides clinical services and collects data for a research study, these two activities require separate informed consent processes. Consent to treatment never implies consent to research participation; clients must be told their care will not change if they decline, and research consent must be documented before any study data are gathered — this is grounded in TCPS2 and the CAOT Code of Ethics principle of autonomy.
questions.explain_differently: Think of it like two separate contracts. Signing one contract (agreeing to receive CIMT therapy) does not automatically sign you onto a second contract (being a research subject). Before the OT can use any of this client's information for the study, the client needs to read, understand, and sign that second contract — with a clear promise that tearing it up will not change a single session of their therapy.
questions.topic: Research ethics and consent when combining clinical practice with a study

options.label: A
options.text: Enter the client's data into the research database, since REB approval confirms the study meets ethical standards and the client already consented to the OT services being provided.
options.incorrect_rationale: REB approval authorises the study to proceed but does not substitute for individual informed consent from each participant; consent to treatment is legally and ethically distinct from consent to research.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask the programme coordinator to obtain the client's research consent, since the coordinator is the study's primary investigator and the OT should avoid a dual role.
options.incorrect_rationale: Delegating the consent conversation does not resolve the fundamental requirement; moreover, the OT remains accountable for ensuring clients on her caseload are not enrolled without proper consent regardless of study role.

options.label: C
options.text: Document the client's CIMT progress in the clinical chart as usual and flag the file so research data collection can begin automatically once the client is discharged and no longer receiving services.
options.incorrect_rationale: Collecting identifiable client data for research purposes — whether during or after the therapeutic relationship — still requires prospective informed research consent; waiting until discharge does not eliminate this obligation.

options.label: D
options.text: Meet with the client to provide full information about the study, explain that participation is voluntary and will not affect the quality of clinical care, and obtain a separate signed research consent before entering any data.
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct answer.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist working in an outpatient hand therapy clinic has received Research Ethics Board (REB) approval to study functional outcomes of a new tendon rehabilitation protocol. The OT intends to recruit current clients who are already receiving treatment using this same protocol. As the OT prepares to obtain informed consent for research participation, which action is MOST essential to protect each client's autonomy?
questions.correct_rationale: When the same OT occupies both the treating clinician role and the researcher role simultaneously, a structural power imbalance and therapeutic misconception risk arise: clients may reasonably fear that declining research participation will jeopardize their clinical care. The Tri-Council Policy Statement (TCPS2, Article 3.1) requires that research consent be free from coercion or undue influence, and CAOT's Code of Ethics obliges occupational therapists to uphold client autonomy and avoid conflicts of interest. The single most essential action is an explicit, unambiguous statement — documented in the consent process — that declining, withdrawing, or modifying research participation will in no way alter the availability, quality, or continuity of the client's occupational therapy treatment. This verbal and written assurance is the ethical firewall that separates the clinical relationship from the voluntary research relationship and is non-negotiable when a treating clinician is also the researcher.
questions.core_concept: When an occupational therapist simultaneously holds the dual roles of treating clinician and researcher with the same clients, the inherent therapeutic power imbalance creates a coercion risk that compromises voluntariness. Canadian research ethics (TCPS2) and the CAOT Code of Ethics require that clients receive an explicit, documented assurance that declining or withdrawing from research participation will not affect their clinical care — this is the foundational safeguard that preserves autonomous, uncoerced consent.
questions.explain_differently: Picture your landlord — who also happens to be your employer — handing you a "completely voluntary" survey. Even if they insist it is optional, you might feel you cannot safely say no. The OT is in an identical structural position: clients may silently fear that saying "no" risks worse treatment. The ethical solution is not a subtle hint but a direct, explicit statement — spoken and written — that says "Your care is identical whether you join or not." That statement is what breaks the coercive dynamic that the dual role inevitably creates.
questions.topic: Research Ethics and Dual-Role Consent in Occupational Therapy Practice

options.label: A
options.text: Explicitly and clearly inform each client that choosing not to participate in the study — or withdrawing at any time — will have no effect on the quality or continuity of their occupational therapy services.

options.label: B
options.text: Combine the research consent form with the standard treatment consent form to streamline the process and reduce administrative burden on clients.
options.incorrect_rationale: Merging the two forms conflates consent for clinically necessary treatment with consent for voluntary research participation, creating implicit coercion and obscuring the distinction — a foundational violation of research ethics under the TCPS2.

options.label: C
options.text: Obtain written co-consent from a family member or substitute decision-maker in addition to the client to reinforce the voluntariness of participation.
options.incorrect_rationale: An adult client who has capacity must give their own independent informed consent; adding a family co-signatory is not required and could itself undermine autonomy by introducing social pressure, unless the client has been found incapable under applicable provincial legislation (e.g., Ontario's Health Care Consent Act).

options.label: D
options.text: Request that the OT's provincial regulatory college review and co-sign each research consent form before it is administered to clients.
options.incorrect_rationale: Research ethics oversight is the domain of the institutional REB, not the provincial regulatory college; no such co-signing requirement exists in Canadian OT regulatory frameworks, and directing this responsibility to the college misrepresents both bodies' mandates.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist (OT) employed by a community home health organization has been providing cognitive rehabilitation to a 72-year-old client over six months following a stroke. At the final discharge session, the client presents the OT with a hand-sewn quilt, stating, "You gave me my life back — I made this especially for you." The OT is aware that her provincial regulatory college's practice standards address the receipt of client gifts. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate course of action?
questions.correct_rationale: Provincial regulatory colleges (e.g., COTO, ACOTRO members) and the CAOT Code of Ethics do not categorically prohibit gift receipt, but they require OTs to maintain professional boundaries and avoid situations that could compromise objectivity, create obligation, or be perceived as exploitative. The correct action is a structured, reflective process: acknowledge the client's intent respectfully; apply clinical and ethical judgment by weighing the gift's monetary value (low-value handmade item is lower risk than cash or high-value goods), the stage of the therapeutic relationship (post-discharge reduces ongoing influence risk), cultural context, and whether acceptance could reasonably be perceived as a boundary violation; and document the decision with explicit rationale. Documentation is what transforms a personal choice into a transparent, professionally accountable act that can withstand regulatory scrutiny.
questions.core_concept: Under the CAOT Code of Ethics (principles of beneficence, non-maleficence, and justice) and provincial regulatory college practice standards, OTs must maintain appropriate professional boundaries. Gift situations require contextual professional judgment — weighing value, relational dynamics, cultural significance, and potential for real or perceived compromise — not a reflexive blanket accept-or-refuse rule, and all decisions must be documented to fulfill accountability obligations.
questions.explain_differently: Treat the gift decision the same way you would a clinical risk screen: you do not say yes or no on instinct. You gather the relevant data (how much is it worth, is the therapeutic relationship ongoing, does accepting create any sense of obligation or power shift, what does this mean in the client's cultural context?), run it against your regulatory college's guidance, make a reasoned call, and write it down. The written rationale is what converts a personal moment into a regulated professional act — it is the difference between a gift and a documented, defensible clinical decision.
questions.topic: Professional Responsibility — Boundary Management and Gift Receipt

options.label: A
options.text: Accept the quilt graciously without discussion, as raising professional standards in this moment would be culturally insensitive and would damage the established therapeutic relationship.
options.incorrect_rationale: Accepting without reflection or documentation fails to uphold the OT's professional accountability obligations regardless of relational warmth; silence does not constitute an ethical decision.

options.label: B
options.text: Thank the client sincerely, acknowledge the gesture's significance, apply professional judgment by weighing contextual factors such as the item's value, cultural meaning, timing, and potential for boundary compromise, and document the decision and rationale in the clinical record.

options.label: C
options.text: Decline the gift immediately and firmly, explaining that the regulatory college's standards prohibit OTs from accepting any gift of any kind from a client.
options.incorrect_rationale: Most provincial regulatory colleges do not impose an absolute prohibition on all gifts; applying a blanket refusal without contextual judgment misrepresents the standards and may cause unnecessary distress to the client.

options.label: D
options.text: Accept the quilt and then delegate the ethical determination to the supervising manager, allowing them to decide in retrospect whether acceptance was appropriate.
